news.Title: 【盤後焦點】國安基金宣示護盤　台股收漲1960點改寫史上次高漲點
news.Content:
（中央社記者江明晏台北2026年11月9日電）國安基金護盤助威，台股今天開高反彈，台積電盤中漲逾7%，多檔跌深權值股與千金股漲停，盤中指數大漲2647點；終場上漲1960.06點，收在41661.7點，創史上第二大收盤漲點，但42000點關卡與5日均線41838點得而復失。投顧分析，台股是否真正落底反彈，仍須觀察美股走勢。

美國科技股上週五止跌反彈，費城半導體指數上漲4.21%，台積電ADR強彈6.33%；加上國安基金上週五宣布史上第10次護盤，金管會也提出限空令等措施，提振台股信心，台股今天開高震盪走高，盤中指數大漲2647.72點，至42349.36點。

台股加權指數終場收在41661.7點，上漲1960.06點，漲幅4.94%，成交值新台幣8379.29億元。電子指數收漲5.49%，金融指數漲2.35%；代表中小型股的櫃買OTC指數強勢反彈5.9%。

觀察權值股表現，台積電收盤上漲100元，收2235元，漲幅4.68%；聯發科、台達電、國巨、大立光等權值股收漲停，一掃先前陰霾；台塑集團股台塑、南亞、台化均以漲停作收。

指標股方面，PCB族群轉強，金像電、華通漲停，ABF載板族群欣興、景碩、臻鼎-KY、南電勁揚；上游族群台玻、金居、富喬漲停，台光電、聯茂勁揚逾6%。

半導體供應鏈股弘塑、萬潤、均華、聖暉、亞翔、環球晶等收漲停；面板股群創漲停，友達漲逾6%。記憶體族群南亞科漲逾7%，華邦電、旺宏、力積電、鈺創、晶豪科、群聯漲停。

高價股今天強勢反彈，股王信驊漲近3%、股后川湖漲逾5%，大立光、鴻勁、聯發科、世芯-KY、奇鋐、精測、聯亞、富世達、群聯、弘塑、智邦、昇達科、台達電、創新服務、光聖等高價股漲停，台股收盤擁38檔千金股。

萬寶投顧執行長王榮旭向中央社記者表示，台股今天強勢反彈，這波反彈並非只有台股，美股、日韓股市也同步回升，不過台股盤中漲幅超過6%，表現明顯優於日韓，除了受惠台灣供應鏈基本面支撐，國安基金宣布進場護盤，明顯發揮提振市場信心的效果。

王榮旭指出，台股行情是否真正落底，仍須觀察美股走勢，目前費城半導體指數尚未站回5日線，也未突破上方壓力區。考量台股與美股連動性高，加上新台幣近期回貶，外資後續動向將是觀察重點。

針對美國民主黨傾向加強AI監管，可能導致資料中心建置放緩，王榮旭認為，目前市場對此議題的反應，情緒面大於實質面，10月以來的股市回檔，已部分反映民主黨勝選預期；此外，近期油價、公債殖利率走跌，對市場而言都是正面因素。

他認為，AI產業並非停止發展，而是投資步調可能適度踩煞車，未必是壞事，反而有助市場重新檢視投資效益與產業發展節奏。

展望後市，王榮旭表示，除非出現新的重大利空，台股短線再度破底的機率不高，但目前融資餘額去化仍不夠充分，預期11月中下旬第3季財報公布後，市場可能進入短暫空窗期；台股後續上漲機率仍高於下跌，但可能以震盪築底為主，個股表現可望優於大盤。（編輯：張良知）

news.Title: 張建一：新台幣貶過頭　台股大漲匯率跌勢可望告段落
news.Content:
（中央社記者潘姿羽台北2026年11月9日電）近期市場對AI產業發展疑慮加深，一度重創股匯市，不過台股今天上演絕地大反攻。台經院院長張建一認為，以台灣經濟基本面來看，新台幣匯率「真的貶過頭」，主要是受外資鉅額匯出影響，但隨股市大漲，新台幣匯率可望逐步止貶回升。

台經院今天舉行「2027年景氣展望與產業趨勢研討會」，張建一於媒體聯訪時表示，台灣今年經濟成長率突破12%，理論上經濟表現強勁，可支撐匯價行情，今年新台幣反而大貶，主要反映台股市值高漲，外資賣股匯出的資金也相當龐大。

張建一直言，台灣經濟成長令人驚艷，新台幣匯率卻相對弱勢，「其實真的貶過頭」，只是外資短線進出主要著眼於自身投資策略，造成匯市劇烈波動，這段期間央行進場阻貶，也比較辛苦。

不過上週隨著台股重挫，新台幣匯率一度摜破33元整數大關，出口商進場拋匯的量能也明顯放大。張建一表示，近期央行道德勸說穩定匯市，加上新台幣貶至近期低點，出口商或許認為「貶得差不多了」，因此當日匯價逆勢走揚。

張建一認為，新台幣匯率具有基本面支撐，加上今年出口暢旺，出口商握有大量美元部位，今天台股已經強勢反彈，相信新台幣匯率也會逐漸止貶回升。

news.Title: Applied Materials, Cisco, Berkshire Hathaway, Nvidia, Micron and Alphabet are part of Zacks Earnings Preview
news.Content:
For Immediate Release

Chicago, IL – November 9, 2026 – Zacks.com releases the list of companies likely to issue earnings surprises. This week's list includes Applied Materials AMAT, Cisco Systems CSCO, Berkshire Hathaway BRK.B, Nvidia NVDA, Micron MU and Alphabet GOOGL.

Q3 Earnings Update: Broad-Based Growth, Key Sector Outliers, and What's Ahead

The bulk of the Q3 earnings season is now behind us, with results from only about 12% of S&P 500 members still to come at this stage. This week brings results from more than 700 companies, including 12 index members. The notable companies reporting this week include Applied Materials , Cisco Systems and Berkshire Hathaway , to name just three.

The picture that emerged out of this earnings season is one of broad-based growth momentum. While the growth pace remains strong, it does not compare favorably with other recent periods, particularly when some of the outlier results are excluded. Most importantly, the revisions trend remains positive, with estimates for 2026 Q4 and full-year 2027 continuing to rise.

Looking at overall expectations for the quarter, combining the actual results from the 441 S&P 500 members that have reported already (through Friday, November 6th) with estimates for the still-to-come companies, Q3 earnings are currently expected to increase by +28.4% from the same period last year on +14.4% higher revenues, the 8th straight quarter of double-digit earnings growth for the index.

The Tech sector continues to be a major growth contributor, but the momentum is broad-based, with 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors on track to enjoy positive earnings growth and 9 generating double-digit earnings growth in Q3.

As noted earlier, the revisions trend has been positive, sustaining the favorable trend in place for almost a year. Estimates for Q3 increased after the quarter got underway, and we are seeing a similar trend at play for 2026 Q4 estimates. We should note, however, that the latest development on this front is negative, with estimates over the preceding week losing some ground.

Since the start of October, Q4 estimates have declined for 12 of the 16 Zacks sectors, with only four sectors enjoying positive estimate revisions. These four sectors are Energy, Tech, Finance, and Conglomerates. Excluding the Energy sector's substantial contribution, the index's aggregate revisions trend would have been negative.

The notable sectors suffering negative estimate revisions since the start of October include Transportation, Autos, Consumer Staples, Construction, and others.

Story Continues

We should note that while Q4 estimates have moved higher in the aggregate since the quarter got underway, the magnitude and breadth of positive revisions are weaker than in the comparable period for Q3.

Sector Focus: Broad-Based Strength

The 9 sectors expected to enjoy double-digit earnings growth in Q3 are Aerospace (up +157%), Energy (+147.9%), Tech (+45.4%), Basic Materials (+34.4%), Transportation (+10.5%), Industrial Products (+18.4%), Consumer Discretionary (+18.5%), Utilities (+14.7%), and Business Services (+12.5%).

Q3 earnings growth for the S&P 500 index drops to +23% from +28.4% once the Energy sector's contribution is excluded from the index. Excluding the Tech sector, Q3 earnings growth for the rest of the index drops to +19.4%. Excluding both the Tech and Energy sectors, Q3 earnings for the rest of the index would be up +10.2% on +7.2% higher revenues.

For the Mag 7 group, we have actual results from 6 members, with Nvidia as the only member left to report on November 17th. Looking at expectations for the Mag 7 as a whole, combining actual results from the 6 members that have reported with estimates for Nvidia, total Q3 earnings for the Mag 7 are expected to increase by +17.3% on +23.5% higher revenues.

Excluding the Mag 7 group's contribution, Q3 earnings for the rest of the index would actually improve to +32.2% (from +28.4%).

The Q3 earnings growth rate drops to +29.5% from +45.4% once the substantial contributions from Nvidia , Micron and Alphabet are excluded.

Q3 Earnings Season Scorecard

Through Friday, November 6th, we have seen Q3 results from 441 S&P 500 members, or 88.2% of the index's total membership. Total earnings for these companies are up +24.8% from the same period last year on +13.4% higher revenues, with 82.1% beating EPS estimates and 74.6% beating revenue estimates.

The very strong earnings and revenue growth pace for this group of 441 S&P 500 members is mostly due to Micron, whose Q3 earnings increased +1075.7% from the year-earlier level. Alphabet's results in the preceding period benefited from a large unrealized gain. Excluding the Micron and Alphabet contributions, Q3 earnings for the remaining index members that have reported would be up +21.5%.

The Earnings Big Picture

Nvidia, Micron, and Alphabet have substantial weightage in the annual earnings growth pace for the index as a whole.

As we noted earlier, estimates for full-year 2027areexperiencing the same positive and broad-based revisions trend that we noted earlier in the context of 2026 Q4.

news.Content:
（中央社記者江明晏台北9日電）國安基金穩住市場信心，台股今天開高反彈，台積電盤中漲逾7%，多檔跌深權值股與千金股漲停，盤中指數大漲2647點；終場上漲1960.06點，收在41661.7點，創史上第二大收盤漲點。投顧分析，台股是否真正落底反彈，仍須觀察美股走勢。

美國科技股上週五止跌反彈，費城半導體指數上漲4.21%，台積電ADR強彈6.33%；加上國安基金上週五宣布史上第10次護盤，金管會也提出限空令等措施，提振台股信心，台股今天開高震盪走高，盤中指數大漲2647.72點，至42349.36點。

台股加權指數終場收在41661.7點，上漲1960.06點，漲幅4.94%，成交值新台幣8379.29億元。電子指數收漲5.49%，金融指數漲2.35%；代表中小型股的櫃買OTC指數強勢反彈5.9%。

觀察權值股表現，台積電收盤上漲100元，收2235元，漲幅4.68%；聯發科、台達電、國巨、大立光等權值股收漲停，一掃先前陰霾；台塑集團股台塑、南亞、台化均以漲停作收。

指標股方面，PCB族群轉強，金像電、華通漲停，ABF載板族群欣興、景碩、臻鼎-KY、南電勁揚；上游族群台玻、金居、富喬漲停，台光電、聯茂勁揚逾6%。

半導體供應鏈股弘塑、萬潤、均華、聖暉、亞翔、環球晶等收漲停；面板股群創漲停，友達漲逾6%。記憶體族群南亞科漲逾7%，華邦電、旺宏、力積電、鈺創、晶豪科、群聯漲停。

高價股今天強勢反彈，股王信驊漲近3%、股后川湖漲逾5%，大立光、鴻勁、聯發科、世芯-KY、奇鋐、精測、聯亞、富世達、群聯、弘塑、智邦、昇達科、台達電、創新服務、光聖等高價股漲停，台股收盤擁38檔千金股。

萬寶投顧執行長王榮旭向中央社記者表示，台股今天強勢反彈，這波反彈並非只有台股，美股、日韓股市也同步回升，不過台股盤中漲幅超過6%，表現明顯優於日韓，除了受惠台灣供應鏈基本面支撐，國安基金宣布進場護盤，明顯發揮提振市場信心的效果。

王榮旭指出，台股行情是否真正落底，仍須觀察美股走勢，目前費城半導體指數尚未站回5日線，也未突破上方壓力區。考量台股與美股連動性高，加上新台幣近期回貶，外資後續動向將是觀察重點。

針對美國民主黨傾向加強AI監管，可能導致資料中心建置放緩，王榮旭認為，目前市場對此議題的反應，情緒面大於實質面，10月以來的股市回檔，已部分反映民主黨勝選預期；此外，近期油價、公債殖利率走跌，對市場而言都是正面因素。

他認為，AI產業並非停止發展，而是投資步調可能適度踩煞車，未必是壞事，反而有助市場重新檢視投資效益與產業發展節奏。

展望後市，王榮旭表示，除非出現新的重大利空，台股短線再度破底的機率不高，但目前融資餘額去化仍不夠充分，預期11月中下旬第3季財報公布後，市場可能進入短暫空窗期；台股後續上漲機率仍高於下跌，但可能以震盪築底為主，個股表現可望優於大盤。（編輯：張良知）1151109

news.Title: 國安基金來了! 台股一度飆2647點 收盤站4萬1
news.Content:
[ 非凡新聞 ]記者謝旻蓁,攝影蘇韋銘

台股周一滿血復活，在國安基金進場護盤消息提振下，指數盤中一度上漲2648點，改寫史上盤中第二大漲點，重返4萬2千點之上。科技類股重拾多頭火種，其中台達電、聯發科亮燈漲停，台積電與鴻海也上漲約半根停板，中小型題材百花齊放，DRAM、光學鏡頭、被動元件面板以及光通訊等族群，多檔亮燈漲停，帶領加權指數終場上漲1960點，收在41661點，成交量達8639億元，櫃買市場漲幅也有5.90%，收在321.97點。不過股匯不同調，新台幣周一續貶，終場收在32.882元，貶值1.14角。三大法人合計賣超945億元，其中外資提款900億元，自營商賣超312億元，投信則是買超267億元。

《非凡新聞》記者 謝旻蓁：「國安基金進場護盤消息，重振市場多頭信心，台股周一盤中狂飆超過2000點，漲點創下盤中史上第二強，指數一口氣收復了，三道整數大關，強勢站回42000點之上。」

盤面一片紅光壟罩，大型電子權值股重掌多頭兵符，聯發科、台達電漲停亮燈，台積電、鴻海也勁揚逾半根停板；中小型概念股更是遍地開花，包含DRAM、光學鏡頭、被動元件、面板以及光通訊等族群都吸引大量買盤進駐；千金股重拾多頭火種，金融與玻璃陶瓷概念股也躍升撐盤要角，顯示股市信心有顯著回溫。

華冠投顧分析師 劉彥良：「（台股）這次剛剛回到年線，國安基金就急著進場，給予投資人非常充足的信心，帶動多方信心回籠，包括空單也被迫大舉回補。上週五台股已經出現一個大量下影線，所以技術面上已具備止跌意義，包括我們盤後看到，融資單日大減超過400億，那使得指數的波段減幅20%，那已經跟融資的，波段減幅18%非常接近，代表說籌碼經過了大幅清洗。」

至於這波反彈續航力有多強，富邦投顧董事長陳奕光認為還是要密切關注新台幣走勢、外資動向，以及科技巨頭信用利差等指標，進一步判斷對大盤走勢 究竟是助力還是阻力。

富邦投顧董事長 陳奕光：「台幣匯率假如這個地方，能夠止貶回升，那代表這個反彈可以進入震盪，震盪進入回升的條件一。外資空單現在還在高高掛，所以外資空單假設，能在反彈過程裡面，順勢地減少他的空單未平倉，也代表說這個反彈是有機會，進入所謂的反轉行情。（CoreWeave）它的殖利率跟這個，所謂的信用利差交易的利率，如果再往上攀高的話，可能要留意信用違約交換這個地方，是否會有違約的情況。」

內資對後市反彈抱持期待，外資圈也維持樂觀看法，高盛看好明年台股最高有機會來到57500點，不過短線最大的不確定性仍在於美國對AI資料中心的監管政策。隨著政策輪廓逐步清晰，台股走勢也有望轉趨明朗（記者謝旻蓁、蘇韋銘／台北採訪報導）

news.Title: Semiconductor Crash: 2 AI Chip Stocks That Could Help Make You a Fortune Following the Pullback
news.Content:
The stock market got crushed on Thursday, Nov. 5, led lower by artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor stocks . The pullback followed the U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats captured both the House and the Senate, as well as key governorships in states like Texas and Pennsylvania. Following the results, many newly elected officials spoke out against the ongoing data center build-out, calling for a moratorium.

However, any further weakness in AI infrastructure stocks could pave the way for an incredible buying opportunity that could help make investors a fortune. Hyperscalers (owners of large data centers) and chip companies have already pre-emptively been planning for a potentially more difficult political environment. Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG), Microsoft , and Amazon have all been investing to expand their data centers overseas, and the backlash in the U.S. could increase this push. Meanwhile, companies are looking at the potential of moving data centers both offshore and into outer space. Earlier this year, China built the world's first offshore wind-powered undersea data center, while SpaceX is aggressively pursuing plans to put data centers in space.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

AI companies are also exploring other ways to navigate the impending political shift in the U.S. Alphabet is teaming up with Bloom Energy on a self-sufficient AI data center with carbon capture that doesn't use any grid power in the Republican stronghold of Wyoming. Meanwhile, Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) is reportedly looking to buy and repurpose old telecom buildings into small data centers. These structures already have access to power and should face a lot less red tape in getting permits.

As such, just because the political climate has shifted against AI data centers, don't expect the AI infrastructure build-out to suddenly slow down. With that in mind, let's look at two AI chip stocks that could help make you a fortune on this pullback.

1. Nvidia

Nvidia remains the leading AI infrastructure company, as its graphics processing units (GPUs) are still the primary chips used to power AI workloads. The company has a wide moat in the training market, as most of the original AI code was written on its CUDA software platform and optimized for its chips. The company has also locked up the most future supply of high bandwidth memory (HBM), which all but assures it will maintain its leadership position.

Story Continues

Importantly, the company has expanded its platform over the years, allowing it to capture an increasing share of the spending pie. With the addition of inference chips, central processing units (CPUs), networking, and an expanded software layer, Nvidia is now capturing around $40 billion per gigawatt for its Vera Rubin platform, up from $18 billion for its Hopper platform.

At a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 12 times fiscal 2028 estimates (ending January 2028), the stock has a lot of upside from both growth and multiple expansion.

AVGO PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

2. Broadcom

While Nvidia dominates much of the AI chip market, large hyperscalers are increasingly turning to custom AI accelerators to help reduce costs, especially when it comes to inference. Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) is the leader in this space, as it provides the necessary IP (intellectual property) and services to help turn customers' designs into AI ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits), which are hardwired custom chips designed for specific purposes.

Broadcom helped Alphabet develop its highly regarded tensor processing units (TPUs), which the two companies are now starting to sell to external customers, with SemiAnalysis reporting that Anthropic, Meta Platforms , OpenAI, and Oracle are all TPU customers. This will be Broadcom's biggest growth driver, with Anthropic expected to become its largest customer, while Alphabet will also remain a major client. Meanwhile, Meta and OpenAI have also developed their own custom chips using Broadcom's help.

Broadcom has said it has a clear line of sight to doubling its AI chip revenue next fiscal year, then doubling it again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Investors seem to have their doubts, with the stock trading at below 10 times fiscal 2028 estimates, so Broadcom could make investors a fortune if it can attain this revenue goal.

news.Title: Chinese robotics stock surge on Apple robotics research
news.Content:
Investing.com-- Chinese robotics stocks rose sharply on Monday after Apple published a research paper unveiling an autonomous humanoid robot control system using technology from Unitree Robotics.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

Unitree– trading as Yushu Technology– was the best performer in the lot, rising over 8% in Shanghai trade.

Ubtech Robotics jumped 8%, Lingyi iTech Guangdong Co added nearly 2%, while Lens Technology and Hesai Group – which both supply robot components– added over 4% apiece.

Alibaba– whose Qwen model was also used to run Apple's system– rose as much as 3%.

Apple researchers last week released a paper unveiling the HALO system– software for humanoid robots that is capable of completing a host of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to objects, and other demonstrations of dexterity.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Apple said the HALO system achieved a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six, real-world environments. The humanoid robot was able to follow plain-language instructions to carry out training tasks.

The system was tested using Unitree's G1 platform, while Alibab's Qwen 3.6 model was used, running locally, in the test.

The test marked more progress towards developing humanoid robots that can operate effectively in real-life environments– which is a major target of the industry at large.

Chinese suppliers– which are viewed as being global leaders in the technology– stand to benefit from any such progress, given that it opens a path to mass market adoption of the technology.

Still, the Apple paper did not mention any direct partnerships with Chinese firms to develop HALO.

news.Title: AMD vs. Intel: Which Is the Better AI Chip Stock to Own for the Next 3 Years Following the Semiconductor Crash?
news.Content:
Chip stocks have been absolutely pummeled recently, with Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) two of the biggest losers over the past month. Meanwhile, the strong Democratic showing in the midterm elections put the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out on notice.

Despite the political shift, I wouldn't expect there to be a major impact on overall AI infrastructure growth in the coming years, with hyperscalers being able to navigate the current environment and shifting some projects overseas. However, between AMD and Intel, I think the clear winner is likely to be AMD. Here's why.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Advanced Micro Devices has been one of the hardest-hit stocks in the semiconductor pullback. However, the company is riding two powerful waves in inference and agentic AI that are just starting to kick in, and its new Helios rack solution could be a game changer.

Helios is AMD's turnkey AI infrastructure solution that incorporates its graphics processing units (GPUs), central processing units (CPUs), and networking components into a single system. The system contains 72 GPUs and 18 CPUs per rack and is designed to provide the "lowest cost per token" to help reduce overall computing costs. The system has already started being rolled out to key customers, including OpenAI, Meta Platforms , Microsoft , Anthropic, and Oracle , and OEM (original equipment manufacturer) and ODM (original design manufacturer) partners will also soon begin to ship Helios.

AMD has two large deals in place with OpenAI and Meta Platforms for 6 gigawatts of compute capacity each. With each Helios system costing between $5 million and $5.5 million and consuming between 225 kilowatts and 245 kilowatts of power, each deal would be worth approximately $120 billion. Meanwhile, Anthropic's 2-gigawatt deal would be worth around $40 billion, with Microsoft and Oracle as smaller customers.

At the same time, the company is seeing huge demand for its server CPUs, given that these chips are needed to help manage AI agents. Its CPUs are helping run Meta's new Muse AI agents, and the company sees server CPUs becoming a $220 billion market by 2030.

As a result, AMD is projecting growth to soar next year, with it recently forecasting revenue to surge 80% in 2027. The pullback has dropped the stock to a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of around 9 times its 2030 analyst estimates, giving it plenty of room to run the next three years.

Story Continues

Intel

While AMD has been the victim of a broader semiconductor stock sell-off, much of Intel's wounds are self-inflicted. This is due to the company's still-outsized exposure to the PC market, which is seeing weak demand as high memory costs have caused computer makers to raise prices, slowing demand.

Intel's client computing and physical AI group (CCPG) remains its largest segment, and revenue for the unit fell 5% last quarter. However, the company is expecting units to drop 10% in 2027 after a 12% decline this year, which will also lead to a large inventory correction that will significantly impact the next two quarters.

Meanwhile, Intel's foundry business continues to produce large losses, including a $1.9 billion operating loss in Q3. The company is struggling to find external customers, in part due to technology and in part due to conflicts of interest, and if the data center build-out shifts overseas, this will likely sting it even more, given its strong domestic footprint.

Intel is the market leader in server CPUs, and like AMD, it's been seeing strong growth in this area. However, the company has been consistently losing shares to AMD and custom CPUs. This is only expected to continue in the years ahead, especially as the company has no turnkey solution like Nvidia and AMD.

As such, I think the stock could continue to underperform over the next three years.

news.Title: Microsoft's Oracle move raises new question for investors
news.Content: For about three years, Oracle servers helped power the AI version of Microsoft's Bing. Now, Microsoft is letting the arrangement lapse and has recently been switching off the rented capacity. It was one of the more unusual partnerships of the early AI rush. The timing could hardly be worse for Oracle. The news landed a day after the Nasdaq dropped more than 5% and slipped into a correction on Nov. 5, as investors bailed out of AI names on fears of slower data center construction. A customer walking away from old hardware is exactly the kind of story bears have been waiting for. Why Microsoft walked away from the Bing deal The deal itself goes back to 2023, when Oracle announced a multi-year agreement for Microsoft to use its cloud AI infrastructure for the AI-assisted Bing, Bloomberg reported. Financial terms were never disclosed. At the time, it looked like a rare case of a cloud giant (Microsoft) renting from a direct rival (Oracle) because it simply could not get enough chips. Also read: Microsoft just gave Nvidia shareholders a reason to pay attention Three years on, the math looks different. People familiar with the matter said the capacity no longer met Microsoft's evolving needs, and the Oracle hardware ran on older Nvidia chips. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. This is not the first time talks between the two have hit a wall. In June, a separate leasing deal that one source said could have been worth more than $3 billion reportedly fell apart over security and compliance concerns, Reuters reported, citing Business Insider. Oracle called the details inaccurate and described Microsoft as both a partner and a customer. The market reaction on Nov. 6 was messy. Oracle traded down about 2% around midday after sliding nearly 10% over the previous few sessions, and Microsoft also slipped. Both names were already bruised from earlier in the week, when the midterm sweep stirred up fears of tougher scrutiny for the AI industry. Oracle's case for older GPUs Oracle is pushing back hard on the idea that ageing chips are dead weight. A company spokesperson said demand for its AI infrastructure "remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs." The company has numbers it likes to point to. In September, Oracle said it was renewing contracts for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium to the original deal price, according to Bloomberg. If that holds, losing one tenant on older hardware may matter less than the headline suggests. It is a bold claim in an industry where most people assume chips lose value quickly, and Oracle will now have to keep proving that its chips are still dependable and in demand. Story Continues There is also a large pile of signed contracts behind the stock. Oracle's remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion, and the company booked more than $30 billion in new AI cloud contracts during the quarter, as reported by TheStreet. The catch is who sits behind that backlog. Reports suggest almost half of Oracle's remaining performance obligations come from a single agreement with OpenAI. That leaves Oracle leaning heavily on one customer at the same moment its oldest gear is losing a big-name renter, which is not a comfortable spot for a company still spending heavily. The bill for Oracle's buildout keeps growing Oracle's balance sheet is where the worry really starts. S&P cut the company to BBB-, one notch above junk, in July, and its reported debt stood at about 4.3 times EBITDA, while peers like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft sat under 1 times, Reuters reported. The funding needs have not gone away. On Oct. 28, Oracle committed to capping new capital raises through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, not counting debt refinancing. Five days later, on Nov. 2, it filed to raise the full amount through a mix of stock and senior notes, and the shares fell sharply that day, according to Oracle. There is also a timing mismatch that the Microsoft news puts in sharper focus. Oracle's data center leases run 15 to 19 years, while many of its customer contracts last only up to five, and some of those leases have yet to even start. If and when a customer decides older chips no longer fit its needs, Oracle is still carrying the building. More Microsoft: Microsoft's Windows sales fell 22% as PC prices climb Microsoft CEO sees a problem ahead for AI stock investors Microsoft just gave Nvidia shareholders a reason to pay attention The selloff has already done a lot of damage––Oracle's stock has roughly halved since June, as investors fret over spending that has pushed its free cash flow negative. But because the shares look like a better deal, since the stock price slide has improved the price/earnings ratio, some valuation screens now rank Oracle ahead of its megacap peers. However, a lower valuation does not necessarily mean a lower-risk investment. What Microsoft's pullback really signals Microsoft is not cutting back on renting computing power in general. Back in October 2025, it committed more than $33 billion to neocloud providers such as CoreWeave, Nscale, and Lambda, with cloud chief Scott Guthrie describing the company as being in "land-grab mode," as reported by TheStreet. Those commitments have since expanded substantially, but Microsoft has grown frustrated with the high costs and delays that came with them. What has changed is how picky the company has become. Microsoft has been tightening oversight of data center projects run by neoclouds including IREN, Nebius, and Nscale. IREN pushed back some deliveries after Microsoft asked for network design changes, Bloomberg reported. Nebius alone signed a five-year deal worth $17.4 billion with Microsoft in 2025. For Oracle, the next real test comes with its fiscal second-quarter report on Dec. 14. Investors will want proof that the 20% renewal story is holding up and that newer chips are finding buyers fast enough to carry the debt. news.Title: 5 Stocks I am Retiring On
news.Content:
A retirement portfolio needs businesses that can keep rewarding shareholders long after the current market narrative fades. Dividends show how important those quieter sources of return can be: according to S&P Dow Jones Indices research cited in our coverage of Dividend Aristocrat stocks , dividends have accounted for roughly 31% of the S&P 500's total return since 1926, with capital appreciation accounting for the remaining 69%. In the 1940s and 1970s, dividend income accounted for more than half of total returns. The lesson is not that every retirement investment must pay dividends, but rather that long-term shareholder gains can come from sources other than rising share prices.

Warren Buffett offers a useful test for that level of dedication. He has advised investors to buy only what they would "perfectly happy to hold if the market shut down for 10 years." Rather than relying on the potential to sell tomorrow, investors should consider how much the underlying business may make over a decade. That business-owner perspective is the common thread running through Insider Monkey's discussion of Warren Buffett's best long-term stocks to buy .

For retirement investors, the distinction between a high starting dividend and an increasing dividend is crucial. The S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats index requires components to have increased dividends for at least 25 years in a row. This is a record that spans numerous economic cycles, though it doesn't guarantee future growth. Insider Monkey's analysis of dividend growth stocks to buy and hold in 2026 looked at 68 such companies and evaluated their five-year average dividend growth rates.

Of course, financial strength is just as important as payout record. A dividend competes with debt repayments, capital spending, and other financial requirements. Liabilities are broader than debt, but the comparison shows the type of liquidity cushion worth considering alongside dividend yield.

So, what are the best small-cap value stocks to invest in now? We provided the expanded list of the 10 Stocks I am Retiring On . The top 5 stocks are provided below:

Our Methodology

For this article, we looked through financial websites such as The Motley Fool, Seeking Alpha, Yahoo Finance, and 24/7 Wall St. for journalists and experts that say a stock is the one they are retiring on, building their retirement portfolio around, or plan on holding for life. We included a stock only if at least two different sources supported it, and for each stock, we explain who made the assertion and what their thesis is. We then rated the 10 stocks that satisfied this criteria in ascending order of hedge fund ownership. We also list each stock's short interest and number of hedge fund holders as of Q2 2026, allowing investors to see whether hedge funds agree with these retirement picks.

Story Continues

Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 599.2% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 372 percentage points ( see more details here ).

5. Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (NYSE: BRK-B )

Short Interest: 0.98%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 135

Berkshire Hathaway Inc. is a rare mega-cap company valued at book value. The third-quarter results, released on November 7, came in soft. Operating earnings fell 5.8% to $12.7 billion, while net earnings fell 28% to $22.1 billion due to lower investment gains. A the same time, insurance underwriting earnings fell 43% to $1.35 billion as a result of Geico losses. Berkshire responded with a record buyback for 2026. It repurchased $9.6 billion in the quarter, more than doubling the second quarter's $4.5 billion, bringing the total for the year to $14.4 billion.

Keith Speights placed Berkshire in his January 2026 "forever" portfolio of equities that he doesn't plan to sell. His conviction is based on the diversification afforded by Berkshire's operating subsidiaries and public-equity investments, as well as his belief that Greg Abel will continue Buffett's business and investing philosophy.

The risk is in the earnings engine rather than the balance sheet. Berkshire's trailing twelve-month operating earnings are down 3.2%, insurance investment income dropped 14% due to lower short-term rates, and the company was a net seller of stocks again. The cash only helps if Abel can find places to put it. Read about whether the capital allocation mechanism can continue to compound after Buffett here .

4. Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )

Short Interest: 0.90%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 169

Apple Inc. is valued as a quality compounder, trading at 32.87x forward earnings. The company's fiscal fourth-quarter revenue increased 12% to $114.5 billion, while iPhone revenue climbed 17% to $57.6 billion, and Services reached a new high of $31.6 billion, up 10%. Speights' January 2026 "forever" portfolio featured Apple as its largest individual stock holding. He stated that he regretted selling shares in the past and didn't plan to repeat the mistake. His theory focuses on Apple's tightly integrated ecosystem of products and services, with future devices and technologies offering opportunities to further consumer interactions.

That said, valuation depends on margins holding. CEO John Ternus referred to memory pricing as "unprecedented," and Apple guided gross margin to 45% to 46%, below the roughly 46.3% consensus. The rise in services was the slowest since 2022, and shares dropped by around 2% the day following earnings before rising again. Insider Monkey looked at Apple's role in helping the mega-cap recovery. Read the analysis here .

3. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM )

Short Interest: 0.57%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 249

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited makes the advanced chips behind most of the AI buildout. Despite 2-nanometer dilution, which accounts for 8% of wafer revenue, the company's operating margin for the third quarter stood at 58.7% while its gross margin came in at 66.4%. Management expects a 44% increase in revenue for 2026 with capital expenditures of $60 billion to $64 billion, while the fourth-quarter estimate calls for $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. The stock is trading at about 16.4x forward earnings, a discount for geopolitical risk that appears modest in comparison to that growth.

Motley Fool writer Keithen Drury chose TSMC in January 2026 as the single stock he would buy and hold if forced to own only one. He contends that since TSMC produces advanced chips for competing clients and stands to gain as overall demand rises, investors don't have to correctly predict which chip designer would take the lead in the AI race. He highlighted the company's manufacturing scale and technological prowess while clearly noting reliance on continued AI spending and the possibility of dispute over Taiwan.

That risk is genuine, as Taiwan hosts the vast bulk of advanced-node capacity. Margins are also under pressure from the 2-nanometer ramp and overseas factories, while capital spending continues to climb. For a retirement investor, the question is whether TSMC's manufacturing size and technological leadership are durable enough to outlast those fundamental risks over time. Bell Global Equities Fund believes they are, and Insider Monkey looked into why the fund continues to favor the stock .

2. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL )

Short Interest: 1.34%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 275

Alphabet Inc. has become cheaper while its business accelerated. The company's third-quarter revenue climbed by 25% to $127.6 billion, while Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion with a 36.2% operating margin, and Cloud backlog reached $561 billion. Search grew 12%, with the fastest query growth in five years, and the Gemini app reached one billion users. Analyst targets for GOOGL sit around 41% over the stock's current price.

Lyle Daly made the retirement connection directly in his May 2026 piece. He named Alphabet the top stock in his retirement portfolio, claiming that it provided the best long-term value in technology. His conviction stemmed from its portfolio of proven businesses, including Search and Google Cloud, rather than pure AI enthusiasm. At the time, he cited first-quarter Search growth of 19% and Cloud growth of 63% as proof that the operating businesses were doing well.

The market is punishing spending. Capex was $51.4 billion in the quarter, while free cash flow came in negative $9.1 billion. Capex for 2026 is expected to be between $195 billion and $205 billion, with an increase in 2027. The reported EPS of $2.12 missed the $3.01 consensus, while Other Bets, which includes Waymo, lost $2 billion. Long-term shareholders face the issue of distinguishing between investments that can boost future earnings and those that may take years to yield a satisfactory return. Waymo catches this trade-off: it offers another potential growth business, but it needs funding before its economics can be validated. Insider Monkey asked whether the valuation reflects Waymo's potential. Read the analysis here .

1. Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN )

Short Interest: 0.95%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 369

Amazon.com, Inc.'s valuation is based on operating profit and AWS rather than earnings per share. The company's third-quarter revenue rose 12% to $201.9 billion, while operating income surged 61% to a record $28.1 billion, representing a 13.9% margin. AWS revenue increased 39.3% to $46.0 billion, the fastest growth in nearly five years, with a 38.7% operating margin and a run rate of $184 billion. CEO Andy Jassy predicted AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028.

Speights selected Amazon as the first company for his "forever" portfolio in January 2026. He ascribed its long-term attraction to Jeff Bezos' "Day 1" culture, which encourages the company to continue chasing new opportunities rather than defending an outdated business model. AWS was his prime example of that culture serving as a major profit engine, while satellite internet and consumer robotics indicated potential future opportunities. Separately, Leo Nelissen identified Amazon as one of three stocks around which he would create an entire portfolio, citing AWS demand and a projected path to $150 billion in annual free cash flow by 2030.

The sell-off was based on cash. Amazon expects $220 billion in capex in 2026 and "meaningfully more" in 2027, with trailing free cash flow turning negative and EPS of $1.89 missing forecasts. The fourth-quarter projection of $240 billion to $247 billion in sales and up to $33.5 billion in operating income fell short of the consensus midpoint. For long-term shareholders, the question is whether increasing operating profits will eventually convert into cash left over after investment. That conflict extends beyond AI infrastructure to projects like Zoox, which drove Insider Monkey's analysis of whether Amazon's cloud and retail cash engines can continue to fund its robotaxi ambitions .

While we acknowledge the risk and potential of AMZN as an investment, we believe certain AI infrastructure stocks offer far stronger long-term potential at a much more attractive entry point. If you are looking for an AI stock more promising than AMZN that operates as a critical AI tollbooth and stands as the most important company in the world, check out our report about this must-own AI stock .

news.Title: Bloom Energy Stock Fell 16% on the Same Day 2 Giant Data Center Deals Named It. Is It a Buy?
news.Content:
Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) turned up in two big data center announcements on Nov. 5. NTT DATA said it had agreed to deploy 900 megawatts of the fuel cell maker's onsite power across data center projects around the world.

And Alphabet's Google said Bloom would build the fuel cells for a 702-megawatt plant powering its first data center in Wyoming, a $17 billion project.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The stock had a bad day anyway. Shares ended at $167.52, off around 16%, amid worries that rising opposition to new data centers after the Nov. 3 midterms might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

The growth stock is still up over 90% this year. But it now sits about 52% below the $345.85 record close it set on June 22.

How much new business did Bloom win on Nov. 5? Less than the headlines may suggest, because just one of the two deals is new. I think the other still matters, though, and the stock looks much more reasonably priced than it did in October.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Google's fuel cells were ordered in January

Google won't buy the fuel cells itself. American Electric Power plans to invest around $4 billion in the 702-megawatt project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, the utility said on Oct. 14. It'll sell the plant's output to Google under a 20-year power purchase agreement, and it expects the plant to be fully running by late 2028.

The fuel cell order came months earlier. In January, an AEP subsidiary agreed to buy solid oxide fuel cells for around $2.65 billion for a plant near Cheyenne. The purchase used most of an option for 900 extra megawatts under AEP's 2024 supply deal with Bloom.

For a sense of scale, that one order is worth over half of Bloom's full-year revenue forecast of $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion for 2026.

So, Google's news didn't add to Bloom's orders. The fuel cells were bought in January, and AEP had already named Google as the plant's customer in October.

That still means something, I think. A fuel cell order backed by a 20-year power contract with Google looks more likely to become revenue on time than one linked to an unnamed buyer.

NTT DATA is the new business

NTT DATA's deal is the new business, and the companies called it Bloom's biggest international project so far. NTT's data center arm plans to use the fuel cells as its main power source, with the relationship meant to reach gigawatt scale across its global portfolio.

Story Continues

What the release didn't say matters, too. It gave no dollar value, no project locations, and no timeline beyond first shipments starting in 2027. This deal shouldn't show up in Bloom's 2026 revenue, and Bloom hasn't said how much of it falls in 2027 or later.

But 900 megawatts is a lot of fuel cells -- nearly a full year of output at the 1 gigawatt of annual production capacity Bloom's Fremont, California, plant had going into 2026. The company planned to double that capacity by year-end.

Bloom needs deals like this, because its quarter-to-quarter growth slowed sharply in the third quarter. Second-quarter revenue of $1.07 billion was 42% above the first quarter's $751 million. Third-quarter revenue then climbed 16% sequentially to $1.24 billion, up 138% year over year. And October's raised outlook (management's third raise this year) implies a sequential gain of 9% to 25% in the fourth quarter.

That's still strong growth. Keeping it up into 2027 and 2028, though, depends on deals like NTT DATA's moving from announcement to shipment.

Is the price finally reasonable?

Based on the midpoint of management's adjusted earnings forecast for 2026 ($3.10 to $3.40 a share), Bloom stock cost around 52 times earnings at its Nov. 5 close. The same forecast had it at around 67 times earnings at the $217.77 close on Oct. 22. On next year's expected earnings, shares now trade at around 31 times earnings.

Still, 52 times earnings is a premium price. It assumes Bloom keeps growing quickly well past this year.

But Bloom landed a big new deal on Nov. 5 as its shares got much cheaper.

Of course, a slower U.S. data center build-out might delay some deliveries. And October's weak spot hasn't gone away. Bloom's operations burned $27 million in cash in the third quarter, mostly because it booked revenue faster than it could bill customers for it.

Is Bloom stock worth buying after a 16% one-day drop? I'd consider buying some shares at this price, a few at a time. And I'd maybe add more when billing catches up with revenue.

news.Title: Cathie Wood buys $17.2 million of tumbling tech stock
news.Content:
Cathie Wood, head of Ark Investment Management, likes to buy and sell shares of her favorite technology companies as stock prices move up and down.

That's what she just did with Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL), selling nearly 59,000 shares before turning around and buying more than 60,000 shares during a broader market selloff.

Last year, her flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is down 1.90% as of writing, while the S&P 500 has surged 7.76 %, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Nov. 6, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -9.05% , while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 9.45% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar .

Cathie Wood says AI boom won't slow down

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott . That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking.

Wood remains optimistic about the stock market despite growing concerns about the Iran war, higher energy prices and the recent U.S. elections.

She rejected recent concerns that Democrats' election victories could slow the AI boom.

Related: Cathie Wood buys $10.9 million of tumbling tech stock

"Can this election derail the AI revolution? We don't think so," Wood wrote in an X post on Nov. 7.

Wood expects companies building data centers to care more for the local economy. The benefits include lower property taxes, higher-paying jobs, commercial developments, and funding for schools and facilities.

Wood also believes AI-driven productivity gains will help ease affordability pressures while boosting corporate profits and investment.

"In our view, those gains will translate into higher compensation—helping to turn around affordability— as well as stronger margins, more investment, and lower prices," she said.

Despite the market's recent uncertainty, Wood believes investors are underestimating the economic growth that AI could deliver.

Story Continues

"We have experienced just a taste of this technology revolution," she wrote. "The market's uncertainty is understandable, but we believe the economy is on a stronger growth trajectory than most investors recognize."

Not all investors agree with Wood's optimism. Over the past month through Nov. 5, the Ark Innovation ETF saw roughly $2.19 billion in net outflows, according to data from ETF research firm VettaFi .

Cathie Wood buys $17.2 million of Alphabet stock

On Nov. 5 and 6, Wood's Ark funds bought a total of 60,553 shares of Google parent Alphabet Inc. (GOOG), according to Ark's daily trading information sent to TheStreet. These shares were worth about $17.2 million based on the latest closing price of $283.93.

The purchases came right after Wood sold a total of 58,694 shares of Alphabet on Nov. 3 and Nov. 4.

Wood made the purchase during a brutal market sell-off on Nov. 5, as investors reacted to the midterm election results and worried that the outcome could cap the expansion of AI data centers. The S&P 500 Index tumbled 4.36% that day and rebounded 0.31% on Nov. 6.

Related: Cathie Wood buys $47 million of popular semiconductor stock

Alphabet stock is down nearly 10% year-to-date. On Oct. 29, the stock plunged 12% after reporting disappointing third-quarter results, with its massive AI spending plans and negative free cash flow overshadowing growth in its Google Cloud business. That was the company's worst post-earnings selloff on record.

Alphabet missed third-quarter estimates on both revenue and earnings, reporting $127.57 billion in sales versus the $128.2 billion expected. Earnings per share came in at $2.12, well below the $3.02 consensus.

Investors have been questioning whether the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion, substantially worse than the $2.70 billion deficit expected by analysts.

The company maintained its full-year capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion, but warned that spending would increase significantly in 2027.

Several Wall Street analysts have lowered their price targets on Alphabet after earnings.

On Oct. 30, Wells Fargo cut its price target on Alphabet to $371 from $417 while maintaining an Overweight rating. The firm said Google's search business was slowing more than expected, particularly compared with Meta Platforms' strong advertising results.

Wells Fargo believes the shift toward AI-powered search is a key reason for the slowdown, even as search engagement continues to grow at record levels.

Citi also lowered its price target on Alphabet to $375 from $447 while maintaining a Buy rating. The analysts said the cut was to "reflect greater overall uncertainty," according to a research note sent to TheStreet.

Citi raised concerns about AI search monetization, rising capital spending in 2027 and pressure on free cash flow.

"While we acknowledge the N-T headwinds at Google, we remain constructive on shares as greater RSI investment should accelerate model velocity, support newer product launches (such as Gemini Agent), and strengthen monetization across its Consumer and Enterprise functions while also improving internal productivity," Citi said.

Alphabet is currently not in the top 10 holdings of the Ark Innovation ETF.

Top 10 holdings in the Ark Innovation ETF by market value and weight as of Nov. 6, 2026:

Tesla (TSLA): $606.12 million, 10.74%

SpaceX (SPCX): $410.80 million, 7.28%

Tempus AI (TEM): $342.01 million, 6.06%

Circle Internet Group (CRCL): $272.64 million, 4.83%

OpenAI (Private): $249.37 million, 4.42%

Nvidia (NVDA): $209.02 million, 3.70%

Shopify (SHOP): $187.15 million, 3.32%

Twist Bioscience (TWST): $176.12 million, 3.12%

Other than buying Alphabet shares, Wood also bought shares of Natera (NTRA), Kratos Defense & Security Solutions (KTOS), 10x Genomics (TXG), Coinbase Global (COIN), Cerebras Systems (CBRS), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Nvidia (NVDA), Tempus AI (TEM), Twist Bioscience (TWST), Scribe Therapeutics (SCTX), Iambic Therapeutics (IAM), AeroVironment (AVAV), Joby Aviation (JOBY), Rocket Lab (RKLB), and Intuitive Machines (LUNR).

Wood trimmed positions in Eli Lilly (LLY), Teradyne (TER), Bullish (BLSH), CoreWeave (CRWV), Broadcom (AVGO), BYD (BYDDY), Personalis (PSNL), and CareDx (CDNA).

news.Title: Here's What a $1,000 Investment in Tesla Stock Could Be Worth in 5 Years
news.Content:
Investors view Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) as a perennial winner. Over the last decade, this is true. Shares have soared 2,630% since early November 2016 (as of Nov. 5, 2026).

But the story takes a dramatic turn if you zoom in. This "Magnificent Seven" stock has actually dropped 16% in the past five years. That performance means that it has significantly underperformed the broader market. Investors are left wondering if the company's shares are staying out of the fast lane permanently.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here's what a $1,000 investment in Tesla could be worth in five years. There is, without a doubt, significant upside. However, uncertainty is sky-high.

The opposite of stable and predictable

One of the core tenets of Warren Buffett's investing philosophy is to own what you know. Investors must be able to confidently figure out what a business will look like in the future. Naturally, this limits the opportunity set to stable and predictable companies.

Tesla is the opposite. It's like the business is always undergoing some sort of strategic restructuring. This makes it extremely difficult to assess what the future will bring.

Five years from now, Tesla's operations could look very similar to what they are today. During the third quarter (ended Sept. 30), 73% of the company's revenue came from selling electric vehicles (EVs). This business continues to struggle, though, as competition diverts consumer spending to rival offerings, which has forced Tesla to lower pricing. Deliveries dipped 2% year over year in Q3.

It also doesn't help that car demand is exposed to changing economic winds, adding volatility to the mix. Just ask the legacy mass-market auto manufacturers how much their profits can fluctuate based on interest rates and other macro variables.

Tesla is working on exciting projects that attract the market's attention. While the Robotaxi service is only running in select markets right now, with Cybercab only in Austin, Texas, the future of the company rests on autonomous vehicle technology. The ultimate goal is to run a global fleet that collects recurring revenue at tremendous scale.

Optimus, the humanoid robot, is another important part of the story . These won't be available for sale until the end of 2027, at the earliest. However, Elon Musk said in 2024 that this product could drive Tesla's market capitalization to $25 trillion one day.

Story Continues

Tesla's future rests squarely on its ability to bring artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities into the physical world. Self-driving EVs and robotics are the avenues. Their market opportunities appear to be massive. But there are an unlimited number of questions surrounding technical advancements, scaling production, regulatory developments, user adoption, safety and reliability, and timelines.

Gauging the market's expectations

If you view them at a high level, it's easy to assume that shares are egregiously expensive. The belief is that this has always been the case. Investors can buy Tesla stock right now by paying a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 151.

That multiple is more than 11 times higher than what Nvidia trades at. The dominant artificial intelligence infrastructure business is forecast to bring in $190 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2027. That's almost double what Tesla will report as revenue this year.

The Elon Musk premium is real. The investment community prizes what he says and does. And the general view is that he's the greatest entrepreneur and visionary ever.

This feeds into the positive sentiment. Tesla's strongest bulls will argue that the company's optionality signals that shares are severely undervalued. Robotaxi and Optimus will usher in a new era of financial prosperity that will contribute to unprecedented profit growth.

The bears point to a track record of over-promising and under-delivering on key milestones and deadlines. It seems that Tesla has always been working toward some ambitious goal that it never fully achieves. And investors are always left having to buy the narrative and ignore the current reality of the business.

An extreme valuation coupled with sky-high uncertainty lead me to believe that the stock will largely stay flat over the next five years, leaving investors with the $1,000 that they started with.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »

Neil Patel has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia and Tesla. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

news.Title: Could HBF be the solution to the Memory bottleneck?
news.Content:
Investing.com -- The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence workloads is creating a growing demand for memory capacity and bandwidth, opening the door for a new storage technology that could ease infrastructure constraints while providing a fresh growth opportunity for the NAND flash industry, Bernstein said.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

In a research report, Bernstein highlighted the potential of high-bandwidth flash (HBF), a technology designed to combine read bandwidth comparable to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) with eight to 16 times greater capacity at a significantly lower cost per gigabyte. The technology could make AI inference more efficient by reducing the amount of expensive GPU memory required to run increasingly large models and allowing AI systems to retrieve previously processed information instead of repeatedly performing costly computations.

The shift from AI training toward advanced inference and agentic workloads is making memory capacity, bandwidth and data reuse increasingly important. Larger models, longer context windows and more complex interactions are pushing data beyond the limits of HBM, expanding demand for conventional DRAM, NAND flash and hard disk drives.

Bernstein said HBF could address this challenge through a tiered memory architecture in which HBM handles frequently accessed and latency-sensitive data, while HBF stores larger model parameters, less frequently used model components and reusable key-value (KV) cache data. This could allow AI infrastructure providers to run larger models with fewer GPUs and reduce computing, power and capital expenditure requirements.

The technology could also create a significant opportunity for NAND manufacturers. Bernstein estimates that HBF could consume approximately 6.5 times more NAND wafer capacity per bit than conventional triple-level cell (TLC) NAND, reflecting its use of higher-performance single-level cell (SLC) flash, additional silicon area and advanced packaging requirements.

Bernstein estimates that HBF manufacturing costs could be roughly 10 times higher than those of conventional enterprise SSDs, depending on the configuration. However, if manufacturers price HBF modules at levels comparable to HBM while offering substantially greater capacity, the technology could generate attractive gross margins. Under its base-case assumptions, Bernstein estimates gross margins of about 86.5% for an eight-high HBF configuration and 88.9% for a 16-high configuration.

Story Continues

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Despite the opportunity, Bernstein cautioned that HBF faces significant adoption hurdles. The technology is not a direct replacement for HBM and has limitations involving latency, write bandwidth, endurance and data access. It would also require changes to processor designs and system software, alongside careful optimization of data placement and memory management.

A key concern is the lack of formal endorsement from Nvidia, which has instead promoted alternative technologies such as Storage Next and its CMX content memory storage platform to address the growing demand for KV-cache capacity. Alphabet Inc Class A (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META), SK hynix Inc ADR (NASDAQ:SKHY) and Tenstorrent are among the companies involved in the HBF ecosystem, but broader industry adoption remains uncertain.

SanDisk Corporation (NASDAQ:SNDK) has moved HBF beyond the conceptual stage toward standardization and initial silicon development, with the company targeting its first product samples for inference applications in 2027. Bernstein said the technology could provide additional upside to the company's financial targets, although HBF is not currently included in those targets.

Bernstein maintained an Outperform rating on SanDisk with a $3,000 price target. It also rated Seagate Technology PLC (NASDAQ:STX), Western Digital Corporation (NASDAQ:WDC), Samsung Electronics Co Ltd (KS:005930), SK hynix and Micron Outperform, while assigning KIOXIA an Underperform rating.

The analysts said HBF could ultimately do for the NAND industry what HBM has done for DRAM by creating a premium AI-driven demand category and tightening supply through higher wafer consumption. However, its commercial success will depend on technological execution, customer adoption and competition from alternative memory architectures.

news.Title: Should You Buy Meta Platforms Before Its Stock Split?
news.Content:
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) has been an up-and-down stock in 2026, and its latest announcement may just add more vigor to its oscillations: The company will enact a 2-for-1 stock split in January. However, this won't be your standard stock split, and it comes with nuances investors need to be aware of.

So, should you buy Meta's stock before the event arrives? After all, stocks often run up significantly when the market is waiting for them to split.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Meta's new Class C shares won't have voting rights

Meta's stock split isn't exactly standard. Instead of splitting its shares 2-for-1 outright, it's creating a new class of shares. For each pre-split Class A share an investor owns, they will be given one Class A share and one new Class C share. The A shares will have voting rights. The C shares won't. This may seem like an odd way to split the stock, but it's easy to see what Meta is trying to do. Meta has told investors that in the future, it will use C shares for employee compensation, acquisitions, and raising cash.

So, with each new C share issued, the shareholder base grows, but the new stock structure locks in majority voting power for CEO and founder Mark Zuckerberg. He already holds more than half the voting power thanks to the super-voting Class B shares that he owns 99.7% of -- those have 10 votes apiece. Now, he can further dilute his 13% financial stake in Meta by issuing more shares without diluting his control of it. He thus can continue to steer the company in any direction he wants without being concerned that the other shareholders might replace him, barring any malpractice.

Bearing in mind that Meta's stock split also locks the company into Zuckerberg's vision for the foreseeable future, the question of whether you should buy it now hinges on whether you trust his long-term vision. If you do, then this move makes a ton of sense. If you don't, now may be the time for you to get Meta's stock out of your portfolio.

However, Zuckerberg's current direction for the company has started to pay off, as its recently launched agentic AI app , Meta Muse, is seeing huge early adoption and could prove to be the very platform the company needs to start making some direct profits from all of its AI spending . Overall, Meta's business is still doing great, with revenue rising 26% year over year. So, Meta is still doing great as a company.

Story Continues

But because it's not yet clear what its path to monetizing AI will look like, the market is still viewing the stock with skepticism. This is reflected in its 1-year forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.

META PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

That's not a particularly high valuation for the company, especially considering the reaction the market has had since Meta reported its Q3 results. If you want to buy, now could be a prime opportunity because it's on sale. However, if you're not sure about Zuckerberg, it's time to move on, because he's about to lock in his majority voting power permanently.

news.Title: Intel Stock Faces a New Threat That No One Saw Coming
news.Content:
Intel (INTC) stock has been one of the wildest rides on Wall Street in 2026. Shares nearly quadrupled by June 2026. Then the bottom fell out. A brutal PC slowdown and a weak fourth-quarter guide erased billions in market value in days.

In simple terms, Intel stock plunged more than 49% over the past month. But a new risk is insinuating itself. The disaster for Trump was that the Democrats swept the midterm elections. Over on Wall Street, the companies that sold shares to the U.S. government may be subject to a new round of hearings and legal action.

More News from Barchart

How to Play SpaceX Stock after Democrats Sweep Midterm Elections

Oracle Just Walked Away From a $7 Billion Tencent Deal. Here's What It Means for ORCL Stock.

Dear Applied Materials Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 12

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

Intel's leading the way on that list. Uncle Sam's stake in the chipmaker, about 10%, goes to the government via an $8.9 billion purchase last year. The rally was the result of that support. It potentially could be a "headliner issue" now.

Potential questions about this investigation will be whether it is going to alter Intel's turnaround narrative or simply dampen down a very volatile stock.

Intel Stock Still Not Cheap

Despite the selloff, Intel's stock does not come in cheap. However, on some metrics it's below the sector median. Its forward price-to-book (P/B) ratio is 2.81 compared to the sector's 4.55, indicating INTC stock is less expensive on this measure.

On the other hand, the forward price-to-sales (P/S) is 5.21 versus 3.31 for the sector, and the forward P/E is 40.73 relative to 21.21 for the sector, suggesting INTC is generally expensive and trading at a premium in most other metrics.

Means, the stock looks cheaper on P/B, but that is a small consolation when the core business is still rebuilding profitability. This is a show-me story trading at a premium.

The Blue Wave Risk

The Democratic sweep puts a new page in the political math books of Washington. The new Congress starts in January. Already, Democrats have indicated they will seek stronger corporate regulation. Firms can be called to appear before hearings or investigations for their past dealings with the Trump administration, and each other.

The largest on that list is Intel. Questions have already been raised in a shareholder lawsuit about whether the Commerce Department had the legal authority to replace chip subsidies with equity. That lawsuit could throw the entirety of the government stake into question if it takes traction. Ultimately, the Commerce Department's scheme could go, but Intel would not. However, it would cause confusion to a major cornerstone of the bull's argument. Government support for Intel's foundry build-out is still required, and long-term planning will be more difficult due to political noise.

Story Continues

A Beat Shadowed by a Weak Guidance

Intel recently reported third-quarter 2026 results, and the headline numbers were strong, yet the stock plunged heavily due to a much weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter outlook, a dim PC market forecast, and persistent supply constraints.

Revenue came in at $16.5 billion, up 21% year-over-year (YoY). Adjusted earnings per share hit $0.52, up 126% from a year ago. Net income attributable to Intel was $3.3 billion, down 18% due to higher taxes and other items.

The data center and AI segment was the star. Revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion. Foundry revenue rose 58% to $6.7 billion. But the client computing business, which sells PC chips, fell 5% to $8.1 billion.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan was blunt about the split. "Despite near-term headwinds across the PC industry, demand for our CPUs remains robust, reinforcing our confidence in the long-term growth opportunities for our business," he said.

The problem was guidance. The company began with a warning for investors, with Intel warning that its fourth-quarter revenue will be $15.5 billion at the midpoint. Analysts were looking for $17.02 billion. The revised $0.25 EPS mark was off by more than four times the $0.44 consensus.

The company also generated $5.1 billion of cash from operations in the quarter and a cash balance of $54 billion at the end of the quarter. It's a shock absorber for that balance sheet. But the guidance scared off the market. INTC stock fell almost 29% the following day, hitting its lowest day since 1974.

What Wall Street Is Saying About INTC Stock

The analyst community seems divided, but most firms are staying on the sidelines. That's why the consensus rating sits at "Hold." But the price targets tell a different story.

Recently, Goldman Sachs slashed its target from $150 to $100. The firm kept a "Neutral" rating. It wants to see real foundry customer traction before getting more positive.

J.P. Morgan actually upgraded the stock to "Neutral" from "Underweight" in mid-October. The firm kept its $85 target. Analyst Harlan Sur said the risk-reward looks more balanced now that shares have pulled back 36% from June highs. He also credited CEO Lip-Bu Tan with improving execution in the core data center business.

BofA took the opposite path. Analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to "Neutral" from "Buy" right after the Q3 print. He cut the target from $145 to $100. Arya said the turnaround is pushed out because of PC and supply headwinds. He also said Intel "has not communicated enough traction with external foundry customers."

The average price target at all coverage is approximately $93.23. That means approximately a 64% upside based on the current price.

Furthermore, there was one important clue hidden within the CEO's recent trading activity. CEO Lip-Bu Tan bought $10 million worth of stock on the open market just days after the crash. He picked up 150,000 shares at prices between $64.70 and $64.74. That's not a ringing endorsement from Wall Street. But those are the words of faith from the person in the know.

news.Title: This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?
news.Content:
The "Magnificent Seven" is a grouping of stocks used to describe some of the largest companies in the world that have helped lead the U.S. stock market higher over the past decade. It is made up of:

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL)

Nvidia

Microsoft

Alphabet

Amazon

Meta Platforms

Tesla

For U.S.-listed stocks, all seven of these are in the top 10, so being on this list is a big deal. However, 2026 hasn't been the greatest year for the Magnificent Seven. The S&P 500 is up about 12.3% this year, and only three stocks are outperforming it: Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. But which one of these is doing the best? It's the non-AI one.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Apple leads all Magnificent Seven stocks

The top performer so far in 2026 has been Apple, up about 29%. That's practically double the second-best performer, Amazon, which has risen around 15%. So, what has separated Apple from the competition? I think there are two reasons.

First, Apple really isn't an AI stock . While its products have some AI features, it's not spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers like every other company on this list (besides Nvidia, which is selling the equipment for these data centers). As a whole, the market has been a bit bearish on the AI buildout lately, and Apple has been a haven for investors who aren't as keen on the long-term prospects of AI.

In fact, Apple is the only stock among the top 10 largest companies on U.S. exchanges that doesn't have significant AI investments or business cases riding on the AI buildout. This has made it a safe haven for non-AI investors and has boosted its stock.

Another reason Apple has done well this year is that its iPhone 17 lineup was the most popular of any of its previous models. This has driven sales growth and has made Apple a respectable business again.

However, Apple's day of reckoning could be coming. Outside of Tesla (which has a sky-high valuation of 424 times trailing earnings), Apple is by far the most expensive stock in the Magnificent Seven.

As a result, I think the stock could be getting a bit too pricey, and investors need to watch out. Apple's strong performance this year hasn't come entirely from business results, and if the market flips its stance on AI and becomes bullish on it again, Apple's stock could sell off in favor of some AI-focused investments. It's about as good as it gets for Apple sentiment right now. As a result, I don't think Apple stock is a buy right now.

news.Title: Why AI investors may favor established data-center owners
news.Content:
Investors in artificial intelligence may see the same sell-off across a wide group of stocks and assume the risk is evenly shared. James Demmert, who has worked in the investment industry for more than 35 years, argues that the data-center debate creates a more useful divide: Companies that already operate major data-center networks may be better positioned than businesses whose growth depends on building many more of them.

Demmert, chief investment officer at Main Street Research, favors putting new money into the broader AI trade, including semiconductors and major cloud operators. He places Alphabet and Amazon near the top of his Magnificent Seven ranking because their stocks have lagged despite healthy cloud results and because each already has substantial data-center capacity.

That strategy suits investors who are seeking long-term AI exposure, can tolerate volatility, and evaluate balance sheets. It is less suited for investors looking for short-term trades tied to data-center construction, where capital requirements can matter as much as demand for computing power.

Here is how Demmert, who spoke in an interview on Street Talk with TheStreet's Caroline Woods, separates established AI operators from more speculative data-center growth stories.

Note: The market musings expressed herein are those of the interviewed guest and should not be treated as professional investment advice. Readers should consult a certified financial planner (CFP) for individualized advice based on their available capital, goals, risk tolerance, and time horizon.

Why AI data-center fears can create a split market

The central worry is straightforward: AI companies are spending heavily on computing infrastructure, while investors question whether the eventual revenue will justify the investment. Demmert said strong results from cloud businesses at Microsoft , Amazon, and Alphabet haven't fully eased investor nerves. In his view, investors remain particularly focused on pressure surrounding Google Search rather than the cloud results that he described as strong.

That skepticism has weighed on valuations. Demmert said the semiconductor industry was trading at 15 times earnings, down from a multiple of 30 a year earlier. A price-to-earnings ratio compares a stock's price with its annual earnings; a lower multiple can make a stock look cheaper, but it doesn't guarantee that its price will rise.

The data center build-out problem, which I frankly think is completely overdone, I think that we can't slow that down if we want to keep up ahead of China.

Story Continues

Demmert's case rests on the idea that AI demand will continue to require more computing capacity and that the U.S. will have a strategic reason to keep building it. That is an investment view, not a certainty. His stated risk is that demand for electricity and data centers could slow more than expected, which would weigh especially heavily on companies tied to the power required for AI computing.

Why existing data centers may offer a safer AI route

Demmert distinguishes between companies that already own large data-center footprints and companies trying to acquire or build enough capacity to scale. He described Alphabet and Amazon as safer AI exposure because existing facilities can serve customers that need computing resources now. He still sees potential returns in faster-growing operators, but said investors must be prepared to wait through a few quarters of uncertainty.

However, there's a trade-off. Established operators may not offer the same upside as a smaller company that successfully expands quickly. Yet Demmert's framework puts financial durability first. A company that needs substantial new capacity must also finance that expansion, and a weak balance sheet can turn a favorable industry trend into a difficult stock-specific situation.

We love strong balance sheet companies, dominant market share, but the balance sheet there just is very concerning.

For instance, Demmert called CoreWeave a trap, citing its need for more data centers and balance-sheet concerns. His conclusion is a company-specific judgment, rather than a verdict on all newer AI infrastructure businesses. But it explains why a data-center theme should not be treated as a single bet: Owning capacity, needing capacity, and financing capacity are materially different positions. Coreweave's stock dropped about 40% in the year to date at the time of the interview.

How to build AI exposure without making one concentrated bet

For investors who want AI exposure, Demmert favors a quality-focused semiconductor group that includes Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices , Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, ASML Holding, and Micron Technology . While their specialties range from chip design and memory to fabrication equipment, all five provide the foundational hardware essential for AI computing.

Demmert is more cautious on the electrification trade, naming GE Vernova and Siemens Energy as companies whose performance could be vulnerable if power demand worsens. This caveat underscores a broader reality: the AI investment theme spans well beyond large technology stocks. Over-indexing to one vertical risks misdiagnosing where supply-chain constraints or execution disappointments will actually emerge.

Demmert adds a word of caution for investors loaded up on tech: Don't make AI your only bet. He sees viable opportunities across healthcare, energy, and financials, though he recommends waiting for pullbacks in energy and healthcare rather than buying at peak momentum. Diversification doesn't wipe away risk, but it cushions the blow if market expectations for AI fail to pan out.

The takeaway for AI investors weighing data-center risk

For your portfolio, first decide whether you want long-term exposure to established AI leaders, a more speculative position in emerging infrastructure providers, or both. Keep those roles separate. Demmert's approach favors dominant companies with existing capacity and durable finances over businesses that must raise capital to make their expansion plans work.

Then revisit the evidence as cloud results, capital spending, power demand, and balance sheets change. If your goal and time horizon support AI ownership, a diversified group of established operators and semiconductor suppliers may fit better than a single all-or-nothing data-center bet.
