news.Title: AI Stocks Are Falling; Bitcoin Is Holding Ground. Here's What Could Come Next.
news.Content:
It's been said that bull markets end when good news fails to boost prices, and that bear markets end when bad news fails to send prices lower. On that note, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) is 33.7% above its bear market lows in late June. Most of the high-flying artificial intelligence (AI) value-chain stocks, on the other hand -- including Intel , Oracle , Micron Technology , and Sandisk -- are down by between 20% and 62% in the same period.

There are plenty of good reasons for those stocks to be down. Yet aside from emerging factors like questionable future demand for some of the technologies those companies make, all of those players, as well as Bitcoin, have faced a constant onslaught of geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty this year. Their diverging prices amid those shared headwinds mean that one thing in particular could be coming next.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Bitcoin's floor hasn't collapsed yet

Bitcoin didn't just start shrugging off bad news in the last couple of months. On Sept. 15, the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, a bill intended to set rules for crypto market structures. It briefly fell below $75,000 that day, then recovered within weeks.

Then, October saw the Nasdaq Composite index fall more than 5%, as big spenders on AI failed to wow the market with their earnings reports as well as their future projections. Bitcoin dropped 10.3% in the 30-day period ending on Nov. 5, but it largely traded in a range: every daily close was between $76,198 and $84,082, regardless of what was happening in the world. That resilience had to face down a handful of problems that also weighed on tech stocks.

For instance, on Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve voted to hold interest rates steady, and the very next day's hot inflation data caused markets to expect a December hike. Rate hikes tend to be bad for risky assets like AI stocks and cryptocurrencies, as higher rates mean investors can earn a better return on low-risk Treasuries.

Before that, Brent crude oil prices climbed in October as the prospect of continued war with Iran contributed to a highly uncertain environment. Uncertainty tends to weigh on riskier assets, and rising energy costs drive inflation, which might prompt the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates further.

Story Continues

As if that wasn't enough, hackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto exchange, on Oct. 29, in what was the largest crypto hack to date. Such hacks tend to make investors skittish about investing in digital currency, and for good reason.

U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds saw $643.3 million in net outflows on Oct. 30. But even after, the token's price didn't do much. And even if investors are skittish about buying it, they don't appear to be dumping their coins.

That suggests great things could be ahead for Bitcoin in the coming quarters.

How much bad news could be left?

Besides the above, Bitcoin is facing down at least a couple more problems right now. Congress will switch over from Republican control to Democratic control in 2027. Democrats are traditionally considered to be less favorable to crypto. Though that characterization isn't entirely fair (historically, digital coins and other cryptocurrencies have performed well under both parties), it is still a factor influencing investor psychology and likely keeping at least some capital sidelined.

In the longer term, the coin is, in theory, vulnerable to its encryption being broken by quantum computers. Those computers might not exist until the early 2030s, but some investors, like Charles Edwards of Capriole Investments, argue that the unaddressed risk of a future quantum-enabled breach is already substantially depressing the coin's price.

On paper, that's a lot of reasons not to own Bitcoin. Yet people keep holding it and buying it for their crypto portfolios.

The bad news didn't crater its price back to bear market lows. Nor is the credible threat of more bad news seriously damaging its price. Especially when viewed against the ongoing decline in AI stocks, this state of affairs suggests there's a reasonable chance Bitcoin will climb once the headlines ease.

After all, it tends to be pretty good news for holders when an asset keeps refusing to make new lows despite bad news.

news.Title: Prediction: Here's What a $1,000 Investment in Rivian Will Be Worth by 2030 if the R2 Ramp Holds
news.Content:
Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) hasn't exactly been hiding the fact that it is using Tesla 's (NASDAQ: TSLA) playbook. And the R2 is a significant step along the path Tesla blazed. Which is why it is such good news that the R2 is now Rivian's best-selling vehicle. If Tesla is the example, investors could see Rivian's stock price rocket by as much as 1,000% if the good news keeps rolling in.

But through 2030, more modest expectations are probably appropriate. Here's why I think Rivian's stock could double or even triple over the next three years or so.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What's going on with Rivian?

Like Tesla, Rivian started out by producing a high-end all-electric vehicle . The R1 truck was well received and won multiple awards. However, the volume was so low that the company lost money on every truck it sold. This is why the second step was to ramp up production, again, just like Tesla. That process went relatively well, leading to Rivian generating a gross profit.

A gross profit simply means that it made more money selling its trucks than it cost to make them. There are other costs to running a business, like selling, general, and administrative expenses and research and development costs. Achieving a gross profit was a huge step, but Rivian was still losing money as a business. That's where the R2 comes in.

To be a sustainably profitable company, Rivian needs to increase the number of cars it sells. That will allow it to spread its costs over more vehicles. However, the high-end of the market is limited, so Rivian needs a successful mass-market vehicle that costs less. That's what it was looking to create in the R2. It delivered, with the new vehicle helping to increase deliveries by 46% year over year in the third quarter of 2026. The R2 was Rivian's most popular model. This is a huge win.

What comes next for Rivian?

Rivian is clearly pleased with its results, but it is also realistic. High demand for the R2 is good, but it still needs to produce more vehicles. That means more capital spending is in the cards as the automaker continues to invest to expand its manufacturing capabilities. To that end, the company is building a new auto plant in Georgia. It probably won't be up and running until late 2028.

So, in the near term, the start-up is likely to continue to bleed red ink. Until it is sustainably profitable, stock gains will likely be limited. But each step closer to the end goal could see investors reward Rivian with a higher stock price. And, assuming the Georgia plant investment goes well, it isn't unreasonable to believe that Rivian could be sustainably profitable by the end of the decade or early in the 2030s.

Story Continues

TSLA data by YCharts

Tesla's stock rose as it neared profitability and then took off like a rocket after it became sustainably profitable. If the same trend were to occur with Rivian, it isn't unreasonable to believe the stock could double or triple by 2030. That would turn a $1,000 investment into $2,000 to $4,000. Even more gains could be on tap thereafter.

Only for aggressive growth investors

That said, Rivian is really only appropriate for more aggressive growth investors. The story sounds good, but a lot could still go wrong. Notably, the R2 is a very new vehicle, and consumer enthusiasm around the product might cool off. That could turn this huge opportunity into a massive bust, which is why more conservative investors should probably stay away. However, if you believe in the Rivian story, the upstart continues to hit the big-picture milestones that propelled Tesla to massive success.

news.Title: 3 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks I’d Buy Without Hesitation in a Market Crash
news.Content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) isn't just a fad. The technology is reshaping the world, and many corporations are helping power this revolution. However, investors chasing life-changing returns have bid up shares of many AI companies, some of which, despite having highly promising prospects, have become too expensive.

In fact, the entire market is arguably overvalued, at least as measured by metrics such as the S&P 500 Shiller CAPE ratio, which is near its highest levels since before the dot-com bubble burst. We may eventually experience a bear market as a result, and if we do, there are three stocks I can't wait to buy on the dip: Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV). Here is why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

1. Space Exploration Technologies

Space Exploration Technologies is best known for revolutionizing space travel . The company helped pioneer reusable rocket technology, thereby significantly reducing launch costs. However, SpaceX's AI business, which it recently renamed Super Intelligence (SI), has arguably been more impressive than its space business since it went public in June.

In the third quarter, SpaceX's revenue increased by 161% year over year to $14.6 billion. Space revenue grew 6% year over year to $1.8 billion, while SI revenue soared 830% year over year to $7.6 billion. The company's connectivity revenue was $5.2 billion, up 69.5% year over year.

So, SI now accounts for more than half of the company's revenue and is growing much faster than other business segments. It is also profitable. SI operating income for the period was $431 million, significantly better than the operating loss of $1.7 billion reported in the year-ago period.

SpaceX's space business isn't profitable, though its connectivity business is. But SI could remain the main growth driver, as SpaceX is experiencing outstanding demand for AI compute capacity.

However, the stock remains fairly expensive -- it is trading at 50.8x forward earnings, and there is significant uncertainty ahead, including with the company's development of its next-gen rocket , Starship, which could support many of its AI-related ambitions.

The business looks promising, but it is too risky at current levels. If the stock falls at least 25%, I'd buy without a second thought.

Story Continues

2. CoreWeave

CoreWeave, a neocloud company, is also seeing booming demand for its services. Second-quarter revenue grew 112.5% year over year to $2.6 billion, while its revenue backlog was $104 billion, up 245.5% compared to the year-ago period. The problem is that CoreWeave is spending significant sums to keep purchasing AI infrastructure.

The company's debt has ballooned as a result, while operating and net losses are worsening year over year. In the second quarter, CoreWeave posted an operating loss of $49 million, down from the operating income of $19 million reported in the year-ago period. Its net loss per share widened to $1.14, compared with $0.60 per share in the prior-year quarter.

CoreWeave has raised more than $30 billion this year. Perhaps that won't be a problem for the company as long as AI spending continues to grow unabated. But if it doesn't, the company could be in trouble.

My view is that CoreWeave is an attractive AI stock, but the mounting debt and customer concentration -- a single customer accounted for 67% of its revenue in 2025 -- leave little room for error at current levels. Investors with an appetite for risk may still consider initiating a small position in the company, but I'd feel even more comfortable doing so if the stock loses 15% to 20%.

3. Tesla

Tesla is a different kind of AI company. It doesn't offer AI compute capacity like CoreWeave and SpaceX, but the technology has become central to its future. Tesla has several AI-heavy projects, including its robotaxi and humanoid robot ambitions. AI helps the company train its self-driving vehicles, and it could also allow Tesla to improve its Optimus robots.

There might be a large market in both cases. Provided Optimus robots are as advanced as Tesla wants them to be, they could be in high demand in factories and warehouses and eventually make their way into the home.

Meanwhile, Tesla's robotaxi business could generate significant profits at scale. However, there is plenty of uncertainty. Regulators will have their say in both markets, and the public may not adopt these technologies to the extent Tesla hopes. Could the business still perform well over the long run?

Absolutely, but to be as sure as possible that I'd earn juicy returns, I'd like to buy the stock at a much lower price -- Tesla is currently trading at 163.2x forward earnings. I'd happily initiate a position in a bear market.

news.Title: Analysts Just Sounded the Alarm on These 5 Overhyped Stocks
news.Content:
Wall Street had a rough week, and the damage came fast. Thursday's sell-off erased $2.3 trillion in market value, pushed the Nasdaq into a correction and sent the VIX, the market's fear gauge, up 70% to 28, Yahoo Finance reported on November 6. A chip-sector index that plunged 12% on Thursday bounced 4% the next day, and oil fell below $100 a barrel.

Politics added to the swings. The Dow roared back on Wednesday after the midterm results removed election uncertainty, and oil fell on hopes of a deal with Iran, according to Yahoo Finance on November 5, though the rally was already cooling.

Interest rates became the bigger worry. Payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, far above the 65,000 economists expected, while unemployment slipped to 4.1% from 4.2%, Reuters reported on November 6.

Hot Jobs Data Raises the Odds of a Rate Hike

Traders read the numbers as a sign the Federal Reserve is not done tightening. Bets on a rate hike at the next meeting rose to 78% from 70% before the report, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.87%. The 30-year yield reached 5.27%.

Chief market economist Peter Cardillo said the labor market is at full employment and that the Fed has no choice but to raise rates in December. Chief investment strategist Susannah Streeter called the report hawkish and said she sees a couple of hikes before late next year, depending on the Iran conflict. Chief economic strategist Brian Jacobsen noted that wages rose 3.1% from a year earlier, yet real wages fell as inflation outpaced them, which he called the affordability crisis in one stat.

What Past Fear Spikes Have Meant for Stocks

Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi pointed to CBOE data showing eight earlier VIX jumps of this size since 1991. The S&P 500 gained an average of 3.0% one month later and 14.7% one year later. Our list of oversold AI stocks where Wall Street analysts are spotting 50%+ upside covers names that have been through a similar reset.

Hiring itself looks steady. Andy Challenger, who tracks corporate job cuts, called the current climate a "low-fire environment," with employers holding on to workers ahead of the holidays, according to Yahoo Finance on November 5.

Not everyone sees a hike as certain. Joe Saluzzi, co-head of equity trading at a New Jersey firm, called the jobs numbers very good but said the recent volatility could lead the Fed to hold off at its next meeting. Readers who follow the market's leaders can see our ranking of the best stocks near all-time highs according to Wall Street .

Story Continues

Click to continue reading and see the expanded list of Analysts Just Sounded the Alarm on These 10 Overhyped Stocks . The top 5 stocks are shared below:

Computer with charts

Our Methodology

To compile this list, we reviewed news coverage and financial websites for analyst downgrades published over the past 20 days. From the stocks that came up, we picked 10 and ranked them in descending order of average upside potential, based on analysts' average price target, as of November 6, 2026. We also list each stock's number of hedge fund holders as of Q2 2026, from our database of 1,006 hedge funds.

Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points ( see more details here ).

Analysts Just Sounded the Alarm on These 5 Overhyped Stocks

5. Fidelity National Information Services (NYSE:FIS)

Average Upside Potential: 26%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 49

J.P. Morgan downgraded Fidelity National Information Services to Neutral from Overweight on November 4 and cut its price target to $38 from $53, citing the company's financial guidance and its chief financial officer's exit. The cash numbers behind the stock tell a steadier story.

CEO Stephanie Ferris said client demand remains strong. Adjusted free cash flow was $862 million in the third quarter, up 8.0%. For the full year, the company expects free cash flow of $2.15 billion to $2.25 billion, a gain of 33% to 39%.

That cash is going toward lowering debt. FIS paused buybacks and small acquisitions to speed up the process and expects to resume meaningful repurchases once leverage reaches its target level. Even so, it returned $248 million to shareholders in the quarter, mostly through dividends. Adjusted earnings per share rose 6.6% to $1.61.

Ferris said investments in security and innovation will build a more recurring, predictable revenue base. The company is also tidying its portfolio. It recently sold a non-core prepaid business in banking, and its strategic review of the rest of the business is still underway.

4. HubSpot (NYSE:HUBS)

Average Upside Potential: 15%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 51

Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Matthew Vanvliet downgraded HubSpot to Underweight from Neutral on November 5 and cut his price target to $170 from $265. The quarter just reported had still beaten Wall Street's numbers.

Analysts expected HubSpot to earn $3.28 a share. It earned $3.81 on an adjusted basis, the Associated Press reported, while revenue of $947.6 million beat the $924.5 million forecast. Net profit came to $83 million, or $1.67 a share.

The beat fits a long record of growth. HubSpot's revenue has grown 28.81% a year over the past five years, and the software it sells keeps most of each sales dollar after the cost of delivering it.

The price looks modest next to that record. HubSpot trades at 15.41 times forward earnings, compared with 18.86 for its sector, and sits 83.99% below its own five-year average, on adjusted figures. For the fourth quarter, the company guided adjusted earnings of $3.85 to $3.87 a share. Bulls see a software company with a long growth record that now trades below its sector's multiple. We recently looked at how HubSpot's rising AI adoption could turn into revenue growth .

3. Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE)

Average Upside Potential: 9%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 81

Citigroup downgraded Adobe to Sell from Neutral on November 4, with a price target of $207. The call sits against a quarter in which the company's AI products grew fast.

CEO Shantanu Narayen called passing one billion monthly active users a defining moment for Adobe. That audience is the base for its AI products, and AI-first annual recurring revenue grew more than 150% from a year earlier.

The core business is growing too. Third-quarter revenue hit a record $6.76 billion, up 13%, and Adobe raised its full-year revenue and earnings targets, with non-GAAP earnings per share now expected between $24.45 and $24.50. Narayen said the quarter reflected the strength of the company's AI innovation.

Total annual recurring revenue exited the quarter at $27.50 billion, so the AI products are growing from a large base. Remaining performance obligations, the revenue Adobe has signed up but not yet recognized, are mostly due within a year, about two-thirds of the total. Adobe also bought back about 9.5 million of its own shares in the quarter. The market's worry about AI is the focus of our look at whether the fear around Adobe is overdone .

2. Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL)

Average Upside Potential: -1%

Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 169

DZ Bank downgraded Apple to Sell from Hold on November 4, with a price target of $300. The call came days after a record quarter, and the numbers behind the company stayed strong.

Apple's installed base now tops 2.5 billion active devices, Yahoo Finance reported, and that base is why the company can post records at its size. In the September quarter, revenue rose 12% to $114.5 billion, a record for that quarter, and iPhone sales set a September-quarter record as well.

Apple returned $28 billion to shareholders in the quarter. Services revenue hit an all-time high, giving the company a growing stream of income from devices already sold. Active devices reached a record in every major product category and every geographic segment, and CFO Kevan Parekh said Apple set September-quarter records for net income and earnings per share. He guided December-quarter revenue growth of 7% to 10%.

John Ternus, who recently took over as CEO from Tim Cook, pointed to the iPhone Duo and a new line of home hardware as what comes next. Whether longer ownership can still raise profit per customer is the question in our piece on Apple's iPhone economics .

Sales are steadier where Nike has focused. Wholesale, its largest channel, brought in $6.8 billion, down just 1%, with North America growing even as Greater China declined. Hill said the push around sport-specific products is driving measurable progress in its performance business, and the company says momentum continued across the sports it has chosen to prioritize, which Hill calls the Sport Offense.

Nike also returned about $610 million through dividends, up 3% from a year earlier. A dividend that keeps growing during a rebuild tells investors management believes the cash flow can support it. We also asked whether Nike's turnaround is worth betting on .

news.Title: Elon Musk Wants to Build an "Enormous Robot Army." Here's What That Means for Tesla and SpaceX Investors.
news.Content:
Last year, Elon Musk stressed his priority of regaining majority voting control over Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA). His biggest concern at the time was control over new products -- humanoid robots , in particular -- that Tesla is expected to produce en masse over the coming years.

"My fundamental concern with regard to how much voting control I have in Tesla is: If I go ahead and build this enormous robot army, can I just be ​ousted at some point in the future?" Musk told investors last October.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Whether investors agree with Musk's concern or not, it is clear that he seeks majority control over Tesla's daily operations. This has one major implication for shareholders of both Tesla and SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX).

A SpaceX and Tesla merger may not be in the interest of shareholders

While a merger between SpaceX and Tesla has not been formally announced, speculation of a potential tie-up has risen sharply after the companies launched independent committees focused on exploring the benefits of a merger.

Musk's negotiated pay package at Tesla originally included key milestones that would trigger additional stock grants, including the deployment of one million humanoid robots. But some experts are claiming that Musk's ambitious "enormous robot army" is a distraction from his true goal.

"It's irrelevant," Charles Elson, ​founding director of the Weinberg Center, told Reuters this week. "This package is a distraction from the real story, which is complete control."

Musk's pay package with SpaceX grants him additional voting power before the shares are even issued. Incorporating the new pay package, Musk now has approximately 85% voting power at SpaceX. With roughly 20% voting power at Tesla, a tie-up between the two companies could ultimately give Musk majority control over the combined entity.

SpaceX's IPO prospectus was replete with bold long-term plans. Tesla, meanwhile, is working to sustain its lofty valuation with promises of robot armies and ubiquitous self-driving cars. Investors, however, should look deeper into these claims, understanding that a mega-merger between Tesla and SpaceX may have more to do with Musk's economic incentives than the best interests of shareholders.

news.Title: These 4 Stocks Are Tied to the Smartphone in Your Pocket
news.Content:
Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM), Corning (NYSE:GLW), and Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) each collect a share of the money spent on smartphones. Apple sells the phone. Qualcomm supplies chips and patent licenses, Corning makes the glass over the screen, and Arm's chip designs turn up in almost all smartphones.

But their latest quarterly reports all vary meaningfully. Apple's iPhone revenue climbed 17% year over year in the September quarter, while Qualcomm's handset chip revenue dropped 26%. And Corning and Arm both said a softer smartphone market hurt their results.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

All four also pointed to the same pressure: memory chips have become much pricier. But I think it matters really differently for each stock.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Apple's iPhone is still growing

Apple makes much more money from the phone than the other three do. iPhone sales were around $254 billion for fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 26. That was 53% of Apple's revenue and 21% more than a year earlier.

But growth is slowing. iPhone revenue climbed 17% year over year to $57.6 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, after gaining around 22% in fiscal Q3. And excluding the benefit of tariff refunds, Apple's gross margin dipped about one point from the June quarter. Management sees it coming in between 45% and 46% in the holiday quarter, mainly because of memory costs.

At roughly $347 as of this writing, Apple trades at about 36 times its expected fiscal 2027 earnings . Investors are paying a premium as its margins fall.

2. Qualcomm's handset slide is getting steeper

Qualcomm's phone business is going the other way. Its handset chip revenue dropped 26% year over year to around $5.1 billion in its fiscal fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 27. It had risen 3% in fiscal Q1, then dropped 13% in Q2 and 20% in Q3. For the full fiscal year, Qualcomm blamed lower shipments to some major phone makers, which cut their build plans as memory got scarcer and pricier.

And Qualcomm expects Apple to rely mostly on its own modems from now on, a change it warns will significantly hit its chip sales.

Of course, Qualcomm still collects from the phone through its patents. It renewed its long-term license with Apple, and licensing kept 70% of its revenue as pre-tax profit in the quarter, versus 24% for the chip business. Meanwhile, auto chip revenue surged 89% to nearly $2 billion.

Story Continues

At roughly $150, Qualcomm trades at about 15 times the earnings it's expected to report in fiscal 2027. I'd say the price already assumes the handset business keeps shrinking.

3. Corning: the glass is the smaller business

Corning's links with Apple stretch back almost 20 years.

"By the end of 2026, all the cover glass for iPhone, including iPhone Duo, and Apple Watch, sold worldwide will be produced at our Harrodsburg, Kentucky facility," chief financial officer Ed Schlesinger said on Corning's Oct. 27 earnings call.

Phone glass, though, is in Corning's glass innovations segment, which also sells glass for TVs and laptops. Segment sales slipped 3% in the third quarter, to about $1.5 billion, and segment net income slid 10%.

Optical communications, meanwhile, grew sales 44% to around $2.4 billion, and Corning's sales linked to generative AI more than doubled. With shares near $104, Corning trades at about 23 times next year's expected earnings, a price I think largely depends on fiber.

4. A royalty on nearly every phone

About 43% of Arm's royalties in the fiscal year ended March 31 came from the main smartphone processors.

In the September quarter, royalty revenue dropped to $670 million, down from $715 million three months earlier, and grew just 8% year over year. Arm said memory prices hit the smartphone market, partly offsetting a doubling in data center royalties.

Around $166 as of this writing, Arm stock trades at about 55 times expected earnings for fiscal 2028, which for Arm ends in March 2028. Investors are probably paying that premium for the data center, where Arm expects Arm-based chips to make up more than 60% of the server market at the largest cloud providers by the end of 2026.

The one I'd own for the phone

Ultimately, of the four, only Apple reported growing phone sales last quarter.

Sure, about 36 times expected earnings isn't cheap, and memory costs might pressure Apple's margins for a while. But Apple sets the device's price, and it raised iPhone prices in September. Qualcomm is much cheaper, but its handset revenue is still falling.

For the phone itself, I'd consider buying Apple.

news.Title: Here's Where I Think Intel Stock Will Be at the End of 2030
news.Content:
Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock has given back a huge part of its 2026 gains. Shares ended at $60.55 on Nov. 3, around 57% under the $140.94 they ended at on June 22. The stock dropped 45% in October alone.

My estimate for $5,000 put into Intel stock at that price is around $5,400 when 2030 ends. That'd be a gain of less than 10% in a bit more than four years, or under 2% a year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What surprised me is that this number assumes Intel's business does well. My estimate has Intel more than doubling its earnings per share from this year to 2030.

Most of what keeps the result down is how much investors pay for Intel's earnings today.

Image source: Intel.

Intel's profits have bounced back fast

Showing how quickly the business has turned, Intel's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share grew from $0.29 in the first quarter of 2026 to $0.42 in the second quarter and $0.52 in the third. A year before, in the third quarter of 2025, it was just $0.23. If Intel meets its fourth-quarter forecast of $0.25, its adjusted earnings per share for all of 2026 would total around $1.48 -- more than triple the $0.42 it made in 2025.

Intel's server chips are doing most of the work. Data center and AI segment revenue jumped 78% year over year to $7.3 billion in the third quarter, the segment's fastest growth in 15 years.

But that fourth-quarter forecast is a big drop from the third quarter, and PCs are the main reason. Intel expects PC unit sales industrywide to shrink around 12% this year. And it's planning for about another 10% decline in 2027. It doesn't expect PC sales to rebound for good until memory supplies improve and prices start to normalize.

What might Intel earn in 2030?

Intel's revenue may hit around $62 billion in 2026 if fourth-quarter sales land at the midpoint of its $15 billion to $16 billion forecast. This would be up about 17% over $52.9 billion in 2025.

Say revenue rises about 10% a year from there. This puts 2030 sales around $90 billion, over Intel's all-time high of $79 billion in 2021.

In the third quarter, Intel kept about 17 cents per revenue dollar as adjusted net income ($2.8 billion on $16.5 billion of revenue). I've assumed that grows to 20 cents by 2030. That's still under the more than 25 cents Intel kept in 2021. And it arguably leaves room for a foundry business that reported a $1.9 billion operating loss in the third quarter.

Story Continues

Intel's fourth-quarter forecast also assumes around 5.44 billion diluted shares, reflecting the $23 billion of new stock it sold in August. I've rounded that up to around 5.5 billion to allow for a bit more dilution.

In all, the estimate is around $18 billion of adjusted net income in 2030, or about $3.25 a share. That means Intel would earn more than twice the $1.48 it's on track to earn this year.

Investors are paying up for the rebound

Of course, the stock isn't priced like a company making $1.48 a share. At $60.55, Intel stock trades at around 41 times earnings, using this year's likely total. It's also at about 33 times expected 2027 earnings.

I've assumed investors pay 20 times earnings at the end of 2030. That could seem stingy for a company growing so fast.

But Intel stock ended 2021 at $51.50, or around 9 times earnings, as Intel made $5.47 a share that year on an adjusted basis. Investors have paid much less for Intel's profits before, even in a record sales year.

At 20 times earnings of $3.25 a share, Intel stock would be worth around $65 at the end of 2030. That's where the $5,400 comes from.

Plus, Intel suspended its dividend in 2024, so the stock price is the whole return.

Yes, Intel might beat my numbers. Intel says its immediate priority is unlocking more supply to meet what it calls extraordinary demand for its Xeon server chips. And a major outside customer for Intel's plants might boost the foundry business faster than I've assumed.

But even a bigger, more profitable Intel may not make up for paying around 41 times earnings today. Ultimately, I think the stock looks more interesting closer to $44 a share, where the same estimate comes to about 10% a year.

news.Title: Is Google's New Cryptocurrency Push a Reason to Buy Alphabet Stock?
news.Content:
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is expanding in crypto via a cryptocurrency custody service for financial institutions that it previewed on Oct. 28. Separately, on Oct. 30, the Binance crypto exchange, the world's largest, said that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from its coffers -- the kind of loss Google says its service is designed to reduce.

Given the obvious and escalating need for secure crypto custody solutions amid widespread, ongoing cybersecurity challenges worldwide, will this be a new reason to buy Alphabet's stock?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What Google is building

The new platform is called Multi-Party Compute (MPC), and it aims to provide more secure custody of cryptoassets by splitting each private key (the code that grants control of a crypto wallet) into several fragments.

Separate, isolated computer systems, which can include servers at rival cloud computing companies , then hold those fragments. Then, before any funds can be spent, Google's system evaluates whether the spending complies with the owner's rules and approves the transaction only if everything checks out.

At launch, MPC will support the transaction signing methods used by Ethereum and Solana , among other cryptoassets, and Alphabet already uses the system to protect its own assets stored on both chains. MPC adds to Google's earlier crypto work, including Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL), a private blockchain launched in 2025.

At first glance, there isn't much to get excited about here for Alphabet shareholders or those considering buying its stock.

There are many existing crypto custody businesses, including those with similar security schemes, and a plethora of blockchains vying for adoption by financial institutions. What's more, it isn't clear that the Google brand is especially valuable or appealing for offering crypto products, so this launch alone shouldn't push anyone to invest in Google stock .

It's hard to make a dent in a top line that's this large

The bigger reason Google's new cryptocurrency efforts are unlikely to be meaningful for shareholders is that the existing revenue base is already so large that it'll be nearly impossible to push it significantly higher.

Google Cloud's Q3 2026 revenue was $30.7 billion, accounting for 24.1% of Alphabet's $127.6 billion total revenue. Assuming MPC brought in $1 billion in 2027, when it's expected to launch, that would equal just 0.8% of Google Cloud's annualized revenue, and a tiny sliver of the company's top line as a whole. Of course, in time that story could change, but again, with so many competitors in the target market, it's hard to see how that would work out given the service's current description and vision.

Story Continues

So, while there's still a strong case for buying and holding Alphabet stock given its other businesses and sources of income, the new crypto push probably shouldn't factor into investors' decisions here.

news.Title: Better Stock Split to Buy: Meta Platforms vs. Sandisk
news.Content:
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) and Sandisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) are each going through a stock split over the next few months. Sandisk is going through a traditional stock split, splitting its shares eight-for-one, effective Nov. 19. Meta's is a bit different. Instead of doing a traditional stock split of its existing stock, it's creating a new share class. This complicates things, but it's still going through a split at the end of the day.

So, which one makes the most sense to invest in? Let's take a look.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Meta's stock split is unique

First, let's look at what's going on with Meta's stock. Its stock split is a bit goofy, but makes sense in the end. Overall, it's splitting its stock essentially two-for-one. It's doing this by creating a new Class C share. Class C shares will have the same value as Class A shares (the same ones any investor can buy on the market) initially, but in practice they will be worth slightly less over the long term.

The difference between Class C and Class A shares is that the new Class C shares have no voting power. This is important for Meta because, as it hands out Class C shares for acquisitions or employee compensation, CEO Mark Zuckerberg doesn't lose his voting control. This could be a red flag for some investors, but it's the direction that Meta is heading.

If you look at other stocks with split-share structures, like Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), one share class trades at a discount to the other, but it's not a big enough price difference to be a big deal. So, if you're fine with the voting power of the company residing in the founder's hands, then this is nothing more than your run-of-the-mill two-for-one stock split. But if you're concerned about where Mark Zuckerberg is taking Meta, then it may be time to abandon ship.

For the remainder of the analysis, I'll assume that the average investor is OK with Zuckerberg's controlling power. But even with that, is it enough to be a better stock to own than Sandisk?

Sandisk and Meta have two widely different growth rates

Sandisk and Meta aren't even close to being in the same industry. The closest relationship is Meta being a customer of Sandisk's, as it would buy solid-state drives (SSDs) from Sandisk for its data centers. Sandisk makes these devices, which have been in short supply due to the intensity of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. This has caused prices on these units to soar, and Sandisk has experienced huge growth as a result. During its latest quarter, revenue soared 378% year over year. That's simply incredible, and trumps anything Meta has delivered.

Story Continues

During Meta's Q3, its revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion. That's pretty fast among the big tech companies, but with how much Meta is spending on AI, investors want to see more. Still, this is a respectable result, and some of Meta's latest AI initiatives, such as Meta Muse, have received positive feedback and have seen heavy use. This could be a sign that Meta is headed in the right direction, and lead to better returns down the road.

Each stock is doing well in its industry, but there's still a huge piece of the puzzle missing: valuation. Sandisk is far cheaper than Meta, but that's because the market is concerned about a cyclical downturn in the industry once demand isn't as rampant.

SNDK PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts

With Sandisk growing rapidly and being priced so cheaply, I think it's the stock that I want to buy and hold right now . However, you'll have to keep a close eye on it to make sure that market conditions don't shift in the memory chip industry. If you're looking for a more set-it-and-forget-it type investment, then Meta makes more sense, as it's still in a great position to profit from the AI arms race if it continues to see success as it has in recent months.

news.Title: 5 Best Stocks To Buy According to Billionaire Armitage
news.Content: John Armitage has managed money since the early 1980s, and the record behind his firm is the reason investors keep an eye on his filings. He started Egerton Capital in London in 1994 with William Bollinger, after a career at Morgan Grenfell that began in 1981. There he ran a unit trust for six years that beat its index by 10% a year and ranked first among 85 funds, which gave him the confidence to go alone. Egerton runs a concentrated, long-biased book. Its third-quarter 13F lists 23 holdings worth $9.82 billion, and the five largest account for 52.4% of that total. Pricing Power, Realistic Managers and Valuation Discipline Armitage laid out his philosophy in a podcast hosted by Nicolai Tangen, who worked for him for five years before running Norges Bank Investment Management. His first question about any idea is whether it is worth the time, since many businesses are fairly priced, and the second is whether he can understand it. He prizes pricing power, the ability to raise prices despite competition, because a company that outpaces its own cost inflation achieves structurally rising margins. He also watches incremental margins, since a high margin on extra sales can swing profit sharply when revenue beats or misses. The balance sheet gets the same attention as the income statement, from inventories to receivables. He wants managers who admit their mistakes and distrusts those who always present a rosy picture or lean on accounting choices to look better. Valuation matters to him, perhaps too much, he admits, because it has made him miss many great growth stocks. He dismisses enterprise value to EBITDA as meaningless because depreciation is a real cost. Readers who want to compare his style with another long-horizon manager can read our ranking of the stocks favored by a different billionaire's fund . Recent Returns Lag the Market, but the Long Record Holds Up He builds positions slowly, starting small and adding as conviction grows, and he usually trims after a disappointment because he prefers confirmation of a thesis to contradiction. At the firm, two people must love an idea before it becomes large, and he prefers thematic diversification to heavy concentration. Schroders manages the Schroder GAIA Egerton Equity fund, which Egerton oversees. Its euro accumulation share class returned 19.0% in 2025, ahead of 18.4% for the MSCI World index, after gaining 20.4% in 2024 against 21.0% for the index. Through the end of September this year it returned 1.8%, while its comparator gained 12.4%. Over three years it has compounded at 15.4% annually, and since its November 2009 launch at 7.9%. Story Continues Schroders called the quarter's stock selection poor, as a violent tech selloff, rising bond yields and a market narrowed to artificial intelligence worked against a diversified book. Armitage told Tangen he stuck to his valuation numbers rather than chase the crowd, which he called lucky. On technology, he dislikes the market's concentration in AI but calls it very powerful, and he wants it to help his team rather than think for them. Investors following that theme can also browse AI picks across two other billionaire portfolios . He also cautions that concentration is marvelous when it goes right and a disaster when it goes wrong, and says he dislikes financial leverage because longs and shorts can both move against a fund at the same time. We shared the expanded list of 10 Best Stocks To Buy According to Billionaire Armitage here . You can find the top 5 stocks below. John Armitage of Egerton Capital Our Methodology For this article, we took the 10 largest holdings in the Q3 2026 13F filing of Egerton Capital, the hedge fund led by billionaire John Armitage, and ranked them in ascending order of Egerton's stake value, as of November 7, 2026. We also list the number of shares held and each stock's percentage of Egerton's portfolio. Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points ( see more details here ). 5 Best Stocks To Buy According to Billionaire Armitage 5. Moody's (NYSE:MCO) Stake Value: $743.52 million Number of Shares: 1,637,246 Percentage of Portfolio: 7.57% Moody's appeared in a Schroders monthly update as a detractor, with the fund citing the potential for reduced debt issuance as interest rates rose. The comment captures the stock's central sensitivity. A large part of the ratings agency's revenue comes when companies and governments borrow in the bond market, and higher yields give borrowers a reason to wait or to borrow less. The company has two engines, though. Its ratings business earns fees tied to issuance, while a second unit sells data, analytics and research on subscription, giving it a steadier revenue base that is less exposed to the borrowing cycle. A rate-driven slowdown in issuance therefore tests only part of the business. Armitage has said that cyclical exposure is important to get right, because a cyclical company often looks its best just before a downturn. For a holding like this, the question is how much of the earnings stream depends on market conditions, and the answer shifts with the mix between ratings and analytics and with how quickly borrowers return once yields settle. Moody's push into private credit is the focus of our analysis of whether it can build a durable subscription business . 4. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) Stake Value: $854.59 million Number of Shares: 3,741,971 Percentage of Portfolio: 8.7% Armitage bought Nvidia early this year after missing its first big move, and it has grown into a top-ten holding. Two developments changed his mind. Evidence of real AI value had built up, including Anthropic adding $5 billion of annualized revenue in six weeks, and the shares had de-rated from 35 times forward earnings to 23 times. He told Nicolai Tangen that he is neither a physicist nor a coder, but wants to feel he can understand why Nvidia might succeed. That means working through its economics. Memory cost inflation matters because of its effect on the bill of materials at a company earning gross margins near three-quarters. His thesis rests on supply. Demand exceeds supply through 2027, management guides to strong sales growth next year, and he expects its share of AI chip spending to slip only gradually. He regards the circular financing around customers as rational and carefully sized. At about 15 times estimated 2027 earnings, he calls the valuation highly attractive. Beyond data centers, a look at how Nvidia is using AI growth to expand in autonomous driving covers a newer growth path. 3. Amphenol (NYSE:APH) Stake Value: $902.74 million Number of Shares: 10,708,713 Percentage of Portfolio: 9.19% Armitage calls Amphenol a brilliant company that supplies into Nvidia, and he named it when asked how Egerton takes part in the AI boom. He said he does not like the concentration of the market in AI but finds it very powerful, and that so much of the US economy now keys off it that every portfolio ends up holding more of it than its manager expects. The stock has been a regular contributor to the fund's results. It helped in the first quarter and again in June, and it was the top contributor in a later monthly update, when Schroders credited increased confidence in AI demand. Armitage has called the connector and sensor maker more diversified than other AI plays, even though it is a core supplier to Nvidia. That diversification fits a stated preference. He has said he likes being thematically diversified, a stance he called unfashionable, and he wants to understand the operating leverage that decides whether a business massively out- or underperforms expectations. For a wider view of the sector, our list of the best AI infrastructure stocks for long-term investors is a good place to start. 2. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) Stake Value: $1.17 billion Number of Shares: 4,714,127 Percentage of Portfolio: 11.96% Amazon is one of the two hyperscalers Armitage says Egerton owns, and he has been candid that it has not been an easy holding. It weighed more than any other position on the portfolio in the first quarter, and it detracted again in a later month when investors argued over whether cloud providers will earn adequate returns on their capital spending. His response has been to lean on the demand data. He cited management comments that most of the capacity for 2027 is already reserved and that demand for 2028 looks striking, and he noted that AI servers pay back in a little under three years. He has also argued that the hyperscalers are a core exposure whose market positions would end stronger if the smaller neocloud rivals suffered. That contrast ties to his skepticism about valuing the neoclouds on earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, since depreciation is their biggest cost. Armitage said he dislikes the market's concentration in AI but finds it very powerful, which is why Egerton participates. Another route to growth is covered in a piece on whether Amazon's cash engines can fund its robotaxi bet . 1. Visa (NYSE:V) Stake Value: $1.47 billion Number of Shares: 4,079,226 Percentage of Portfolio: 14.93% Visa is Egerton's largest holding, and Armitage used it to illustrate how he thinks about modeling a company. He pointed to its margins of roughly 67%, saying the drivers of the top line and the costs are clear enough that mix effects matter far less than they do at businesses whose economics are private. That transparency lets him judge whether the valuation numbers underpinning the position still hold. Those numbers were tested this year. Armitage said there was a time when the shares could hardly be given away, and that sticking with the position, rather than chasing the crowd at the point of maximum gloom, turned out to be fortunate, as the stock has since risen about 20%. A later Schroders monthly update listed it as a detractor on concerns about consumer health, a reminder that its revenue follows spending volumes. Egerton also owns Mastercard, giving it exposure to the broader payments network. The pressure point for any payments leader is how much of each dollar flows back to large clients, an issue explored in our look at whether bigger client rebates are worth the valuation . news.Title: Think Arm Is Too Expensive? 1 Thing You Need To Understand About the Chip Stock
news.Content:
Like the rest of the semiconductor sector, Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) endured a brutal sell-off on Thursday.

Shares of the chip stock , which is best known for licensing its power-efficient CPU architecture, lost 13% on Thursday following its fiscal second-quarter earnings report.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

That sell-off was largely driven by the broader plunge in tech stocks on concerns about potential data center restrictions following the midterm elections, though Arm shares fell in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the report came out.

Arm topped estimates on the top and bottom lines, but investors were disappointed with weak growth in royalty revenue, which rose 8% to $670 million, a function of a slow smartphone market. Arm dominates the smartphone CPU market with virtually 100% market share, and it's still the biggest source of royalty revenue for the company. However, higher memory prices have pressured smartphone shipments, and smartphone royalty revenue was roughly flat in the year.

Nonetheless, the company's growth markets continued to deliver strong results. Data center royalty revenue doubled year-over-year, and now makes up roughly a quarter of total royalty revenue. Physical AI royalty revenue, meanwhile, was up 50%, driven by growth in the auto market.

Guidance for royalty revenue growth in the third quarter was also disappointing, as the company forecast just low-single-digit royalty growth due to weakness in the smartphone segment and tough comparisons with the quarter a year ago.

License revenue in the quarter was strong, up 50% to $773 million, driven by an increase in long-term agreements. Arm's total revenue rose 27% to $1.44 billion, topping the consensus at $1.38 billion. On the bottom line, adjusted earnings per share rose from $0.39 to $0.52, which beat estimates at $0.48.

Image source: Getty Images.

What was missing from the quarterly numbers

Arm stock soared in March when the company announced that it was getting into silicon for the first time. Historically, the company has just licensed its CPU architecture and collected revenue on royalties. Now, it will design its own chips like fabless peers such as Nvidia , AMD , and Broadcom .

Arm introduced the Arm AGI CPU with Meta Platforms as its lead partner. The data center CPU has a higher performance per watt than any current competitors on the market, and will go into production in Arm's fiscal fourth quarter, which ends next March. The company already has more demand than it can handle and raised its revenue guidance from the chip through fiscal 2028 from $1 billion to $2 billion. By fiscal 2031, it expects $15 billion in annual revenue from Arm AGI CPU.

Story Continues

The company said in its shareholder letter that it's more confident in hitting that $2 billion forecast, and it's focused on "expanding capacity to meet growing customer demand."

CPU demand is directly correlated with AI inference, which is what powers agentic AI. There's a lot of upside potential for the new AGI CPU if a product like Meta's Muse gains significant adoption.

Arm CFO Jason Child explained that every Muse user required a single CPU core devoted to it. If Meta were able to convert every one of its roughly 3.5 billion social media users into Meta users, it would need to buy 3.5 billion Arm AGI CPU cores from Arm. Child said that cores are priced between $10 and $20, which would translate into $35 billion-$70 billion in revenue.

That's the ceiling from Muse, and not every Facebook user is going to adopt Muse, of course, but the example is illustrative of Arm's potential growth with the new CPU. It also shows that the addressable CPU market is potentially much larger than the $100 billion or $200 billion previously estimated, as there are several personal AI agents on the market and agentic AI products will certainly expand.

Is Arm a buy?

Arm stock has fallen sharply since it peaked in June, following a broad rally in chip stocks and excitement about CPU demand. It's still expensive, with a price-to-earnings ratio of around 80, but the discussion of the stock seems to ignore the upside potential related to the Arm AGI CPU.

While investors will still have to wait a couple of quarters to get some meaningful numbers on the AGI CPU, it could bring in much more than $15 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031. At this point, owning Arm for some exposure to the agentic AI upside makes sense, even if the stock otherwise looks expensive.

news.Title: Elon Musk says Tesla will stop making iconic vehicles
news.Content:
The Ford F-Series truck, which includes the Ford F-150, has been America's best-selling truck for 49 years and the best-selling overall vehicle for 44 years, the automaker said in a December 2025 statement.

The popularity of the Ford F-Series prompted the company to launch its Ford F-150 Lightning electric truck in April 2022, which became a rival of EV company Tesla when it rolled out the Cybertruck in November 2023.

In less than five years, both products would end production as the companies seek both affordable and profitable electric vehicles that the public will embrace.

Elon Musk's Tesla discontinues Cybertruck

The world's richest man, Elon Musk , said that his electric vehicle company Tesla will cease making Cybertruck's three models in mid-2027, according to the billionaire's X post.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said in his X post on Nov. 5.

Cybercab is Tesla's newest addition to its Robotaxi fleet, which also includes its autonomous Model Y sedan and the Robovan, an autonomous microtransit van suitable for large groups, according to the vehicle's website.

Gigafactory Texas in Austin is the only manufacturing plant where Tesla produces the Cybertruck. Musk did not say if production would be moved to another factory.

Cybertruck has three models

Tesla manufactures three Cybertruck models: Dual Motor All-wheel Drive, which starts at $82,490; Premium All-wheel Drive, which starts at $92,490; and Cyberbeast, which starts at $102,490.

In addition to the Robotaxi and Cybertruck, Tesla lists three other vehicles on its website: the Model 3, Model Y, and Roadster.

Cybertruck's sales decreased significantly year-over-year by 48%, from 38,965 vehicles in 2024 to 20,237 in 2025, according to Kelly Blue Book data reported by Reuters.

Head of Cybertruck program left in 2025

Compounding the vehicle's problems with sales, the head of the Cybertruck program since 2022, Siddhant Awasthi , left the company on Nov. 10, 2025, after over eight years at Tesla. Awasthi joined Tesla in 2018 and in four years he was running the program.

When production began in 2023, Musk projected the vehicle would generate 250,000 in annual sales.

Tesla's end of Cybertruck production follows a surprise decision earlier in 2026 to stop production of its Model S and Model X vehicles by mid-2026.

Tesla ceased production of other vehicles

Musk announced during a Jan. 28, 2026, Tesla earnings call that the company would "basically stop production of Model S and Model X next quarter," Musk said.

Story Continues

Tesla launched its limited release Roadster in 2008, then rolled out Model S in 2012 for mass production. The EV company joined the SUV craze in 2016 when it introduced its Model X, then a year later launched its popular Model 3 sedan in 2017.

Tesla's decision to end production of the Cybertruck follows Ford's announcement in December 2025 that it would discontinue production of the F-150 Lightning electric truck.

Ford, which launched the Lightning in April 2022, said it would continue to provide parts and service for the Lightning for 10 years. It would also continue software updates for the vehicles, Ford Authority reported.

news.Title: Lassonde Industries Inc (LSDAF) (Q3 2026) Earnings Call Highlights: Margin Pressure and ...
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Release Date: November 06, 2026

For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript .

Positive Points

Lassonde Industries Inc ( LSDAF ) delivered gross profit growth to $206 million and adjusted EPS growth of 2% to $5.94 despite a challenging operating environment.

Favorable commodity costs for orange and apple concentrates, along with a positive shift in sales mix, contributed to higher gross profit.

The Apple and Eve brand gained distribution with national retailers in the U.S. Midwest and West, and benefited from innovation in reduced-sugar juice box formats.

In Canada, Oasis achieved volume and market share gains in the chilled category, and the company sustained its market leadership despite category volume declines.

The new $200 million New Jersey facility remains on track and on budget, with production transfer starting near the end of Q4 2026 and continuing through 2027.

Lassonde Industries Inc ( LSDAF ) received industry recognition, including being named a Sysco Canada Top 10 supplier and receiving a Gordon Food Service 2026 VIP award.

The company repurchased over 68,000 shares for $15.8 million under its normal course issuer bid, demonstrating confidence in its financial position.

Net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio remained low at 1.25:1, well below the internal maximum threshold of 3.25:1.

Negative Points

Third quarter sales decreased 2.3% year-over-year (excluding FX), driven by retailer promotional strategy changes, product line discontinuations, and suboptimal production levels.

Temporary production issues in the U.S. Beverage network, including a 20-day shutdown at the North Carolina single-serve line and end-of-life asset disruptions in New Jersey, constrained growth opportunities and increased conversion costs.

Adjusted EBITDA margin declined to 11.7% from 11.9% last year, reflecting higher conversion costs, increased PET resin and freight costs, and lower sales volumes.

Operating cash flow fell to $63 million from $118 million last year due to working capital requirements, and capital expenditures are projected to be elevated at around 7% of sales for 2026.

Management expects consumer demand and volumes to remain under pressure, with fiscal 2026 sales slightly below last year's level excluding FX, and uncertainty remains about replacing lost specialty food volume at historical business terms.

Higher crude oil prices are expected to continue pressuring transportation and PET resin costs, while conversion costs in the U.S. Beverage network may remain elevated through early 2027.

The company faces persistent category headwinds, with Canadian volumes down about 5% and U.S. volumes down about 3%, and private label volumes remained soft due to a major customer's go-to-market strategy change.

The transition to the new New Jersey facility cannot be accelerated, and the company will continue to manage end-of-life equipment risks and potential disruptions until the transfer is complete.

Story Continues

Q & A Highlights

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Sign with LSDAF.

Is LSDAF fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Q : Can you quantify the Q3 EBITDA impact from the North Carolina and New Jersey production disruptions, and how much will linger into Q4? A : CFO Francis Trudeau declined to disclose a specific figure but pointed to conversion costs and freight as the two main components, noting the margin impact was significant. He flagged a risk that suboptimal production continues into Q4, as the company is still working to resolve the issue and is currently operating at reduced levels.

Q : With roughly 70% of the specialty food volume secured for 2027, how much of the associated earnings contribution has been replaced, and what is the remaining risk to 2027 profitability? A : CFO Francis Trudeau said the impact from the lost customer began in Q3 and Q4 of 2026, as previously guided. While the company has done a good job replacing 70% of the top-line volume, he flagged a risk in replacing that volume at similar business terms, which is expected to weigh on Q4 and early 2027 results.

Q : What drove the private label weakness, and which components do you expect to improve as operations normalize? A : CEO Vince Timpano attributed the softness to category headwinds (Canadian volumes down about 5%, U.S. down about 3%), retailer strategy shiftsincluding a move from high/low promotions to EDLP in Canadaand, in the U.S., consumers shifting from grocery toward discount, mass and club channels. He expects some of these retailer-driven volume issues to be cycled in 2027. The CFO added that a better sales mix and innovation are already contributing positively.

Q : What exactly happened in North Carolina, and was the 20-day downtime on the line established last year? A : CEO Vince Timpano confirmed the roughly 20-day shutdown affected the line established last year and described it as a temporary equipment challenge. He said improvements are being seen but the company is planning prudently, leveraging network redundancy to meet existing customer demand. The main cost is a reduced ability to pursue growth, plus higher freight from shifting production to other markets and overhead absorption challenges in North Carolina.

Q : Industry volumes are down about 5% in Canada and 3% in the U.S.how do your own volumes compare, and are you gaining share? A : CEO Vince Timpano said the company is gaining share on the branded side in the U.S., particularly with Apple & Eve's reduced-sugar format. In Canada, category headwinds and a retailer shift away from promotional frequency and depth are weighing on performance, though he called that reset nearly complete and cyclable in 2027. He noted share is above 2024 levels despite a recent decline, with solid improvement in the chilled category over the last four weeks.

Q : Given the disruptions at the legacy New Jersey facility, could you accelerate the transfer to the new facility to reduce risk over the next 12 months? A : CFO Francis Trudeau said acceleration is not feasible because the new plant is still being built, though the project remains on time and on budget, with test runs underway and production transfer starting at the end of fiscal 2026 and continuing through most of 2027. CEO Vince Timpano emphasized the $200 million U.S. investment is on track, with first runs expected in late December or early January, and that the company will manage end-of-life equipment challenges in the interim.

Q : In the sales breakdown, private label was down about $21 million on volumes versus a $7 million$8 million per quarter SKU-cut impactwhat makes up the balance? A : CFO Francis Trudeau confirmed the balance is mainly due to the change in one Canadian customer's go-to-market strategy, with the previously announced discontinuation of selected product lines also falling into the private label category. Those are the two main elements to consider.

Q : Has the value spread between private label and branded products changed over the past few quarters given the value-seeking consumer environment? A : CEO Vince Timpano said the spread has not changed materially.

Q : Pasta sauce has grown mid-single digits in Canada versus a declining industrywhat is driving that? A : CEO Vince Timpano credited growth in the premium-to-super-premium segment, where the company's participation through the brands it packs is performing exceptionally well. Strong brand partners in a segment outpacing the category average are the key driver.

Q : Can you quantify the benefit from lower orange and apple concentrate costs in Q4 or 2027? A : CFO Francis Trudeau said it is difficult to quantify because purchase price adjustment mechanisms create lags, and the commodity benefit must be viewed against massive inflation in freight and PET resin costs since June last year, which has significantly offset the gains. He noted the company has been on the right side of commodity costs for several months and that commodity management will be important in the outlook period.

Q : Given persistent demand pressure, do you expect prolonged promotional behavior in the industry, or will margin discipline prevail? A : CEO Vince Timpano said the environment remains highly uncertain due to commodity gains offset by fuel and freight costs from the Middle East crisis, plus tariff uncertainty, and he expects current conditions to persist for the foreseeable future. He stressed maintaining pricing discipline while using smart promotions to appeal to value-seeking consumers in discount, mass and club channels, and leveraging the portfolio's diversity and innovation to participate where consumers are going.

Q : What is your exposure to mass and club channels in the U.S., and can you benefit from consumers shifting away from traditional grocers? A : CEO Vince Timpano described the company as fairly evenly exposed across channels, with a diverse portfolio well represented across all of them. He said the focus is on maximizing participation in the channel shifts as consumers move, rather than being structurally over- or under-exposed.
