Q & A Highlights

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with WULF.

Is WULF fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Q : With so many data center projects seeking hyperscaler backstops, how long will that appetite last, and how does TeraWulf plan for a market without an investment-grade backstop? A : CEO Patrick noted that demand from hyperscalers and semiconductor companies remains robust, and the "version 2.0" of the company's wrap shows hyperscalers are willing to put their balance sheets to work. He likened the arrangement to training wheels: once a customer like Anthropic achieves a certain investment-grade rating, the Google backstop falls away, leaving that balance sheet for the hyperscaler's own use. He expects this maturation pattern to become more common across the space and welcomes it.

Q : Would TeraWulf consider selling stabilized assets to recycle capital into new development, given the many vehicles in the market buying such assets? A : CEO Patrick said the business is to build and own these assets long-term, but pointed to precedents such as Blackstone's investment in FirstEnergy's transmission business, where an infrastructure fund bought into an operating business at a significant multiple and proved out equity value at the parent. He said a sale is a possibility if the market continues to reward companies building data centers for NVIDIA, AMD, Amazon, Google and Microsoft, but the number one priority remains executing, bringing buildings online, converting them to cash flow and repeating that process in a financially efficient way.

Story Continues

Q : How sensitive are project yields and spreads to changes in the rate environment, and what pricing dynamics or escalators should investors watch? A : Management said it avoids focusing on current market pricing and instead builds shareholder value by protecting the economics of its deals, so the only real risk taken is execution risk. On new projects, TeraWulf signed Fluor as EPC contractor with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP) at Clawsville and expects to do the same at Muskie. On the debt side, the company requires investment-grade support from customers, since the business is about financing efficiently. Management said the combination of protected economic spreads, execution skill and investment-grade-backed debt gives it a lock on creating shareholder value.

Q : What is the status of the Chesapeake acquisition and its regulatory approvals? A : Chesapeake is under a purchase and sale agreement, and most regulatory approvals are in hand, with a couple outstanding, including one from the SEC. However, conditions precedent to close have yet to be fulfilled by the seller, and management said those conditions are important to TeraWulf. If they are met, the company is ready to proceed; if not, it will rethink the deal. Management said it will not bring anything into its pipeline that is not accretive and a promising data center development, adding that it likes Maryland, citing Governor Wes Moore's progressive approach to data center contributions and the state's position on a transmission superhighway.

Q : Given the changing political landscape, how do you view the shape of lease rental rates over the next 12 to 24 months? A : Management said it focuses on its own portfolio, which it believes is "a lot more valuable than it was last week," citing tremendous demand for partner-now and prompt power. The phone has been "ringing off the hook" regarding the Muskie facility, and management feels good about its side of the table in negotiations with potential customers there. It also stressed being thoughtful about where to develop, noting the company has spent 25 years building energy infrastructure in places where it can navigate the politics and regulatory framework, and that approach will continue as it builds out its pipeline.

Q : As hyperscalers and developers face pressure to contribute to incremental power costs and local communities, who bears those costs and how does that affect development yields? A : Management said customer Anthropic is socially conscious and wants to contribute to communities, and TeraWulf shares that approach, since its employees live and work in these communities and the facilities will operate there for the next 20 years. The company has historically focused on teachers, kids, education and first responders, and management expects contributive host agreements to become common. It cited giving a new fire engine to the fire department in Hawesville, Kentucky, where the fire chief personally called to express gratitude, and said both parties should be responsible participants in their host communities.

news.Title: 5 Latest Jim Cramer Stock Picks on Twitter and Mad Money
news.Content: Markets are trembling amid the latest AI stock sell-off, which has sent shares of major AI players deep into the red. But CNBC's Jim Cramer believes the downturn is not another dot-com crash. Cramer warned that AI stocks could fall further, particularly semiconductor companies whose shares surged during the AI boom. However, he argued that unlike the speculative businesses that collapsed in 2000, many of today's AI companies are highly profitable. His biggest concern is smaller AI infrastructure companies such as CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius, which have borrowed heavily to finance data center projects that could face regulatory delays. Before the election too, Cramer was more careful about tech. On Mad Money, he said the Nasdaq had just closed its worst month since March 2025 and that the week ahead "might be even worse." He said he wanted to see a "crescendo" before putting more money into tech, which he described as stocks getting crushed in the morning and then rallying on big volume to finish higher. He also warned that anti-data center politicians could stop projects if Democrats took control, and data center stocks fell on Wednesday on fears of tighter AI regulation, Reuters reported. We recently ranked 10 stocks Cramer sounded positive about, based on his posts on X and his comments on CNBC. Click to see the full list of 10 stocks Cramer likes here . We ranked them in ascending order by the number of hedge fund holders at the end of the second quarter of 2026, according to Insider Monkey's database of 1,006 hedge funds. Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points ( see more details here ). GE Vernova (NYSE:GEV) is one of the names he is watching closely. Barometer Capital Management pointed to the company's gas turbine and grid backlog in its second-quarter 2026 investor letter. He likes how the chipmaker's stock is performing and sees it helping lift the tech sector. Fidelity Dividend Growth Fund said in its second-quarter 2026 investor letter that not owning AMD was its largest relative detractor. See the full letter here. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) recently reported quarterly results with revenue up 45% from a year ago, its best quarter ever. Data center sales nearly doubled, and CEO Lisa Su said on the call that AMD now expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. Bulls say the report shows demand for AI chips is still strong. Chip stocks have fallen because some big cloud companies burned cash in the quarter, but those companies still plan to spend more on data centers in 2027, and that spending becomes revenue for AMD. news.Title: Sandisk Stock Has Lost About 64% Since June. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy It.
news.Content:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock sank about 22% on Thursday, Nov. 5, adding to a painful stretch for the flash memory maker. At roughly $806 as of this writing, shares are down about 64% from their June 25 close of $2,335, a record.

Thursday's slide continued a sell-off in AI data center stocks that started after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, as investors weighed whether the outcome might slow data center construction.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

And it's been quick. Sandisk closed around $1,330 on Oct. 29, the day it posted fiscal first-quarter results and guided for even higher profits in this quarter. So the growth stock has fallen about 39% over the past week, even though the company's outlook calls for earnings to keep rising.

I think the sell-off has finally brought the stock to a price worth paying. And Sandisk's guidance is what I'd use to set it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Earnings are still rising, just more slowly

Showing how much the company has changed, Sandisk's earnings per share on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis grew 26% sequentially, to $49.51 in its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (which ended Oct. 2, 2026). That followed sequential gains of 278% in fiscal Q3 of 2026 and 68% in fiscal Q4. Fiscal Q1 revenue came to $11.0 billion, up 23% sequentially and 378% year over year, and data center customers accounted for about $4.8 billion of it. For fiscal Q2, management guided to adjusted earnings of $55 to $57 per share, implying about 13% growth over fiscal Q1 at the midpoint.

Put simply, profits are still climbing. But the growth rate is slowing quickly, and it might keep falling from here.

After all, memory profits can swing fast. A year before, in fiscal Q1 of 2026, Sandisk earned just $1.22 per share on an adjusted basis, with a gross margin of around 30%.

And in the three months ended March 28, 2025, it had an adjusted loss of $0.30 a share.

True, the company looks different now. Data center revenue was under $300 million in the year-ago quarter, and the gross margin has since climbed to 85%. But flash memory is still a product whose price can fall when supply outruns demand, and Sandisk's earnings would probably drop with it.

The stock is priced for a brief boom

Sandisk's guidance covers only one quarter, so the simplest way to use it is to annualize it. Four quarters at the $56 midpoint would total about $224 per share in adjusted profit. At around $806, the stock trades at under 4 times those annualized earnings.

Story Continues

In other words, a buyer at today's price is paying for less than four years of profits at the current pace. Even on actual results, shares sell for about 7 times earnings over the last four quarters.

By comparison, at the Oct. 29 close, shares traded for about 6 times annualized guided earnings.

With a valuation this low, investors seem to expect the boom's profits to fade within a few years. I think that's a fair worry for a memory company. It's also why I wouldn't pay much more than the stock goes for now.

What would I pay for the stock?

My price is around $900 per share -- the point at which four years of earnings at the fiscal Q2 guidance pace would equal what I'd pay. Asking a company this cyclical for much more than four years of boom-level profits feels like too much to me.

The coming stock split changes how that number looks, but not what it means. Every shareholder of record on Nov. 9 gets seven extra shares for each one held. The new shares arrive after the Nov. 19 close, and split-adjusted trading is expected to start Nov. 20. Divided by eight, my $900 price comes to about $112, and the $56 guidance midpoint becomes $7 a share.

At roughly $806, Sandisk is under that price. Sure, a stock that has dropped this far this fast can keep falling. And if flash prices start to slip, the earnings behind my price might follow.

With that in mind, I'd consider taking a small position now, maybe adding to it over time rather than all at once. If the stock gets back above $900 (or $112 after the split) before I buy, I'd hold off.

news.Title: Microsoft and Oracle's AI ambitions are suddenly a lot more expensive
news.Content:
The AI data center boom is not cooling off, even if the buildings themselves badly need to. Microsoft and Oracle are sitting on huge contract backlogs, and the only way to turn those promises into revenue is to build more capacity, fast. That rush is also lifting suppliers like Vertiv Holdings, which sells the cooling and power gear every new facility needs.

The money involved keeps getting bigger. Goldman Sachs expects the five largest U.S. hyperscalers to lift AI infrastructure spending to $1.2 trillion in 2027 from about $800 billion this year. The bank also estimates these companies need about $300 billion in yearly AI revenue just to break even.

Microsoft's backlog keeps growing

Microsoft has more signed business than it can serve today. Its commercial remaining performance obligation, which tracks contracted revenue not yet recognized, jumped 73% to $677 billion in the quarter ended September 30, while Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion. "We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost efficiency for customers across our entire stack," CEO Satya Nadella said.

Also read: Microsoft just gave Nvidia shareholders a reason to pay attention

The quarter itself beat expectations. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion, and Azure grew 48%, ahead of the roughly 45% Wall Street had expected. CFO Amy Hood defended the heavy spending, saying "each dollar of CapEx has the potential to support more revenue and higher returns over time."

The spending bill is rising quickly. Microsoft put $45.2 billion into capital projects in the quarter, with about three-quarters going to short-lived assets such as GPUs, CPUs and networking gear. Hood expects capex to top $50 billion in the second quarter, with Azure growth guided to 49% to 50%. She said, "We still have demand that exceeds supply."

Microsoft also has room to keep paying for it. The company uses leasing and debt markets as part of its funding mix and expects to stay free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. Nadella added that Microsoft will sell capacity when the pricing is right.

Oracle's backlog also goes all in

Oracle's backlog is nearly as large. The company reported remaining performance obligations of $664 billion in its fiscal first quarter, up $209 billion from a year earlier. Total revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion, while cloud infrastructure revenue more than doubled to $7.4 billion, according to Oracle .

"Customer demand for AI Cloud Training and Inferencing Services continues to grow faster than supply," Oracle said. It booked more than $30 billion in new AI cloud contracts in the quarter and expects about half of its backlog to turn into revenue over the next 36 months. Management raised its full-year revenue guidance to at least $90 billion and called fiscal 2028 its peak spending year.

Story Continues

Paying for that build-out is the hard part. On November 2, Oracle filed to raise $10 billion in senior notes and another $10 billion in common stock. It expects free cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028. The shares fell that day, leaving them well below their September 2025 peak.

Oracle is getting creative too. It is using a $35 billion AI purpose vehicle with Apollo and Blackstone to keep some deployments off its balance sheet. At the same time, a force majeure notice has delayed payments on its Project Jupiter data center in New Mexico.

Goldman Sachs data also shows AI-related issuers paying about 115 basis points on new debt, compared with 78 for the broader investment-grade market, TheStreet reported .

The cooling bottleneck lifts Vertiv

All that new capacity creates a heat problem. Standard data center racks run at about 10 to 20 kilowatts, while racks built around Nvidia's Blackwell chips can need 100 kilowatts or more, pushing operators toward liquid cooling.

The market for fixing that problem is growing fast. The global data center cooling market was worth about $18 billion last year and is forecast to reach roughly $141 billion by 2036. AI servers, denser racks and a move toward direct-to-chip and immersion cooling are behind that growth, according to Research and Markets .

Vertiv is riding that wave. The company sells power, thermal management and liquid cooling gear, and its third-quarter revenue jumped 61% to about $4.31 billion. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.21 a share, and organic orders more than doubled from a year earlier.

More Microsoft:

Microsoft's $665 target hinges on a new AI advantage

Meta and Microsoft just sent employees a memo about Anthropic

Microsoft just sent a strong message to Anthropic

The company also raised its full-year outlook. Vertiv now expects 2026 revenue of $14.65 billion, up $650 million from its July forecast, and adjusted earnings of $7.15 a share. It plans to double its chiller production capacity by year-end to keep up with orders.

What this means for Microsoft and Oracle investors

Wall Street is rewarding Microsoft for now. Its shares rose more than 5% after hours following the October 28 results, even as Alphabet fell about 10%. Capital.com analyst Daniela Hathorn said the two reports offered "competing narratives" on whether AI is paying off, as reported by TheStreet .

Microsoft investors still need to watch where that backlog comes from. In January, Hood said about 45% of the company's remaining commercial performance obligation came from OpenAI. Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges, who rates the stock a Buy, lists weaker-than-expected OpenAI revenue as a key risk.

Oracle investors face a longer wait for the payoff. The company targets more than $225 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings above $21 a share by fiscal 2030, but Scotiabank and Wells Fargo both trimmed their price targets in late October. Oracle's next test comes when it reports fiscal second-quarter results on December 14.

Related: Jim Cramer sends strong signal to Oracle stock investors

news.Title: Google buys Wyoming data center site as hyperscalers move to own AI capacity
news.Content:
Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

Investing.com -- Alphabet is buying the site it could have rented. Google has acquired Crusoe's southeast Wyoming data center site, a day after announcing a $17B investment in the project ( Reuters, Nov 6, 2026 ). Crusoe is a private AI infrastructure developer, and the search returned no listed shares for it. The deal's financial terms were not disclosed. Read alongside Microsoft (MSFT)'s pullback from some neocloud projects, it points to a shift in strategy. The largest buyers of AI capacity increasingly want to own it, because the permitting, power and construction risks of renting it have become harder to price. (Prices as of Nov 6, 2026, about 3:28 PM EST.)

From Landlord to Owner

Crusoe was not simply bought out of a finished project. According to Bloomberg reporting relayed by Investing.com (Jul 2, 2026), Crusoe was pressured to leave the Wyoming campus in June after Google raised concerns about costs and timetable. Crusoe has now handed over the pre-development work, which included site selection, government approvals and power strategy. Google is building with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital. Crusoe says it is separately developing another Google campus in Armstrong.

That sequence supports the thesis. Google is no longer simply contracting for capacity delivered by an intermediary. It wants direct control of the timeline.

Power Is the Product

The power setup shows what Google is buying. In October, Alphabet (GOOGL) agreed to directly finance a $1.8B, 564-megawatt natural gas facility with Black Hills (BKH), part of a ring-fenced Wyoming microgrid ( Oct 8, 2026 ). The Wyoming project will also draw on a planned 702-megawatt fuel-cell development supplied by Bloom Energy (BE) ( Reuters, Nov 5, 2026 ). Control of generation, not just buildings, is what lets an owner promise delivery dates. Alphabet guided 2026 capex to roughly $195B to $205B, so it has the balance sheet to carry that ownership.

The Political Squeeze

The midterms made timing risk worse. Of 41 data-center ballot measures this week, all but one went against data centers , according to Ballotpedia. Candidates opposed to expansion also won key races in Texas and Georgia. In Texas, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she would ban new projects until lawmakers pass rules for the industry. A renter exposed to a developer's permitting or power delays can end up holding capacity that arrives years late. An owner at least controls which sites to pursue, how to sequence them, and how to arrange power.

Story Continues

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Microsoft's Parallel Retreat

Microsoft has not announced a new strategy, but its recent decisions point the same way:

It declined to exercise an option to more than double its Nscale Texas lease ( FT via Investing.com, Nov 5, 2026 ).

It tightened oversight of some projects from Nebius (NBIS), IREN (IREN) and Nscale, and is debating whether to sign new neocloud deals ( Reuters, Nov 5, 2026 ).

It withdrew from an Essex anchor deal after power connection delays pushed supply into the 2030s.

Its fiscal quarter capex of $45.2B missed the $50.7B consensus, partly because of timing of third-party capacity ( Oct 29, 2026 ).

Microsoft's spokesperson said its approach combines owned, leased and partner capacity, which is a reminder that neoclouds are not ruled out. Microsoft also plans about 38 gigawatts of capacity by 2032, more than triple the current footprint (Sep 10, 2026). It still needs a lot of supply from somewhere.

Neocloud shares fell Nov 5, with Nebius down about 14%, IREN about 17% and CoreWeave about 10%, according to Reuters. Today's gains look like relief rather than a change of trend.

Bull, Bear and Bottom Line

Bull case for ownership: more control over deployment, utilization and unit economics, and less exposure to third-party pricing. If Alphabet delivers Wyoming on time, it gains a cost advantage as rivals queue for power.

Bear case: ownership concentrates execution risk on the owner's balance sheet. Construction delays, cost overruns or an AI demand slowdown would hit Alphabet directly rather than a landlord. Microsoft's own caution on neocloud costs also shows that tenants can walk. Owners cannot.

The nuance: the Crusoe deal looks less like a rejection of third-party developers than a division of labor. Crusoe did the pre-development work, and Google took the asset once it was de-risked. Neoclouds that can't secure customers and power will struggle to keep borrowing. Hyperscalers that can finance and operate their own capacity gain leverage.

news.Title: Amazon's CEO Andy Jassy Just Announced Huge News for Amazon Investors
news.Content:
Andy Jassy is the CEO of Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), succeeding founder Jeff Bezos a few years ago. Jassy used to lead Amazon Web Services (AWS), and his appointment as CEO a few years ago clearly indicated that this was the direction Amazon's business was heading. Bezos was correct in this assessment, as AWS has become a huge part of Amazon's business.

However, it's about to get even bigger. Andy Jassy made a bold prediction during Amazon's third-quarter earnings call that investors need to digest, as it could have big implications for the stock.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

AWS is headed to the $1 trillion mark

During Amazon's Q3 earnings call, Jassy noted that AWS could grow by more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, driven by significant investments in the platform. Over the next five to 10 years, that could grow to become a $1 trillion business. For reference, AWS, Amazon's cloud computing unit , grew at 39% in Q3, and its trailing-12-month sales totaled $161 billion.

That's huge news for investors, but what does it mean for the stock?

The biggest thing investors must realize is just how much better of a business AWS is than commerce. Commerce businesses in general operate on razor-thin margins, and while Amazon is one of the best at maximizing its margins, it's still much lower than what AWS puts up. During Q3, AWS' operating margin reached 39% on operating income of $17.8 billion. Its North American commerce segment delivered $8.7 billion in operating income on a 7.7% margin.

That's a huge mismatch, and it shows why Amazon is investing in AWS so heavily: It has a superior operating profile. As Amazon leans more heavily into AWS, it will be great news for the stock. Let's assume AWS hits a $1 trillion run rate a decade from now. If Amazon can maintain a 39% margin, that's $390 billion in operating income. Over the past 12 months, Amazon has produced $106 billion in operating income.

AMZN Operating Income (TTM) data by YCharts.

That means its operating income could more than quadruple over the next decade, which would result in huge returns for shareholders. AWS headed to $1 trillion in annual revenue would be huge news for investors, and if Jassy is right, could indicate that Amazon is a top stock to buy in the market now .

news.Title: What TeraWulf (WULF) Said on Its Q3 Earnings Call
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in TeraWulf Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

Q3 revenue rose to $76.2 million from $44.8 million in Q2, with high-performance computing leases contributing $63 million, or about 83% of revenue. TeraWulf expects Lake Mariner capacity additions to lift annualized leasing revenue to approximately $700 million by the end of Q1 2027.

For its Justified campus, TeraWulf plans to finance remaining costs with project-level debt and has Google credit support tied to Anthropic's 20-year lease. A Fluor construction agreement covers all three buildings, with phased service deliveries targeted from late 2027 through Q2 2028.

TeraWulf reported $2.4 billion in cash and restricted cash and said current liquidity plus expected asset-sale proceeds should cover planned Lake Mariner and Justified spending, as well as interim Muskie requirements, without issuing equity. The company is also working toward up to 1 gigawatt of power service for Muskie, with the first 500 megawatts targeted for 2028.

MarketBeat Week in Review – 11/2 - 11/6

TeraWulf (NASDAQ:WULF) reported higher third-quarter revenue as high-performance computing leases expanded, while executives outlined financing and construction plans for its data center projects in New York and Kentucky.

Revenue rose to $76.2 million from $44.8 million in the second quarter. HPC lease revenue nearly doubled to $63 million and accounted for approximately 83% of the total, Chief Financial Officer Patrick Fleury said on the earnings call.

→ Amazon Has Erased Its Earnings Sell-Off, But Is the Biggest Opportunity Still Ahead?

Google's Credit Backstop May Be TeraWulf's Biggest Advantage

Chairman and CEO Paul Prager said TeraWulf expects additional capacity at its Lake Mariner campus to begin generating revenue over the coming months. The company also is pursuing project-level debt financing for its Justified campus in Kentucky, where Google has agreed to provide credit support connected to a 20-year lease with Anthropic.

Lake Mariner capacity and revenue ramp

At Lake Mariner, the CB3 building is online and earning revenue under a lease with Fluidstack. Its lease commenced July 13, and third-quarter results reflected 102 megawatts of operating capacity generating lease revenue, Fleury said.

→ Washington Made a $2 Billion Quantum Bet, But Can Either ETF Match It?

Riot Platforms Re-Wires the Ledger for a $9B AI Power Play

Chief Technology Officer Nazar Khan said the first two of four data halls in CB4 had tenant equipment deployed and energized, with commercial operation and rent commencement expected shortly. The remaining two halls were scheduled to come online during the fourth quarter.

Story Continues

Fleury said TeraWulf expects to exit the fourth quarter with an additional 168 megawatts online at CB4, followed by another 168 megawatts at CB5 by the end of the first quarter of 2027. Prager said the company expects to exit that quarter with approximately $700 million in annualized run-rate leasing revenue.

→ Energy Transfer's Earnings Miss May Be Hiding Its Strongest Advantage

Fleury estimated total WULF Compute project costs at approximately $8.9 million per critical IT megawatt, within the company's original $8 million to $10 million guidance range. Approximately $2.9 billion of project capital spending had been completed as of September 30, with about $1 billion remaining, he said.

Google support and Fluor agreement advance Justified

At the Justified campus in Hawesville, Kentucky, TeraWulf has an Anthropic lease representing approximately $19 billion of contracted revenue. Prager said the company has the equity required under its current plan and expects to fund the remaining capital requirement with project-level debt.

Fleury said Google's support will protect against an Anthropic default after lease commencement through either a mandatory lease assumption or a debt-reducing termination payment. The cost of the support is recoverable from the tenant, and the support falls away if Anthropic achieves specified investment-grade credit ratings, he said.

TeraWulf also signed a definitive engineering, procurement and construction agreement with Fluor covering all three Justified data center buildings. Khan said the agreement includes cost and schedule protections, with guaranteed maximum pricing being established as engineering and procurement advance.

Construction pilings are underway, and the company continues to target phased ready-for-service deliveries from late 2027 through the second quarter of 2028. It expects costs of approximately $10 million to $12 million per critical IT megawatt.

During the question-and-answer session, Khan said Justified's engineering and drawings were approximately 90% complete, with completion expected by December 1. He said the project was more than 80% complete on long-lead equipment and expected to reach 100% by year-end.

Muskie power plans and financing discipline

For its Muskie site in Kentucky, TeraWulf is working with Kentucky Power and AEP on a path to an initial gigawatt of electric service. Khan said the first 500 megawatts are scheduled to begin delivery in 2028 under an electric service agreement.

The next 500 megawatts requires new generation, Khan said. He said the companies plan to seek Kentucky regulatory approval for Kentucky Power's proposed 760-megawatt Big Sandy combined-cycle gas plant, with approval expected by mid-2027. TeraWulf is working on the potential to bring portions of the second 500 megawatts forward into 2029, ahead of the plant's anticipated 2031 delivery.

Prager said TeraWulf is in discussions with prospective Muskie customers but declined to predict when it might sign a lease. The company would not sign a deal that forces it to issue equity at a valuation management believes does not reflect TeraWulf's value, he said.

Fleury said potential funding options include customer prepayments, customer equity investments, additional leverage and project-level investment in stabilized assets. He said TeraWulf intends to build and own assets long term but would consider investment in operating assets as a way to recycle capital.

Third-quarter results and liquidity

TeraWulf reported net income attributable to the company of $709.9 million, compared with a $939.9 million net loss in the second quarter. Fleury attributed the change primarily to a noncash fair-value adjustment associated with Google warrants and a gain on the sale of an equity interest in the Abernathy joint venture. Non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA was negative $12.8 million, compared with negative $18.3 million in the prior quarter.

Reported HPC leasing segment profit margin was approximately 17%, below the company's long-term target of approximately 85%. Fleury said the reported figure included tenant fit-out, pre-revenue and development costs; after adjustments and excluding certain power costs, the margin was approximately 83%.

Cash and restricted cash totaled approximately $2.4 billion at September 30. Based on current plans and assumptions, Fleury said existing liquidity and expected Abernathy sale proceeds would fund remaining Lake Mariner commitments, the remaining Justified equity investment and interim Muskie letter-of-credit requirements without accessing equity capital markets.

About TeraWulf (NASDAQ:WULF)

TeraWulf Inc is a digital asset infrastructure company focused primarily on developing and operating environmentally conscious data centers for bitcoin mining and other high-performance computing applications. The company emphasizes the use of low-carbon energy, including nuclear and hydroelectric power, to support energy-intensive computing operations.

TeraWulf operates mining and data center facilities in the United States, including the Lake Mariner site in New York and the Nautilus Cryptomine facility in Pennsylvania.

news.Title: 5 Companies Buying Back Their Own Stock Hand Over Fist As the Stock Market Sells Off
news.Content:
When the stock market falls sharply, as it did on Nov. 5, when the Nasdaq Composite dropped nearly 6% in a single day and closed in correction territory, most investors focus on what they should buy. But some companies are aggressively buying back their own stock, and some can now buy it at a discount, which could help deliver even more shareholder value.

The math is simple. A company that spends $1 billion on its own stock retires more shares when the price is lower, which increases each remaining shareholder's ownership stake. Lam Research, for example, bought back stock in September at prices that look to be around $326 per share. At Thursday's close of about $203, each $1 billion spent on buybacks would retire about 60% more shares.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

With that in mind, here are five companies buying back their own stock aggressively right now.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. PayPal

PayPal (NASDAQ:PYPL) has been one of the most aggressive repurchasers on the market in recent years. Over the past 12 months, the fintech giant has spent $6 billion buying back about 117 million shares, and its diluted share count has fallen by about 11% from a year ago. The business is improving, too, as new leadership focuses on efficiency and growing the core branded checkout business. I own PayPal stock , and with the stock trading at about 10.5 times forward earnings, these buybacks look like a smart use of cash.

2. General Motors

General Motors (NYSE:GM) just finished a $6 billion buyback program and immediately authorized a new $20 billion one, which is about a quarter of its market value. That's an aggressive buyback pace. GM had 849 million shares outstanding at the end of September, a figure well over 1 billion just a few years ago. With adjusted automotive free cash flow guidance raised to $11.5 billion to $12.5 billion this year, GM can afford it. The automaker is one of the largest holdings in my portfolio, and at about 6 times forward earnings, I'm happy to see it reduce its share count.

3. EPAM Systems

IT services company EPAM Systems (NYSE:EPAM) recently raised its buyback authorization to up to $1.8 billion and plans a $500 million accelerated share repurchase this month. It has also committed to returning at least half of its free cash flow to shareholders every year from 2027 through 2029. Its diluted share count is already down about 8% from a year ago, and it's likely to decline further. Unlike most of the market, EPAM's stock jumped 21% on Nov. 5 after earnings, but it remains well below its 52-week high.

Story Continues

4. Lam Research

Semiconductor equipment maker Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) announced a new $25 billion buyback authorization on Nov. 5, the same day its stock fell sharply. That's roughly 10% of the company's market value. CFO Doug Bettinger said Lam's "robust cash generation" gives management confidence in the aggressive repurchase plan. Lam's revenue grew about 54% last quarter, and the stock is now more than 50% below its 52-week high.

5. Airbnb

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) paired a strong third-quarter report with a new $12 billion buyback authorization, on top of the $2.7 billion remaining under its existing program. With $4.9 billion in free cash flow over the past year and billions on its balance sheet, it has the cash to back it up. One caveat: Airbnb says it uses buybacks partly to offset dilution from stock-based compensation, so its share count is down only about 3% from a year ago.

The bottom line

Let's be perfectly clear. We have no idea whether any of these companies are buying back stock right now or how much they're buying back while the market is down. We simply know their aggressive buyback authorizations, and these are companies that are dramatically reducing their share counts.

To be sure, buybacks aren't automatically good for shareholders, and most aggressive buybacks carry risks. To name three, EPAM is funding part of its accelerated buyback with borrowed money, Lam's business is cyclical, and PayPal's free cash flow fell 17% last quarter. But companies with strong balance sheets that buy back stock during sell-offs tend to reward patient shareholders. These five are putting real money behind their confidence.

news.Title: These 4 Trump-backed chip stocks have seen steeper losses than the beleaguered sector
news.Content: Chipmaker Intel ( INTC ) is putting a notable drag on the burgeoning US government investment portfolio, shaving close to $20 billion off the government's stake in the chipmaker. But it's not the only one. The Trump administration's other semiconductor investments have also incurred sharp losses that outpace the beleaguered sector. Chipmaker GlobalFoundries ( GFS ), photonics company Aeluma ( ALMU ), and silicon carbide specialist Wolfspeed ( WOLF ) have all seen losses of at least 40% over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance data. That's in excess of PHLX Semiconductor ( ^SOX ), a capitalization-weighted index of the semiconductor sector, which is down about over 18% over the same span. The government's portfolio, which spans 41 companies and includes industries from critical minerals to drones, according to a CATO Institute tracker , has taken investors on a wild ride since the Trump administration started buying up stakes last year. Semiconductor stocks have proved especially volatile, with sharper ups and downs, including a bounceback in evidence Friday . All four were up more than 5% at midday, and some by double digits, as the sector as a whole jumped a more modest 4%. The price action in these public chipmakers doesn't capture the private companies that have also negotiated equity stakes with the US government. Trump and his team have placed extra focus on semiconductors, leveraging funds made available by the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act to acquire equity stakes in a host of private chipmakers, including Commonwealth Fusion Systems and xLight. The Trump administration has also negotiated stakes in quantum computing companies using CHIPS Act money that have similarly struggled amid headwinds facing the tech sector as a whole. The government portfolio of quantum computing companies includes publicly traded companies like D-Wave Quantum ( QBTS ), Infleqtion ( INFQ ), Quantinuum ( QNT ), and Rigetti Computing ( RGTI ). The price oscillations could give ammunition to critics of the administration's investing approach. Economic research shows that full or partial government ownership in companies has historically led to worse outcomes for the companies and their stakeholders. In a 2025 survey of economists , a large majority said that a government taking equity stakes tends to be detrimental to both a company's performance and its governance standards. The mixed results of the government's investments at the moment also fly in the face of the outsized returns for taxpayers that Trump and his team often promise. Story Continues The president in September posted an image on Truth Social depicting himself as a stock trader in the Oval Office and noting Intel's stock price of $95 per share at the time. "I've made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U.S.A., not myself," Trump wrote at the time in a record that is very much in question at the moment, with Intel trading on Friday at about $55 per share, even as that price level is still an increase over what the government paid for it. news.Title: Not Alphabet. Not Meta. This Is the Digital Advertising Stock I'd Buy Right Now.
news.Content:
Alphabet and Meta Platforms may dominate digital advertising, but there's another company building an impressive advertising business. Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) is expanding its e-commerce ecosystem, artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, and streaming platform, making it a top pick for investors in digital advertising right now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

In its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29, Amazon reported advertising revenue growth of 12% year over year, excluding foreign exchange effects. Looking ahead, management expects advertising growth to accelerate into the high teens in the fourth quarter.

In fact, growth is becoming harder to overlook.

Amazon's ad business is becoming a growth engine

What makes Amazon's advertising business stand out is its direct access to shoppers who are already looking to buy something. That edge is what sets it apart from traditional digital advertising platforms.

The company has turned that advantage into a growing advertising ecosystem. For example, Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands allow businesses to promote their offerings directly in shopping results, while display and video advertising extend their reach beyond Amazon's marketplace.

Plus, the business is becoming increasingly sophisticated, combining shopping behavior, browsing activity, streaming engagement, and purchase information to help advertisers target consumers more effectively. With the rise of AI, Amazon's advertising capabilities just got an upgrade.

AI is making Amazon's ad platform more powerful

One of the biggest developments is Amazon's push to integrate AI into its advertising process. For example, in September, the company introduced Amazon Ads Agent, an AI-powered platform designed to help advertisers plan, create, and optimize campaigns. As a result, instead of requiring advertisers to manually manage multiple campaigns and advertising formats, they can outsource much of the work to Amazon's AI.

Today, its new Full-Funnel Campaigns feature brings sponsored ads, display advertising, video, and streaming television together in a single campaign. In other words, advertisers can simply provide their objectives, products, and creative materials, while AI handles campaign planning, execution, and optimization. This could be a game changer for smaller businesses that lack the resources and expertise to manage larger advertising campaigns.

Story Continues

Amazon is also using AI to simplify creative production. Its advertising tools can help businesses generate video advertisements, images, storyboards, and other marketing materials using existing product information. With that, Amazon isn't just selling ad space. It's also providing the technology that businesses need to advertise more efficiently.

Prime Video and live sports are extending Amazon's ad reach

Meanwhile, Amazon is expanding its advertising footprint through its other product lines. For years, Amazon's biggest advertising opportunity was closely tied to its e-commerce marketplace. Now, the company is going beyond that, with Prime Video being central to its new strategy.

By introducing ads to its streaming service, Amazon has created another way for brands to reach consumers beyond traditional search. Its growing sports programming also gives advertisers access to valuable audiences that are difficult to reach through traditional digital formats.

Thursday Night Football is one example. The program averaged 17.7 million viewers through the first six games of the 2026 season, marking its strongest start yet. Amazon is also expanding its NBA coverage, giving advertisers more opportunities to reach sports audiences.

But the bigger opportunity now is how Amazon connects these advertising formats. For example, a consumer might see a brand during a live sports broadcast, encounter a sponsored product while browsing Amazon, and eventually complete a purchase through the marketplace.

The company, however, still faces intense competition from other hyperscalers, especially those with massive advertising ecosystems and strong AI capabilities. Regulatory scrutiny, privacy concerns, and potential changes in consumer shopping behavior could also affect its business.

Still, Amazon offers something far bigger than traditional advertising: the ability to reach customers, influence their purchasing decisions, and measure sales within a single ecosystem. That raises the question of how much investors are paying for Amazon.

Is Amazon stock a buy at its current valuation?

At a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 22, Amazon is reasonably priced, especially with many Wall Street analysts rating the stock a buy. Not only that, the average price target is $327, implying a 33% upside over the next year.

These targets are possible as Amazon becomes more than an e-commerce and cloud computing giant. Its advertising business is emerging as another powerful growth engine, making it a solid investment in the next phase of digital advertising.

news.Title: Sandisk Stock is Falling Sharply. Here's the Price at Which I'd Buy.
news.Content:
Western Digital (NYSE: WD) spun off Sandisk (NASDAQ: SNDK), one of the world's largest flash memory chipmakers, in Feb. 2025. Sandisk's stock started trading independently at $36 per share, but it eventually soared to a record high of $2,335 per share on June 25, 2026.

That rally was driven by the explosive growth of the AI market , which forced data centers to upgrade their servers with faster solid-state drives (SSDs). But as of this writing, Sandisk's stock trades at $835. Let's see why its stock was cut in half -- and if it's becoming too cheap to ignore.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

How fast is Sandisk growing?

For years, Sandisk was a cyclical producer of NAND chips, which are used as flash memory in SD cards, USB drives, and SSDs. Western Digital, a leader in platter-based hard disk drives (HDDs), acquired Sandisk in 2016 to increase its exposure to SSDs -- which were smaller, faster, more power-efficient, and less prone to physical damage than HDDs.

As the data center market expanded, Sandisk launched ultra-dense enterprise SSDs to consolidate dozens of hardware server racks into single drives. But when WD spun off Sandisk, the AI market's expansion hadn't generated massive tailwinds for that business yet.

In fiscal 2025 (which ended in July 2025), Sandisk's revenue rose 10%, its adjusted gross margin jumped from 14.8% to 30.3%, and it returned to profitability on an adjusted basis.

But in fiscal 2026, its revenue surged 176%, its adjusted gross margin more than doubled to 71.6%, and its adjusted EPS skyrocketed 2,271%. That explosive growth -- which was entirely driven by the AI market's insatiable demand for high-density enterprise SSDs -- propelled Sandisk's stock to its all-time high this June.

For fiscal 2027, analysts expect Sandisk's revenue and adjusted EPS to rise 145% and 220%, respectively. Yet its stock trades at less than four times this year's adjusted EPS.

Is Sandisk's stock ridiculously undervalued?

Sandisk's stock trades at such a low multiple for three reasons. First, it's still valued as a cyclical chipmaker rather than a high-growth AI stock. Looking past its current growth spurt, analysts expect its revenue to only rise 22% in fiscal 2028 and less than 1% in fiscal 2029.

Second, the AI market will face unpredictable challenges after the Democrats swept the House and Senate during the midterm elections. Several prominent Democrats -- including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa -- want to pause the construction of new data centers.

Story Continues

Lastly, rising interest rates are making it difficult for AI infrastructure companies to secure fresh funds. All of those challenges could finally cool the AI market -- and the current chip shortages could quickly turn into supply gluts as the market gets saturated with excess chips.

The bulls expect these headwinds to dissipate as more companies overcome the macro and regulatory challenges and ramp up their AI spending again. The bears warn that Sandisk -- and other AI memory chipmakers like Micron (NASDAQ: MU) and SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY) -- could sink a lot lower if the AI growth cycle doesn't last as long as expected.

Over the past three months, Sandisk's insiders sold nearly 23 times as many shares as they bought. There were also 8.5 times as many sellers as buyers over the past 12 months. That chilly insider sentiment suggests Sandisk might struggle to revisit its all-time highs.

When would I buy Sandisk?

Sandisk's stock looks shaky right now, but I think the mid-$830s is actually a good entry point for long-term investors who can tune out the near-term noise.

Sandisk has a limited trading history, but Micron's forward price-to-earnings ratio has usually bottomed out at 3x-4x during cyclical downturns. Therefore, Sandisk's downside potential could be limited at these levels, even if the AI boom abruptly ends. But if the AI boom accelerates, its current growth cycle could last a lot longer -- and its stock could fetch a higher valuation.

Brazil's political environment, especially the presidential runoff on Oct. 25, added another source of pressure. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's unexpected reelection triggered a broad sell-off in Brazilian assets, including Mercado Libre shares, and heightened concerns about currency volatility. The sell-off pushed MELI toward its recent lows, raising the possibility that the stock is establishing a bottom.

→ Google's Credit Backstop May Be TeraWulf's Biggest Advantage

At least one analyst called out MELI's post-election plunge as an overreaction: BTIG's Marvin Fong also pointed to foreign exchange (FX) conversion as the near-term risk and said investors should look to the Q3 and Q4 results for clarity. Morgan Stanley's Andrew Rubin echoed the sentiment, highlighting FX risk alongside the company's strengths.

Story Continues

Among those strengths is its expanding credit portfolio, which is not tied to local rates.

Rubin also views a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 27 times projected 2027 earnings as an attractive entry point. That would put the stock in the $ 1,500 to $ 1,600 range, depending on the estimate—lower than the early-November price action, but aligned with a technical bottom. The technical support is approximately $1,540 and has been tested through by two successive rebounds, including one triggered by the election sell-off.

Analysts' price targets remain attractive, with the lowest target at $1,750 and the consensus target near $2,200, reflecting about 45% upside.

Recent revisions, however, have been mixed. Following Q3 earnings, BTIG lowered its price target to $2,050, while Cantor Fitzgerald reduced its target to $2,000. Both firms maintained bullish ratings, suggesting continued confidence in Mercado Libre's longer-term prospects despite near-term profitability concerns.

The question is what might put analysts in a more bullish posture. Signs of strength would likely alleviate fear of near-term margin compression and improve long-term visibility.

Institutional data suggests this group will limit downside risk as the year progresses. Institutions own approximately 88% of the stock, a sign of strong conviction, and have accumulated on balance this year.

The red flag is that early Q4 activity has been relatively balanced, reflecting uncertainty ahead of the Q3 earnings release on Nov. 4, and could easily tip into distribution if the company's outlook deteriorates.

Mercado Libre's Q3 Earnings Reveal the Cost of Aggressive Growth

Mercado Libre'sQ3 results failed to trigger an immediately bullish stock price response, but that doesn't make them any less impressive in terms of growth.

The problem is profitability. Net margin came in at 4.2%, while operating margin declined to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier, reflecting the costs of aggressive investments in shipping, fulfillment, and marketing. Revenue grew 45.1% year over year (YOY) to $10.75 billion, driven by strength in both operating segments and outpacing MarketBeat's reported consensus.

On the retail side, total payment value grew 53% YOY to $109 billion, gross merchandise volume grew 38%, and the number of products sold increased 36%. User growth and penetration were also solid, revealing the success of management's strategy. Unique average buyers increased 22%, itmes per buyer increased 12%, and same- and next-day shipping improved 49%, revealing the rapid integration of MELI services into local lifestyles.

On the fintech side, assets under management rose 67%, the credit portfolio grew 62%, and monthly active users grew 29%, fueling strong cash flow and a positive outlook.

Could Mercado Libre's Investment Strategy Unlock Higher Profits?

One risk for investors is the timing and peak of spending. The company has not established a clear timetable for when its aggressive investment cycle will moderate, and elevated spending could continue for years. In this scenario, spending fears and margin compression could keep MELI shares from reaching their full potential.

The opportunity, however, is the transition from aggressive investment to harvesting profits. Eventually, spending could slow, allowing margins to widen and MELI to experience a strong surge in earnings growth, potentially unlocking price-multiple expansion.

Spending headwinds aside, Mercado Libre continues to generate strong earnings per share (EPS). In Q3, the company reported $8.83 in GAAP EPS and $285 million in adjusted free cash flow, helping to sustain balance sheet health and advance its strategy.

The majority of the company's debt is tied to fintech and offset by corresponding receivables and low net leverage. Net debt, including fintech debt, runs at about 2x adjusted EBITDA, a manageable level given the company's financial position. Excluding fintech debt, the company maintains a net cash position. Major credit rating agencies rate it investment grade, though on the low end of the investment-grade spectrum.

Mercado Libre's biggest threat is competition. Now that it's opened the e-commerce gates, companies like Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Temu (NASDAQ: PDD) are moving in. The risk is lost share, sluggish growth, and persistently compressed margins as the company fights to retain leadership.

news.Title: 4 Stocks I'm Not Selling Even If the Fed Keeps Raising Rates
news.Content:
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September, and another hike is widely expected by the end of the year. The relationship between higher interest rates and stock market returns is complicated, but because higher rates raise the cost of borrowing, they can put downward pressure on equity markets as investors brace for lower corporate earnings.

This is certainly a meaningful risk worth monitoring, but there are plenty of stocks that could perform well over the long run regardless of whether the Fed raises interest rates again soon. Four of my holdings fit the bill, in my view, and I intend to keep all four intact well beyond the next interest rate increase. Here are these four stocks: Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT), and Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

1. Johnson & Johnson

Johnson & Johnson's business is relatively insensitive to interest rate hikes, a tool the Federal Reserve uses to slow spending and economic activity and rein in inflation. This can lead to lower demand for many products and services, but not for the kind that Johnson & Johnson offers. The pharmaceutical giant boasts a deep pipeline of lifesaving drugs, which should remain in high demand regardless of economic conditions. Johnson & Johnson's medical device business is also fairly resilient. And on top of that, Johnson & Johnson boasts a rock-solid balance sheet.

Perhaps the best evidence for that claim is the company's AAA rating -- the highest rating possible -- from S&P Global. Of course, none of that guarantees that Johnson & Johnson will perform well over the next year. But the company's business is well-equipped to navigate a high-interest rate environment and continue performing well long after, as it expands its product lineup through innovation. Finally, Johnson & Johnson is a fantastic income stock. It has increased its dividends for 64 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King , or a stock with at least 50 straight annual payout hikes.

2. Amazon

Amazon has a vast business that spans e-commerce, cloud computing, advertising, video and music streaming, and more. Some of the company's segments could experience lower demand if interest rates continue to rise. For instance, corporations may reduce their advertising budgets and demand fewer cloud services as customers cut retail spending. This may lead to lower revenue and earnings than the tech leader would otherwise generate. But I'd stick with Amazon through thick and thin. Here's why.

Story Continues

First, the company has a resilient business that can withstand challenging economic conditions, as it has demonstrated in the past. Consider, for instance, that Amazon had $114.23 billion in cash, equivalents, and marketable securities as of the end of the third quarter. This grants the company significant financial flexibility. Second, Amazon is a leader in some industries, such as cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI), with massive long-term opportunities. It could tap into these markets for years after interest rates have risen and fallen. I am staying put.

3. Walmart

The retail landscape could experience lower demand in a high-interest rate environment. At first glance, that could mean trouble for Walmart, but there is more to the story. The Federal Reserve's efforts to combat inflation may push consumers even more toward companies that offer them the most bang for their buck. In the retail industry, few can beat Walmart at this game. One of the company's most important strategic advantages is its EDLP (Every Day Low Price) strategy.

Walmart's ability to offer competitive prices could help it withstand a higher-rate environment and perform relatively well, especially compared to most of its retail peers. The company also boasts attractive long-term prospects. Its e-commerce and advertising businesses have performed well and should help increase margins over the long run. Finally, Walmart is also a Dividend King, having raised its payouts for 53 consecutive years. It is a top pick for long-term income seekers.

4. Berkshire Hathaway

Berkshire Hathaway has several strengths that could keep it relatively insulated from the negative impact of higher interest rates. First, its operations are fairly diversified and include some businesses that tend to perform particularly well when interest rates rise. Consider the company's insurance operations, which are its single largest source of revenue. Insurance companies make money by investing insurance premiums in fixed-income assets, including bonds. Higher interest rates mean higher yields on newly purchased bonds.

Second, Berkshire Hathaway is sitting on a ton of cash and other highly liquid assets. The company ended the second quarter with $365.5 billion in cash, equivalents, and Treasury bills. In a higher-interest rate environment, Berkshire Hathaway can invest its maturing Treasury bills at higher yields.

The company's massive liquid assets also give it the flexibility to invest in stocks on dips in case challenging macroeconomic conditions trigger a sell-off. Berkshire has gone through significant changes in recent years. Most notably, Warren Buffett is no longer its CEO. But the underlying business remains solid, and the culture hasn't changed. That makes Berkshire a great stock to hold onto.

news.Title: TSMC Makes the Chips for Both Nvidia and AMD. Here's What a $5,000 Investment Could Be Worth by 2030.
news.Content:
When you hear investors talk about AI, names like Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) pop up all the time. While those are great stock picks, investors can also go a layer deeper and look at a stock like Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE: TSM). Taiwan Semiconductor is a chip foundry, which means that it manufactures the chips that giants like Nvidia and AMD design.

Because it's selling its services to most of the competitors in the AI chip race, TSMC is set to keep profiting from the infrastructure build-out no matter which of them is gaining or losing ground. All TSMC cares about is whether companies are spending more and more on data centers each year. If they are, then TSMC will need to produce more chips to meet demand. Considering the language the market has heard from some of the AI hyperscalers and computing unit providers recently, I'd say it's a safe bet that 2027 will be another year for the record books.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That bodes well for TSMC, and I think a $5,000 investment made now could be worth far more by 2030.

Taiwan Semiconductor's scale is unmatched

Taiwan Semiconductor is the giant in its industry. Nobody else comes close to the chip production capacity that it has, and it accounted for over 70% of global third-party foundry revenue during the second quarter. So, if Nvidia or AMD wanted to switch a large share of their business away from TSMC to another foundry, they likely couldn't. Only TSMC has the production capacity necessary to meet the insatiable demand for AI computing power.

However, neither of these two would likely dream of switching foundry partners. Leadership teams at both have many times discussed how valuable their companies' relationships with TSMC are. Since TSMC always has innovative chip fabrication technology combined with excellent manufacturing yields, it has become a strong partner to many companies.

For years, the only thing about TSMC that investors could find fault with was the proximity of most of its foundries to mainland China. The Chinese government has long made clear that it wants to take control over the island of Taiwan, and concerns persist that it will at some point attempt to do so. Such a military conflict would put TSMC's foundries and exports at risk, and that will remain an issue. However, TSMC is in the midst of investing $265 billion in U.S. chip production facilities, which will help geographically diversify its operations. That's a huge deal and helps solidify TSMC's future.

Story Continues

As for future growth, a while back, TSMC management forecast that its AI-related chip revenue would grow at a compound annual rate in the high 50% range through 2029. When asked on last month's earnings call if he could offer an update to that figure, CEO C.C. Wei said that the company doesn't have one, but that demand is robust, and TSMC will probably grow even faster than that.

I think that pretty much confirms that TSMC will stay on its current growth trajectory through 2030, providing investors with large gains.

Taiwan Semiconductor's business will drive stock results

Currently, TSMC trades at 26 times trailing earnings, which is lower than where it has traded for the majority of the past three years.

TSM P/E Ratio data by YCharts. P/E = price-to-earnings.

This means that today's stock price is attractive, and that future share price moves will be driven by business growth. Next year, the company expects about 38% revenue growth, on top of the 47% expected for 2026. For the remainder of the AI build-out, I think a companywide growth rate of 35% through 2030 isn't out of the question, especially considering the increased production capacity that is coming online in the U.S.

Should TSMC's stock grow at the same pace as its business, a 35% annualized growth rate from 2027 to 2030 would cause the stock to rise 232%. That would turn a $5,000 investment made today into a stake worth over $16,000 in 2030.

That's a great return in just a few years, and as long as the AI build-out stays strong through 2030 (and many projections indicate that it will), Taiwan Semiconductor will remain a great stock holding.

In the meantime, Nvidia had two of the top five unusually active options yesterday, with Vol/OI ratios of 144.55 and 78.03. Both expire in a week. The two calls point to a Bull Call Spread.

Story Continues

The options flow confirms it.

As you can see above, two trades for 4,113 contracts occurred at 10:48:35 ET yesterday. They were part of a new multi-leg trade. In this example, the institution bought a Nov. 13 $192.50 call for $4.04 per share and sold a Nov. 13 $197.50 call for $2.49 per share in premium income to partially offset the cost of the long call for a net debit of $1.55 per share.

Here's how the bull call spread looks today. As you can see, the net debit has increased by 90 cents to $2.45, which pushes the breakeven to $194.95, up from $194.05. You'll achieve the maximum profit of $2.55 is achieved if Nvidia's share price is above $197.50 at expiration next Friday. Even with the 90-cent move, the likelihood of making money on the bull call spread is 45.9%, so you've still got time to make this bet.

AT&T Is a Better Short-Term Bet

AT&T (T) had two unusually active options yesterday. Both puts. The options flow set up either a Bear Put Spread or a Bull Put Spread. The two trades for 898 contracts happened at 14:47:44 ET.

Based on yesterday's trade, the bull put spread involves selling the Nov. 13 $21.50 put for $0.34 in premium income and buying the Nov. 13 $21 put for $0.20, for a net credit of $0.14. The trader makes money if the share price is $21.37 [$21.50 strike price - $0.14 net credit] or higher a week from today.

The maximum profit of $14 per contract occurs if the share price is at $21.50 or higher at expiration. The maximum loss of $0.36 [$21.50 strike price - $21 strike price - $0.14 net credit] occurs if the share price is at or below $21 on Nov. 13. The likelihood of making or losing money on this bet is 55%/45%.

The bear put spread involves buying the Nov. 13 $21.50 put for $0.34 and selling the Nov. 13 $21 put for $0.20 in premium income, for a net debit of $0.14. If the share price is below the breakeven of $21.36 [$21.50 strike price - $0.14 net debit] a week from today, the bear put spread makes money.

The maximum profit of $14 per contract occurs if the share price is at $21 or lower at expiration. The maximum loss of $0.36 [$21.50 strike price - $21 strike price - $0.14 net debit] occurs if the share price is at or above $21.50 on Nov. 13. The likelihood of making or losing money on this bet is 34%/66%.

The odds say the bull spread is the way to go.

Is Alphabet's Terrible October in the Rearview Mirror?

Alphabet (GOOGL) had 10 unusually active options in yesterday's trading, with DTEs (days to expiration) ranging from 8 to 161. However, the Jan. 15/2027 $325 call caught my attention.

Looking at the options flow for GOOGL for Jan. 15/2027, the two calls shown below traded at the same time yesterday and the trade sizes matched. This multi-leg trade was the highest volume for the $325/$360 combination. Eight other multi-leg trades had trade sizes above 1,000 and the same $325/$360 combination.

I haven't looked at the other eight, but these two scream a bull call spread. The institution that made these trades bought 7,500 Jan. 15/2027 $325 calls for $4.75 per share and sold 7,500 Jan. 15/2027 $360 calls for $1.28 per share in premium income, for a net debit of $3.47 per share. The bull call spread lowered the long call cost by 27%, or $960,000.

The net debit today for the $325/$360 combination is $3.76. It's a low-risk, high-reward bet.

The profit/loss picture chart is shown below. For every call, you're risking $376 to generate as much as $3,124 [$360 strike price - $325 strike price - $3.76 net debit * 100] in profit, an 830.85% return over a little more than two months. You make some money if the share price is $328.77 or higher at expiration, maxing out at $360.

It's probably better odds than a Powerball ticket.

news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ) is starting to look uncomfortably similar to Cisco at the peak of the dot-com boom, according to veteran investor George Noble.

Noble warned Thursday that Nvidia is increasingly helping finance the same ecosystem buying its AI hardware, creating what he sees as a potentially dangerous feedback loop.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with NVDA.

Is NVDA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

His concern centers on customer financing, lease guarantees and equity investments in startups that ultimately spend heavily on Nvidia chips.

The comparison is important because Cisco used aggressive vendor financing during the late 1990s to help customers buy networking equipment. When many of those customers later struggled, demand collapsed and Cisco shares eventually fell about 89% from their peak, according to Noble's analogy.

Nvidia's model is not identical.

The company announced in August that it was partnering with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to establish AI-compute financing platforms capable of mobilizing more than $500 billion of third-party capital over time. Nvidia says those vehicles are designed to independently finance AI infrastructure and broaden access to compute.

That distinction matters because much of the capital is expected to come from external investors rather than Nvidia's own balance sheet.

Still, Noble's argument is that the ecosystem becomes more fragile if chip vendors, infrastructure financiers and AI startups become increasingly dependent on one another to sustain ever-larger spending commitments.

He also pointed to weakening technical signals in Nvidia shares, including a rising-wedge breakdown and the stock moving below its 200-day moving average.

Investor Takeaway

I think the most important part of Noble's warning is not the Cisco comparison itself.

It is the question behind it: how much of AI demand is truly end-user driven, and how much is being accelerated by financing structures that make enormous infrastructure purchases easier to fund?

There is an important counterargument.

Nvidia is not simply lending money directly to weak customers. Its financing initiative involves some of the world's largest asset managers and banks, with those institutions expected to independently underwrite AI infrastructure.

That makes the setup materially different from a simplistic Cisco repeat.

But if AI customers eventually struggle to generate enough revenue to support their capital commitments, financing availability could tighten quicklyand hardware demand could fall with it.

For investors, the key things to watch are AI-cloud utilization, customer cash flow, financing terms, hyperscaler capex, startup defaults and whether Nvidia's ecosystem investments continue expanding faster than end-market monetization .

Noble sees Cisco all over again.

The real test is whether AI customers can eventually pay for the infrastructure without needing the boom to finance itself.

Microsoft has been turning off computing capacity rented from Oracle in recent months after declining to renew the contract, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. The rented capacity became less useful over time because it no longer met Microsoft's specifications, the people said. The Oracle hardware relied on older-generation chips from Nvidia, which may have limited its suitability for Microsoft's evolving AI workloads.
