news.Title: Microchip (MCHP) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Senior Vice President and CFO - Eric Bjornholt

President and CEO - Steve Sanghi

Head of Investor Relations - Sajid Daudi

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Eric Bjornholt, Senior Vice President and CFO. Thank you, Eric. You may begin.

Eric Bjornholt: All right. Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone. During the course of this conference call, we will be making projections and other forward-looking statements regarding future events or the future financial performance of the company. We wish to caution you that such statements are predictions and that actual events or results may differ materially. We refer you to our press releases of today, as well as our recent filings with the SEC that identify important risk factors that may impact Microchip's business and results of operations. In attendance with me today are Steve Sanghi, Microchip's President and CEO, and Sajid Daudi, Microchip's Head of Investor Relations.

I will comment on our second quarter fiscal year 2027 financial performance, and Steve will provide commentary on our results and discuss the current business environment as well as our guidance. We will then be available to respond to specific investor and analyst questions. We are including information in our press release and on this conference call on various GAAP and non-GAAP measures. We have posted a full GAAP to non-GAAP reconciliation on the investor relations page of our website at www.microchip.com and included reconciliation information in our earnings press release, which we believe you will find useful when comparing our GAAP and non-GAAP results.

We have also posted a summary of our outstanding debt and leverage metrics on our website. I will now go through some of the operating results, including net sales, gross margin, and operating expenses. Other than net sales, I will be referring to these results on a non-GAAP basis, which is based on expenses prior to the effect of our acquisition activities, share-based compensation, and certain other adjustments as described in our earnings press release and in the reconciliations on our website. Our non-GAAP financial results met or exceeded the guidance we provided on August 6, 2026. Net sales in the September quarter were $1.622 billion, which was up 9.2% sequentially and up 42.2% from the September 2025 quarter.

We had several infrequent items that positively impacted net sales by about $53 million in the September quarter that we do not expect to repeat in the December quarter. These items were all at 100% gross margin and included approximately $21 million impact of our pricing change on inventory in the distribution channel, $22 million in licensing revenue from patent licensing transactions in excess of what we expect in the December quarter, and a $10 million benefit from a long-term contract with a customer. We have posted a summary of our net sales by product line and geography on our website for your reference. On a non-GAAP basis, gross margins were 66.5%, including capacity underutilization charges of $26.6 million.

Story Continues

Non-GAAP gross margins were positively impacted by higher licensing revenue in the quarter, as well as the impact of our pricing change that was implemented in the September quarter. Non-GAAP operating expenses were at 27% of sales, and operating income was 39.5% of sales. Non-GAAP net income was $559.2 million, and non-GAAP earnings per diluted share were $0.97, which was $0.04 above the midpoint of our guidance. On a GAAP basis in the September quarter, gross margins were 65.9%.

Total operating expenses were $603.5 million and included acquisition intangible amortization of $90.2 million, special charges of $7.9 million, which was primarily driven by our activities associated with our closure of Fab 2, and acquisition-related expenses, share-based compensation of $62.2 million, and $5.3 million of other expenses. The GAAP net income attributable to common shareholders was $373.6 million, or $0.68 per share, and included a tax benefit of $0.13 per share related to a valuation allowance release on tax attributes. Our non-GAAP cash tax rate was 5.7% in the September quarter, and we expect to have a tax rate of about 6.5% for fiscal year 2027.

Our tax rate is down from our previous forecast for a variety of reasons, including the impacts of a reduction in inventory reserves and a higher percentage of our taxable income being in jurisdictions with lower tax rates. Our inventory balance at September 30, 2026, was $1.117 billion. We had 184 days of inventory at the end of the September quarter, which was up nine days from the end of the June quarter. Inventory increased in the quarter as we received some high-dollar-value wafers from our foundry partners in anticipation of future growth and built some finished goods inventory.

Included in our September quarter ending inventory was 12 days of long life cycle, high-margin products whose manufacturing capacity has been end-of-lifed by our supply chain partners. Inventory at our distributors in the September quarter was at 25 days, which was flat compared to the June quarter and at the lower end of what we have experienced historically. Our cash flow from operating activities was $419.2 million in the September quarter. Our adjusted free cash flow was $377.1 million in the September quarter. As of September 30, our consolidated cash and total investment position was $457 million. Our net debt decreased by $31.7 million during the September quarter, and this is after funding the acquisition of Hailo.

Our adjusted EBITDA in the September quarter was $705.4 million and 43.5% of net sales. Our trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA was $2.162 billion. Our net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 2.36 at September 30, 2026. We expect our net debt to adjusted EBITDA to continue to reduce as we progress through fiscal year 2027. Capital expenditures were $23.1 million in the September quarter, and we expect capital expenditures for fiscal year 2027 to be about $100 million. Depreciation expense in the September quarter was $36 million. I will now turn it over to Steve, who will provide some additional commentary on our September quarter results and our guidance for the December quarter. Steve?

Steve Sanghi: Thank you, Eric, and good afternoon, everyone. I will reflect a bit on our performance in the September quarter. The September quarter was an excellent quarter for Microchip, with broad-based growth as we beat the high end of our guidance in net sales, and our non-GAAP financial metrics like gross margin percentage, operating expense percentage, operating profit percentage, and earnings per share all met or beat our guidance. Our industrial and data center end markets were the two biggest drivers of our growth. Across our end markets, new design wins are increasingly supporting that growth.

Our end market split for the September quarter as a percentage of net sales, excluding licensing revenue, was industrial at 34.6%, data center at 16.7%, aerospace and defense at 16.1%, automotive at 14.2%, communication at 8.2%, consumer appliances at 7.3%, and compute at 2.9%. From the September quarter 2025 to the September quarter 2026, net sales from industrial grew 50.3%, data center grew 55.7%, aerospace and defense grew 41%, automotive grew 19.3%, communication grew 43.5%, consumer appliances grew 26.7%, and compute declined 1.6%. Net sales from our data center business unit was over $250 million in the September quarter and is well on its way to be $1 billion in calendar year 2026.

For calendar 2026, about half of our data center business comes from our standard products, and about half comes from our Data Center Solutions Business Unit. On the standard product side, design wins are building across many products. In power, our digital power controllers are winning across AI data center power applications, from server power supplies to battery backup units. In system management, we offer the parts that sense, control, and connect a server or rack, and our Gigabit Ethernet switches and USB hubs are gaining design win momentum in management networks.

With respect to our Gen 6 PCIe switch and retimer products, we had 19 design wins at the end of September quarter, up from 12 design wins at the end of June quarter. As of today, we now have 24 total design wins. These incremental wins will begin to ramp net sales next year and help position us across a growing range of next-generation data center platforms. As these deployments scale, so does our opportunity across the broader data center portfolio, including timing, security, and networking. I would like to give one more organizational update. As you know, after my return to Microchip as CEO two years ago, I reorganized the company into five pillars.

These pillars were microcontrollers, analog and power, networking and connectivity, high-performance compute, and AI on the edge. There is a Senior Vice President heading up each of these pillars. Our Data Center Solutions Business Unit reports into the networking and connectivity pillar. Because of our focus on our Data Center Solutions Business Unit, called the DCS, I have decided to pull up the DCS business unit to report directly to me at the executive staff level. The head of that business unit is Brian McCarson, who has spoken at these earnings calls before and will now report directly to me. Our design wins are not limited to data centers.

In aerospace and defense, we are winning designs across regions, products, and applications, from satellite communications and laser terminals to unmanned systems, by adapting our commercial technologies for space and defense. In one recent case, a defense technology company selected our radiation-tolerant-secure FPGA over its incumbent supplier for two space avionics programs. As defense production rates ramp, so does our opportunity. Security requirements are also growing across our markets, from data centers to defense to the edge. At the edge, a leading enterprise network provider recently selected our security solution to protect its wireless networks, where quantum-resistant encryption became a requirement.

Together, data center, aerospace and defense, industrial, robotics, automotive, and the intelligent edge are the secular trends we see driving growth over the long term. I will now talk about our business environment and the guidance going forward. Our bookings were very strong in the September quarter, and our book-to-bill ratio remained well above one. We started the December quarter with a higher backlog compared to when we entered the September quarter. The September quarter saw a pivot in the business environment, with customers completing their inventory digestion to shortages appearing in certain areas because of lengthening lead times at foundries, OSAT suppliers, and in our own fabs.

Lead times for the majority of our standard products historically have been four to eight weeks. But now, with our die inventory substantially reduced and foundry and OSAT capacity constraints, we are seeing lead times broadly stretch out on many of our products. Our customer requests for expedited shipments have increased significantly from a few quarters ago. We are receiving many orders for requests inside the lead time, and they are going unsupported in the quarter. We are advising our customers to give us longer-term backlog to help better match our new lead times, which vary a lot across our product lines. Our new lead times are anywhere from six weeks to 32 weeks.

Eric just explained three infrequent items in the last quarter. First, it was an unusually strong quarter in our licensing group, with a couple of large deals closing in the September quarter. Our licensing business is usually lumpy. The second item was the one-time effect of our recent price increases, which raised the value of our distribution inventory. The third was a revenue recognition from a long-term customer contract. Those infrequent items are not present in the December quarter. Our December quarter is also our weakest quarter seasonally, because there are a lot of holidays in the quarter. Therefore, the guidance for December quarter should be viewed in that context.

Our December quarter also includes the impact of two small acquisitions that we completed, Hailo in the AI on the edge space and VORAGO in the A&D space. We expect that Hailo will add about $4 million to our sales in the December quarter, and VORAGO will add about $6 million to our net sales in the December quarter. Taking all of these factors into account, we expect our net sales in the December quarter to be between down 3% and up 1%, with a midpoint of -1%. At the midpoint, this would be up 35.4% from the year-ago quarter. December quarter is usually seasonally down 3%-5%.

This seasonal effect, combined with the infrequent items we experienced in the September quarter, puts our December quarter guidance about 5%-7% above normal seasonality. We expect our non-GAAP gross margin to be between 64%-65% of net sales. This is because of several reasons. First, the three infrequent items in the September quarter were all at 100% gross margin. Secondly, our net sales guidance is lower than what we would have expected a quarter ago. Thirdly, we have substantial unsupported backlog on high-margin products that our supply chain cannot fulfill. And finally, we're running lower level of utilization internally than what we were planning a quarter ago. All these factors are impacting our gross margin guidance.

We expect our non-GAAP operating expenses to be between 26.5% and 27% of sales. We expect our non-GAAP operating profit to be between 37% and 38.5% of sales. We expect our non-GAAP diluted earnings per share to be between $0.87 and $0.95 per share. At the midpoint, non-GAAP earnings per share would be up 107% over the year-ago quarter. Regarding our long-term model, we maintain our long-term model on a non-GAAP basis to be 65% gross margin, 25% operating expense, and 40% operating profit. With that, operator, will you please call for questions?

Operator: Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. So that we may address questions from as many participants as possible, we ask that you limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. If you have additional questions, you may requeue, and time permitting, those questions will be addressed.

One moment, please, while we poll for questions. Thank you. Our first question comes from the line of Timothy Arcuri with UBS. Please proceed.

Timothy Arcuri: Thanks a lot. Steve, I was wondering if you could help unpack a lot of these puts and takes. It seems like you said that December revenue is a little lower than what you would have thought three months ago, and fab utilization's also a little lower, yet bookings are stronger. Is this due to constraints that are downstream from you? Maybe, does that give you more visibility into March, so you could maybe give us a sense, maybe, normal seasonal, I think in March is up like 3%. Sounds like maybe you feel a little bit better about March as a result of all this. If you can just unpack that for us, that'd be great. Thanks.

Steve Sanghi: Yeah. So I think if you look at the last quarter, it was kind of noisy. The three items that we talked about were in our guidance. The licensing deals were in our guidance, the recognition of $10 million of customer contract was in our guidance, and so was the price increase. So the upside last quarter came from product sales, so we did very well. Now, when you look at the current quarter, lead times have stretched out, and a lot of the high-margin bookings we received on a lot of advanced products in pretty much every business segment cannot be fulfilled in this quarter. So, some of them are scheduled for next quarter.

As a result, I think we're guiding the December quarter to be a tad lower than we would have thought about a quarter ago. The backlog for March quarter today is much better than December quarter was at the same point in time. So, currently we're optimistic. We're not giving any guidance for the March quarter, but I think some of the constraints we're talking about are now scheduled into March quarter. So, we are hopeful that March quarter will be a stronger quarter.

Timothy Arcuri: Thanks a lot. Then maybe just as a quick follow-up. So, on the PCIe Gen 6 wins, I think, Steve, you said 14 design wins coming out of June, and it's now up to 24. Sounds like you're building some high-value inventory for that stuff too. So, when does that start to become really big revenue? If you can kind of size what the incremental could be from those wins, if possible, that'd be great.

Steve Sanghi: We are unable to dollarize the wins. The part went into production last quarter, and we have small amount of shipments in the current quarter, and they will increase every quarter from here on. Actually, there is sizable shipment this quarter, and they start increasing then from the next quarter on. The design wins are very strong, and they are turning on at various times next year. By the start of 2028, you can expect almost all 24 designs to be in production, and we are winning essentially a design a week almost.

Eric Bjornholt: Yeah, just one clarification to the way Tim asked that question is he said PCIe Gen 6, and the 24 design wins is both PCIe and the retimers. Just wanted to clarify that.

Steve Sanghi: That is correct. I think we are basically keeping them together. They are very much in the same application. Many times, retimer goes with the PCIe. We don't always win them both. In some cases, customer doesn't need the retimer, they only need the PCIe switch. But they are pretty much products are in sync. In the past, we have broken out how many on PCIe Gen 6 and how many on retimer, and I don't have that today, but we have no problem in breaking that out.

Timothy Arcuri: Okay, Steve. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Matthew Prisco with Cantor Fitzgerald. Please proceed.

Matthew Prisco: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking the question. I guess to start, if you could maybe discuss order linearity in the quarter and maybe what you've seen through October and November thus far, and any color you can offer on those booking trends across end markets would be appreciated. Thanks.

Eric Bjornholt: Bookings were quite strong all the way through September, so nothing really to point out there. And then October was another good month of bookings where backlog, overall backlog continued to grow. November's just been a few days, but nothing odd to report.

Steve Sanghi: Yeah. Bookings have continued well. The backlog has continued to build. The best way to look at our December quarter is to take the $53 million out of the September quarter, which were the three infrequent items. And if you do that, then our December quarter is up about 2.3% from our September quarter, versus normal seasonality for December quarter is down 3%-5%. Therefore, I think we got no issues in how the quarter is, how the product chip backlog is, how the bookings are. All that continues well.

But the two licensing deals, a unique customer program that added $10 million of revenue recognition last quarter, and this strange effect of when you ship the inventory to distributor, you assume there's a certain amount of disti price out protection on that, and then the rest of it you recognize as a revenue. When you increase the price, then that disti price protection becomes less, and you have to capture that as a one-time revenue in the quarter. That was about $21 million. Those items made it very noisy. If you peel through all that, and we're giving you complete visibility, if you take those out, then the quarter is up 2.3%.

In that 2.3%, there's $10 million from two acquisitions, $4 million from Hailo and $6 million from VORAGO. We broke that out too, so take that out too if you like, and the 2.3% will go down to maybe 1.5% or something, versus down 4% at the midpoint. There's no problem in how the business is doing, and we remain optimistic for the next quarter. Backlog is good, bookings are coming in. That's how you should view the quarter in that context.

Matthew Prisco: Very helpful. Thank you. Maybe you can offer some more color on what you're seeing in terms of those constraints today, how those foundry OSAT constraints changed over the last 90 days. I believe you added internal constraints this quarter. How are you responding to these constraints overall, and how do you expect that situation to evolve as we look into 2027? Thank you.

Steve Sanghi: Incrementally, we have additional capacity allocation every quarter, which will continue to provide growth. But we could use more than that. On various different nodes, we have more capacity the following quarter. Therefore, some of the orders from this quarter are scheduled into next quarter, and I believe some of the orders from the next quarter will move into the June quarter, where we have more capacity. We're not unique. I think the entire industry is seeing it. Demand is stronger than the capacity available. With whatever is happening in the market right now with data center, AI infrastructure, concerns whether they will all be built or not built, I think there's a silver lining in it.

The whole thing was just too much hot air, and if some air comes out and capacity becomes available at OSATs and foundries for broad-based business, I think there is still silver lining in it.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Joe Quatrochi with Wells Fargo. Please proceed.

Joe Quatrochi: Yeah, thanks for taking the question. You saw a nice acceleration in the industrial demand this quarter. I was wondering if you could just talk about what you're seeing there, and maybe just on that last line you said, how do we think about your exposure to just everything around the data center infrastructure build, maybe outside of the data hall?

Steve Sanghi: I think, when it comes to industrial is the broadest market segment there is. I mean, what is industrial? It's not a narrow set of things. Industrial is factories, cities, hotels, lighting, robotics, medical. Industrial is very, very broad, and we're seeing opportunities in industrial. Some of it got driven by industrial was sort of the last one to recover, I think, two or three quarters ago. So, it's seeing substantial recovery from that point, and a lot of new design wins in every single area, robotics, medical, process control, factories, farming, equipment, appliances. Everything is growing, so it's very, very difficult to kind of explain industrial beyond that because it's so broad.

The second point of your question is on the data centers. We are early in the data center penetration, because we didn't have a lot of Gen 5 switch revenue, and you've known from past that we were very late to market on it, and therefore, we lost the Gen 5 business. With Gen 6, we are regaining a lot of the market share, and a lot of it is not in our revenue. So, for us, it's all upside, where if it slows down, it could be downside for the people who have a lot of that business.

In terms of our other half of our data center exposure, which is through microcontroller, analog, power, switches, security, USB, Ethernet, these are very broad-based products where data center is really a small portion of the overall shipments to all the end markets. If certain data centers won't get built, a lot of that upside is not in our forecast.

Joe Quatrochi: Thanks. As we're thinking about just kind of the gross margin puts and takes into the December quarter, how should we think about this underutilization charges? There's a nice improvement this quarter. Do we keep thinking that's somewhat linear as we move forward?

Eric Bjornholt: It will not be linear. This quarter, we are not anticipating any sort of big improvement. We actually built finished goods last quarter and don't really want to do that again this quarter, so we're slowing down some of the assembly and test operations. We're still doing the ramp in our wafer fabs, where Steve had mentioned in his prepared remarks that die inventory is getting low in certain cases. It's a balance, but you will not see the large reduction in utilization or underutilization charges this quarter that you saw last quarter. That's still upside in front of us in future quarters.

Steve Sanghi: December quarter historically is kind of weak, so we took that in cautiously, but it will accelerate again next quarter because then we go into good March quarter followed by two strong June and September quarters before we get another weak December quarter next year. So utilization should start to improve, but not linearly.

Joe Quatrochi: Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Chris Caso with Wolfe Research. Please proceed.

Chris Caso: Yes, thanks. Good evening. The question is on pricing and the impact on the December quarter from some of the pricing actions that you took previously. What was the magnitude of that in December quarter? I seem to recall from last quarter that was one of the factors you had expected to be an offset because, as you said, you knew some of those three items that would not recur in the December quarter. I seem to recall that pricing was going to be one of the offsets for the December quarter.

Steve Sanghi: You are correct. We expected that to be offset, and the remaining pricing is being effective this quarter because pricing change was done in the middle of the last quarter. However, because of what we described before, some of the fairly large dollar item products with very high margin, supply chain cannot fulfill this quarter, which is kind of offsetting the improvement we would have seen.

Chris Caso: Right. Okay. Would it be right to assume that as supply improves, as you get the ability to supply some of these higher-margin products, perhaps some of the products where the price has gone up but you can't ship it right now, that you would see some of that benefit as you go into calendar 2027? Is that the right way to think about it?

Steve Sanghi: Are you talking about benefit in revenue or benefit in something else?

Chris Caso: Well, I guess benefit in revenue from obviously being able to ship the product and the higher price, and then I guess more importantly from the margin side, because I think I understand what you're saying is that you didn't see as much of the pricing benefit that you had expected in the December quarter because you couldn't ship those products, therefore, as you finally were able to ship those products, you get that margin benefit.

Steve Sanghi: We certainly get the revenue benefit and we get some of the margin benefit, but the pricing in the industry from our suppliers has continued to go up. There's another round of price increase across the industry starting basically in January from most major foundries and OSATs. Because some of that we counted in our price increase when we did the price increase, that's why you're seeing a very good gross margin for the September quarter and pretty good gross margin in December quarter. If you're expecting it to go back to 66.5%, we're currently not projecting that.

Our long-term target is 65%, and we think we're going to have to fight that price increase with the suppliers and figure out how we deal with it, whether there is a check on our gross margin or we pass that on to the customers further. We haven't figured all that out yet.

Chris Caso: Okay. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Vivek Arya with Bank of America Securities. Please proceed.

Vivek Arya: Thanks for taking my questions. Steve, I wanted to start with more of a macro question based on your industry experience. Do you think that signals to you there are earnings cuts coming? Are we at peak demand? Just kind of what is your crystal ball telling you in terms of where we are in the cycle, and do you think all these worries are justified based on what you are seeing on the ground?

Steve Sanghi: Well, Vivek, I think there is data center and non-data center. There is nothing to worry about in the non-data center. Industrial is doing fine. Automotive is continuing to recover. Its unit count is not growing as much, low single digit, but the content is growing significantly. We are winning across new car architectures across the board. We are doing very well. Aerospace and defense is doing well. Industrial is doing well. Automotive is doing well. Communication is doing well. The issues in data center, it was all that I have been kind of saying it could not be true. The demand was explosive.

You cannot just have that large of a percentage of economy at a rate everybody expected it to grow. I think some of that is coming in check, whether it comes in check that the real estate of data centers cannot be built, or the power cannot be supplied, or the new Congress would not let it happen, or circular financing finally, you cannot do it anymore, it is not cost-effective, or people cannot monetize. Whatever the reason is, or the combination of reason is, the second derivative on data center has to come down substantially. I think you see market voting on it. To me, it is not new. I think it was predictable.

Vivek Arya: Right. What do you think that means for Microchip? Because I think in your commentary, you used the phrase that you thought September was a pivot, right? You are seeing lead times get stretched out. Do you think a lot of that demand is coming because there is a crowding out from the data center, or do you think there is kind of real kind of demand upturn? More specifically, if you look at the next several quarters for Microchip, do you think there is still the possibility of above-seasonal growth?

Steve Sanghi: Yeah, I think yes. Like I said, there is data center and non-data center. The non-data center demand is normal. It is doing well. Data center demand has been explosive. If that comes down, its effect on us would be very small because we are very much in the early stage. We are not doing billions of dollars of revenue in the data center, and all of our rest of the markets are growing, and data center is 16.7% of our business, not 100% like many of the other companies. Where the crowding out is not in demand. The crowding out is in capacity.

Data center has been crowding out capacity for trailing edge nodes because of power requirements and analog requirements and all these other things, microcontrollers and others. So, data center has been crowding out capacity at the OSAT, and in many cases, we have lost capacity, where some of it we had to bring it inside, some of it we had to move it elsewhere, and it takes time to requalify. Therefore, the backlog could not be served and will be served some in the next quarter, some in the quarter after. I think a deceleration on the data center will probably have a positive effect on our business because some of that capacity frees up.

Vivek Arya: Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Vijay Rakesh with Mizuho Securities. Please proceed.

Vijay Rakesh: Yeah. Hi. Just a quick question on the aerospace and defense side. It's kind of grown in line with Microchip's overall growth. When do you actually see aerospace and defense orders start to come back? Are these long lead orders where you have good visibility? And a quick follow-up.

Steve Sanghi: Well, aerospace and defense grew 41% September over September, so we think it is growing very well. The demand for aerospace and defense is very strong at the primes, but primes have to build up capacity, some starting from real estate. Some of them are being asked to increase the missile production by 5x or 4x. Well, they do not have the floor space to ramp the production to 4x, so they are adding capacity, buildings and machinery and all that. We are starting to get the orders, but they are scheduled out when they need it. I think aerospace and defense is not a data center kind of business, $10 million today and $200 million tomorrow.

It will grow consistently, but it is not a hockey stick because the industrial complex cannot grow at that rate.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. On the price increases, you mentioned foundry OSAT price increases. How much flexibility do you have to kind of pass through, or what are you anticipating in terms of the impact of those as you look at 2027 in terms of margin or any headwinds there? Thanks.

Steve Sanghi: Well, we consider our gross margins very healthy. Our last quarter, because of some infrequent items, was higher than target. Otherwise, it is very close to target, within 100 basis points of that. We do not want to take a second price increase to our customers so quickly when we just did a price increase in the middle of August. Just like we did that last time, we absorbed it for a while, and if the cost kept going up, then we passed the price increase. We are kind of doing similar. Right now, we are planning to not do a price increase and absorb it.

At these kind of gross margins, we do not feel that our gross margins are low.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. Thanks.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Harlan Sur with JPMorgan. Please proceed.

Harlan Sur: Yeah, good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. Book-to-bill is strongly above one. Your backlog even now continues to grow. I assume that this strong demand profile is across not just advanced foundry-based products, but across your internally manufactured products as well, right? Your overall lead times are extending. Your front-end utilizations, I would have expected to move higher this quarter, especially with your commentary on low die bank inventories as well. Why wouldn't front-end utilization charges continue to decrease this quarter? I understand back-end utilizations might be stepping down a bit, but why aren't front-end utilizations continuing to increase here in December, and therefore lower underutilization charges?

Eric Bjornholt: Harlan, the front end is reducing in the current quarter, but the back end is not going to be as fully utilized as it was the quarter before. It's the combination of those things, and we don't expect a material change in the overall underutilization charge in the quarter.

Steve Sanghi: I think one other point is that there's a perception that on in-house built fab products. There should be no constraint and there should be no lead time issue. The problem is, the inside-produced wafers also go through the OSAT. Some of it goes through our internal factory, but some of the packages we don't do, it goes through OSAT. So it sees the same constraints that our foundry wafers see. In a lot of cases, some of the capacity at our major OSAT suppliers has been displaced. AI companies, you know which ones, came in and took over the whole factory, and they pushed everybody out.

We brought some in, we brought it some to other OSAT manufacturers, but that is the crowding out of AI. It's affecting processing of inside wafers as well as outside wafers in assembly and test. We are rapidly improving that situation. Ordinarily, we do an inside versus outside analysis when there's a payback to do inside. Not everything we can do cheaper inside. Sometimes we cannot keep the tool fully busy because we could not fully utilize the tool, so therefore we keep it outside. But when we get displaced outside, we can't produce it, a very good margin product, then cost doesn't matter, then we want to bring it in and produce it.

So we're making those moves, but those moves take six months. Some of this displacement only happened just a couple of months ago. So those are the things we are struggling with, and that's why I said that some deceleration of the AI demand actually would be quite positive early on.

Harlan Sur: Got it. Okay, and I appreciate that. As my follow-up, Steve, we are seeing a lot more adoption overall of integration of machine learning and AI capabilities into all of these sort of embedded applications across industrial, automotive, even consumer, right? For many of these applications, you don't need a standalone NPU, like your acquired product family from Hailo, but you could leverage embedded NPU accelerators, right? Can you just remind us, your 32-bit MCU product lines, do you have product families with embedded NPU, and are you seeing accelerated adoption of NPU-based MCUs for these types of embedded, like machine learning AI applications?

Steve Sanghi: Our in-house microcontroller and microprocessor product lines did not have AI acceleration in them. No hardware acceleration. We had some software acceleration. We did have some hardware acceleration available on our FPGAs and our Data Center Solutions Business Unit, but not on our microcontroller business units and the microprocessor business unit, we did not. When we bought Hailo, in our microprocessor business unit, we were developing products. The first of those products was going to be available in about two and a half, three years, and the second of them was going to be available in about four and a half years, because they were serial in nature.

The product line that Hailo brought to us accelerates the roadmap by five years. Therefore, we have canceled the two products that we were developing in the NPU business unit because they have been replaced by Hailo. In fact, I have merged the Hailo and NPU business unit together, and we are advancing the Hailo roadmap, and we have canceled our NPU roadmap in the microprocessor business unit. That's how important Hailo has been for us.

Harlan Sur: I see. Okay. That makes a lot of sense. Thank you, Steve.

Steve Sanghi: Yeah.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Jim Schneider with Goldman Sachs. Please proceed.

Jim Schneider: Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. I was wondering if you could maybe broadly characterize the customer willingness to build, the OEM customer willingness to build inventory on the balance sheet at this point, given the extended lead times. Is that something that some customers and some verticals are willing to do, or is it more broad-based than that? And maybe just give us a sense about, are they even able to do that given the supply constraints you've talked about?

Steve Sanghi: I mean, right now, in broad base of customers, we do not see a desire by them to build inventory. We can hardly get them to place orders with our new lead time. Seems like, number one, lead times are moving rapidly. Secondly, semiconductor manufacturers are always telling their customers, "I want more backlog, I want more backlog." It kind of becomes a broken record, like the wolf is coming, wolf is coming, and they don't respond to it. They don't.

They don't respond to it till they get in trouble, where lead times rapidly go out, they don't have the product, they try to expedite it, we cannot serve it, the lines are down for eight weeks, and that's when there is a fire behind them and they start to place orders. We are not seeing that yet.

Jim Schneider: That's helpful color. Then just as a follow-up, just going back to the gross margin question, it seems like previously you talked about some of the higher-margin products, what you thought would benefit you in the December quarter. You talked about the reasons why those are constrained. Just wanted to make sure that I understand, is the new piece of information that those higher-margin products will come back into the mix over the next couple quarters, but perhaps the input cost increases are not going to be offset on the broader base of products? Do I have that right?

Steve Sanghi: Yeah, I think our assessment last quarter that we can keep the gross margin in the 66% range by more high-margin products coming in, the rest of the price increase kicking in, and completely offsetting the high licensing revenue and couple of other infrequent items, I think that turned out to be more aggressive than the reality has turned out. So we have backed off from that assumption. Now, we still told you always that our long-term gross margin was 65%, and there'll be times in the good times when it will go over, there'll be times in the bad times when it will go under, but we didn't guide you to a higher than 65% gross margin.

But we did say that we could maintain it in the December quarter. Now, various things have happened, partially driven by some of the high-margin products pushing out because of constraints. We can't quite get there. Question is then, why we're not getting there in March or June? Because some of the further price increases from our suppliers is kicking in. Whether we're able to offset that or not, we're not able to model it today. So that's why we're basically resetting that and saying, "Think of 65% as a long-term gross margin, and we will work very hard to get there and maintain it, but not any higher than that.

Jim Schneider: Very clear. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Blayne Curtis with Jefferies. Please proceed.

Blayne Curtis: Hey, good afternoon, guys. I wanted to ask on the trigger to pull back the utilization. Is there a certain level of inventory you don't want to grow it on an absolute basis or a certain number of days you're targeting? Just trying to understand that trigger. I think most people, I know the stock market's terrible lately, but expect a continued recovery, so I'm just trying to understand how you're thinking about managing that.

Steve Sanghi: I think the equation is very, very complex. We build hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Our product, including internal fabs and outside foundries, come from almost 40 different factories around the world, and it's a very complex equation. On some nodes, we have plenty of capacity. On other nodes, we are heavily constrained. Some of the nodes where we have enough capacity, it's a kind of product goes into our packages, like BGA and others, where the capacity is constrained. In some cases, we cannot get the substrates. In some other cases, we don't have the assembly capacity. In other cases, our test capacity has been confiscated by the AI crowd. It's a very, very complex equation.

Despite that, I think we're growing our businesses up nicely. We'll be up again next year. We're solving these problems, bringing some inside, some moving it from foundry to foundry. It's noisy. I get it. I'm frustrated by it too, and with the kind of questions you guys are asking, I get it. The only thing that's going to help is AI decelerating.

Blayne Curtis: Got you. Thank you. I wanted to ask on the auto channel. I think there's some hope that maybe that could be better. I'm kind of curious what you're seeing. Any evidence of restocking in any areas of strength in auto?

Steve Sanghi: Our auto business was up 19.3% year-over-year. I mean, for auto, that's very good. For auto, that's excellent. Auto is never going to grow 100%, 50%, 40%. The auto unit volume grows 2% or 3% best case. Our auto was up 19.3%. We're getting lots of auto design wins, and when you get a design win, it goes to production in three years. So we are harvesting some of that was designed two, three years ago, and there's a good amount of growth coming in with future designs next year and year after. But don't expect any more out of auto. It grew 19.3%. In fact, that's more than entitlement in auto.

Blayne Curtis: Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of William Stein with Truist Securities. Please proceed.

William Stein: Great. Thanks for taking my questions. First quick one is, I'm wondering if there's any meaningful influence of the two acquisitions on either cost of goods or OpEx in the near term?

Eric Bjornholt: There is. I mean, there's OpEx that come along with both of these acquisitions. We aren't going to break out profitability for either of these small acquisitions, but Hailo is investing pretty significantly in their R&D efforts, and we are definitely doubling down on that. And the VORAGO products are good products in aerospace and defense with high gross margins, and we're excited about the opportunity on that. But there absolutely is an impact on OpEx in the current quarter by having a full quarter of Hailo and almost a full quarter of VORAGO in the numbers, and that's obviously built into our guidance.

Steve Sanghi: I think to give you a little more color, VORAGO gross margin is higher than Microchip, but with $6 million revenue contribution, it doesn't move the needle in the current quarter. Hailo margins are lower than Microchip, but with $4 million in revenue, that doesn't move the needle either. In the area of OpEx, VORAGO OpEx is small, and gross margins are very high, so VORAGO is actually very profitable. So that's doing very well, but with such a small revenue, it doesn't move the needle. Hailo doesn't make money yet. They have very high R&D and small amount of revenue, and we're seeing huge opportunity.

There is a multi-hundred million dollar funnel on it already in a very quick period of time. So we will do very well in Hailo over time, but short term, we're having to absorb its higher OpEx.

William Stein: Yeah, that's very helpful. Thank you. Steve, I wanted to follow up on another question you answered earlier. You didn't quite say that, "Hey, we've been in an AI bubble," but effectively, what one might infer from what you said about all the various challenges with data center, and when you responded about how to think about the influence on your business, you—

Steve Sanghi: I didn't say it, then you said no.

William Stein: Okay.

Steve Sanghi: I'm sorry, go ahead.

William Stein: No, no. Okay, that's good. I appreciate that. But in terms of how to interpret, how to think about the go-forward model, you encouraged us to think about data center versus not, and you talked about the silver lining, but I wonder if you consider or if you think your business may be influenced from a couple of other factors. For example, data center drives some industrial demand probably for your business. Probably, it's certainly responsible for some of the price inflation we've seen.

By the way, there's a similar dynamic in aerospace and defense if you consider a lot of what's going on now, the unwind potentially related to lower spending in aerospace and defense to which you're highly exposed. So, if we were in a bubble in AI data center, couldn't this be more broadly problematic for your business?

Steve Sanghi: No, I don't think so. Data center is 16.7% of our business, and half of that 16.7% is broad-based products, and half of that are the Data Center Solutions Business Unit. The Data Center Solutions Business Unit is in the retooling phase, having lost the Gen 5, regaining market share with Gen 6. So there's all upside. In the broad-based business that we have, there would be roughly 8% of our business out of the 100. So I think this is a time, if the data center were to correct, our broad-based exposure in industrial, in automotive, in aerospace and defense, in appliances, in consumer, in computing would be very, very helpful.

Microchip should outperform in that kind of environment compared to the companies that are kind of all data center.

William Stein: Got it. Thank you.

Steve Sanghi: Yes, if I didn't say it, I'll say it again. I have been saying it, that data center is in the bubble.

William Stein: There we have it.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Joshua Buchalter with TD Cowen. Please proceed.

Joshua Buchalter: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question. Steve, you mentioned sort of a reluctance to raise pricing so close to the previous increase. In the spring, you were also mentioning, given some of the relationships you were trying to rebuild after PSP, that reluctance. I guess big picture, you are seeing pressure from input costs rising. How are you philosophically thinking about pricing from a high level? How should we expect you, from a competitive standpoint, to react as a lot of your competitors are raising prices? Thank you.

Steve Sanghi: I think we were very careful in raising prices. We immediately didn't jump on it back in January, February. We were in the process of repairing our relationships, which we have done it very successfully. That's delivering 40% growth year-over-year. When we became comfortable that our relationship was such that we can handle a price increase, we implemented it very carefully. It was small in nature, and we've been successful. We haven't lost customers. Now we're in the same mode. I think we don't want to push the luck so much. We're not greedy. We are comfortable and happy with the gross margins we have.

The other point I would make is our operating margins are higher than some of our competitors' gross margins. I mean, look at STMicro. It's not that our product prices is low. We are a premium price company. We make very good product, high quality. We fight for every cent. Our margins are very high, which means, I don't know if our costs are lower than those companies. Actual costs are very hard to compare. We don't really know. But if the costs were to be equivalent, our prices are very good. Our operating margin is higher than STMicro's gross margin. You got to give us some credit for that.

Joshua Buchalter: No, I hear you on that. Maybe for Eric, leverage is down at below 2.4x. How should we be thinking about when's the right time when you'll be able to start returning cash to investors via raising the dividend and repurchases again? Thank you both.

Eric Bjornholt: Yeah, it's a good question. We get it a lot, and it is a discussion in the boardroom. But the board definitely wants us to continue to take leverage down. We had a pretty big scare during the last downturn, and leverage went way too high. I think we're going to take a cautious approach, keep the dividend where it's at for now, and probably evaluate this as we move into next fiscal year, have a good discussion with the board, and keep investors abreast of our thoughts. But next couple of quarters, for sure, continue to get the leverage metrics down.

Joshua Buchalter: Thank you.

Eric Bjornholt: You're welcome.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Christopher Rolland with Susquehanna. Please proceed.

Christopher Rolland: Thanks for the question. Steve, you are always good with insights on the cycle. This one seems hot and maybe getting hotter. If you could probably talk about how you see or when you see the cycle perhaps ending. It does not seem like we have inventory builds and safety stock building and stuff like that we had in COVID, so probably we have some to go. Maybe adding in there, if the AI data center bubble does slow here, in your words, is that going to be enough to prolong this cycle?

Steve Sanghi: I will go back to data center and non-data center. I do not see any issues in non-data center. Like I said, even our current quarter on a product basis is sequentially up 2.3%, where seasonality is down 3%-5%. I do not see any issues. We have a very good March backlog. I think cycle continues on the non-data center. On the data center side, like I said, on our solutions business unit, Data Center Solutions Business Unit is in the retooling phase. I mean, they are winning lots of designs. If we had those designs all on Gen 5, and we are re-winning them on Gen 6, it will not be incrementally as positive.

We would have gotten revenue before, it would be a lot higher. But we lost them two years ago, and now we are winning it. We have won 24 designs on Gen 6. For us, I think it is incrementally positive. If the cycle decelerates, much of that upside and bubble is not in our numbers. It is in everybody else's numbers. It is not in our numbers.

Christopher Rolland: Understood. Given the constraints that you guys have in the expanding lead times, it does seem like this is from external manufacturing as opposed to internal. Does any of this give you reconsideration on the mix of external versus internal? It was a long time ago that you were potentially considering a 300 mm fab, but would you consider even at the front end, perhaps planning for a new fab?

Steve Sanghi: I mean, we are an IDM, integrated device manufacturer. Our bias always is what we can produce inside, we produce inside. Let's take package first, and I'll take the fab. We largely do packages where we do not have enough volume to do it cost-effectively inside. In some cases, our volume are such we can't even keep one set of tools, one pilot line busy. If you can't, then your utilization will be very low and the cost will be higher. So those are the ones we do outside. Never had an issue with it.

This is sort of the first time where AI is crowding it out and having us think through even bringing some things inside, which may be slightly higher cost, but at least we'll have the capacity. Now, if you come on the fab side, when we were considering a 300 mm fab during the post-COVID years, our plan was to do it under a license with a major foundry. Because all our wafers ran in that foundry, and the foundry was saying they will not add any trailing edge capacity, therefore, they were agreeing to give us a license at 300 mm to bring those processes inside.

When the COVID cycle busted and they had enough capacity, then we didn't want to spend a couple of billion dollars or more of CapEx, nor did they want to give the license, so that program went away. Today, the problems are not as big, and they're not as severe, and they're not multi-year problems where we have to go back and build a few billion dollars of capital to build a 300 mm fab and seek a license again. We're not thinking that because we don't think the problem is that long. It's just a short-term issue.

Eric Bjornholt: I just want to add one piece of clarification to the way you asked the question. We do have capacity constraints with some of our internal production also. There are certain products where we are behind, we cannot meet customers' lead times, and we are working as hard as we can to bring on capacity. As Steve mentioned before, even when we bring on that capacity, sometimes if it is outsourced for assembly test, we have capacity constraints even when it comes out of our fab. These constraints have grown beyond just being an outside foundry issue for us.

Christopher Rolland: Thank you, guys.

Operator: Thank you. Our last question comes from the line of Tore Svanberg with Stifel. Please proceed.

Tore Svanberg: Yes, thank you. Steve, I had a question on the OSAT capacity, the external capacity that is impacting your front-end capacity. How much visibility do you have there? I mean, is it a matter of just being on a location and waiting to get the allocation, or do you have a fairly good feel for when that is going to open up so that you can actually start ramping your own front-end utilization?

Steve Sanghi: There are multiple answers to that question. In some cases, our allocation at that OSAT is not increasing, so we are qualifying a different OSAT in a different country, and some of that is scheduled to be in production in the middle of next quarter. We will get some incremental for half the quarter and then have more even in the June quarter. In some other cases, the current OSAT is asking us to load it with a minimum batch size. Because when the batch sizes are smaller, it takes more capacity, it is less efficient for the manufacturer. So they are asking us to do minimum batch sizes.

Our volume on those packages is small, and we cannot meet the minimum batch size. Therefore, either you pay the extra price for breaking the batch size, or you load it infrequently, once every two weeks, so you can bundle up and meet the minimum batch size, which again then pushes some revenue outside the quarter because you cannot meet the batch size. In some other cases, we are tooling up that capacity inside, and several different programs, and some are in production next quarter, some will even take a quarter longer. It is all over the place. But more capacity becomes available next quarter, June quarter, and from there on.

Tore Svanberg: That is very helpful. Thank you. As my follow-up, and maybe back to the sort of AI bubble and rebalancing of data center across your seven segments, is there anything that you could give us confidence that, if data center does slow down, I understand that it will not impact you as much as others, but what about, let us say, the 24 design wins you have in PCIe Gen 6? Are they still going to go to production? Any sort of color you could share with us there to give us that confidence?

Steve Sanghi: Yeah. So 24 design wins will go to production, but its volume could be slightly lower than if the bubble were to continue. We do not always know the customer who we have design wins with, when they go to production, are they shipping into a data center which already exists, or they are shipping into a data center in Ohio that the local governor is going to put on hold. We do not know that, right? It is all over the place. But it is much smaller portion of our business, so the impact on us from that slowdown would be a fraction of what it would be compared to somebody who is 100% business is in data center.

Tore Svanberg: Yeah. That's fair. Thank you very much.

Steve Sanghi: The fact that on many of the products, like the Gen 6 switch and retimer, it's largely all upside for us because we have no business in it. The other comment I want to make is, if you conservatively model fiscal year 2028, that begins on April 1, with whatever assumptions you have, even in the extreme conservative case, I come up with over $4 of earnings. The stock is at 15x earnings.

Tore Svanberg: Sounds good. Thank you.

Steve Sanghi: I tell you, I'm tempted to buy it myself. [I might].

Operator: Thank you. That concludes today's question and answer session. I would like to turn the floor back over to Mr. Sanghi for closing comments.

Steve Sanghi: Thank you for attending our conference call. I think next conference we go to will be UBS, right?

Eric Bjornholt: Sanghi is at a conference next week. But yeah, we'll have a large Microchip presence at UBS with a larger group of executives.

Steve Sanghi: We'll see some of you there. Thank you very much.

news.Title: 永豐期貨：費半崩跌12%！台股狂瀉3738點、收盤失守4萬點
news.Content:
【財訊快報／編輯部】指數週五下跌1873.08點，收在39701.64點，成交量1.31兆元。台指期下跌2230點至39652點，逆價差為-49.64點。籌碼面部分，三大法人賣超1140.07億元；而在台指期淨部位方面，三大法人淨空單增加4775口至-7813口，其中外資淨空單增加4279口至-99930口；十大交易人中的特定法人全月份台指期淨多單減少5105口至3857口。美股費城半導體指數昨晚暴跌12.25%，台股今日跳空開低。早盤開在38,916點，開盤後隨即下探至37,837點、盤中跌點一度達3,738點，改寫歷史盤中最大跌點；低點過後買盤持續回補，指數一路震盪走高，上午最高攻上40,436點，午後於39,700點附近震盪整理，終場重挫1,873點（-4.51%），收在39,702點，失守40,000點整數關卡。今日成交量1.2兆元。盤面上下跌家數1,215家（其中跌停24家），遠多於上漲132家。

個股表現上，散熱指標奇鋐(3017)摜跌停，ABF載板指標欣興(3037)狂瀉9.13%，日月光投控(3711)跌7.87%，PCB指標台光電(2383)重挫6.83%，台達電(2308)重挫6.64%，聯電(2303)重挫6.50%，AI伺服器指標緯穎(6669)重挫5.76%。前一交易日撐住指數的兩個位置今天同步失守，台積電(2330)跌4.69%、收在2,135元；金融股全面走弱，國泰金(2882)重挫5.36%，富邦金(2881)跌4.82%，台新新光金(2887)跌4.11%。全場只剩中華電(2412)逆勢上漲1.24%。

整體來看，前一交易日還撐在指數下方的台積電與金融股今天同時失守。賣壓的源頭也相當明確：費半單日崩跌超過一成，市場對AI資料中心投資放緩的疑慮擴大，韓股開盤一度重挫逾8%並觸發熔斷，三星、SK海力士同步重挫，半導體權重高的亞洲市場首當其衝。量能放大到10/15以來最大，收盤跌點則是台股史上第四大。外資匯出的壓力也反映在匯市上，新台幣同步貶破33元，創一年半以來新低。 這波賣壓同時壓在台、韓兩地的半導體權值上，後續可留意費半與韓股的表現，作為判斷亞洲半導體賣壓是否告一段落的參考。

選擇權未平倉量部分，11月買權最大OI落在50000點，賣權最大OI落在40000點；11月F1買權最大OI落在40000點，賣權最大OI落在37400點。全月份未平倉量put/call ratio值由0.44下降至0.4。VIX指數上升6.6至46.52。外資台指期買權淨金額0.1億元；賣權淨金額3.78億元。

news.Title: Prediction: November Will Be a Huge Month for Broadcom
news.Content:
Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) hasn't been the best stock to own lately. In June, it hit an all-time high, but it has basically gone straight down from there. It's now down by about 38% from its all-time high, but all that could reverse in November. While Broadcom doesn't have any big events of its own coming this month, there are some others that could drive it higher, like the Anthropic IPO.

Broadcom is a major computing unit supplier to Anthropic, as Anthropic has chosen to deploy a large quantity of Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) that were developed by Broadcom and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL). This could drive heightened awareness around Broadcom's stock, but the reality is that it's a viable investment in its own right and shouldn't need the hype of a new IPO to boost its stock.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Broadcom is a great buy in November, and it's easy to see why if you listen to management.

Broadcom's client list is growing

Broadcom's custom AI chips fill a niche that graphics processing units (GPUs) cannot. GPUs are the industry standard in AI computing because they can be programmed to handle nearly any type of parallel-processing workload. But that type of flexibility costs money.

When a computing unit is designed around a narrow workload, it can be optimized to provide superior performance in that application.

This isn't a new concept. These types of chips, known as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), have been around for a while. However, the concept has now made its way to the AI world, and Broadcom has been the primary chip design company to usher it in.

Broadcom's client list is growing. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) now has a custom AI chip in the works, and so does AI lab OpenAI. However, Alphabet has also started to sell more of its TPUs to external customers (rather than solely installing them in its own data centers), and those sales benefit Broadcom as well.

These are all major growth opportunities for Broadcom, and could lead to massive stock returns if management's forecasts pan out.

During Broadcom's latest conference call, CEO Hock Tan discussed the long-term outlook. He noted that its AI semiconductor revenue is expected to rise to $58 billion in 2026, then double to $115 billion in 2027. The company then predicts another doubling to $230 billion in 2028. That's an incredible growth trajectory. To wrap up this projection, Tan noted that Broadcom has secured the supply chain necessary to produce enough computing units to deliver that level of growth.

Story Continues

That should be music to shareholders' ears, as it shows that Broadcom is on top of its game and well positioned for major growth over the next few years. However, the market hasn't taken much heed. None of this forecast growth is currently priced into Broadcom's stock.

Broadcom's stock is priced cheaply

At first glance, you might not think a stock trading at 38 times trailing earnings is cheap, which is fair. However, the trailing P/E ratio doesn't consider future growth at all. Valuing Broadcom stock in relation to the earnings it's expected to have in 2027, it trades at about 10 times earnings.

AVGO P/E Ratio data by YCharts. P/E = price-to-earnings.

That's a very attractive price tag, and if a fair value for Broadcom's stock is about 30 times trailing earnings, that suggests that if the company delivers on its guidance, the stock could easily more than double by the end of 2027. That's a pretty attractive investment proposition, and that doesn't even factor in that Broadcom's AI semiconductor business is expected to double again in 2028.

All this points to Broadcom being an excellent AI stock to own for the next few years. With the stock down around 38% from its all-time high, now is the perfect time to scoop up shares. The market may realize what a great value it is, and buy in November to start prepping for what could be an incredible 2027 for the stock.

news.Title: ePlus Inc (PLUS) (Q2 2027) Earnings Call Highlights: Record $1 Billion in Gross Billings and ...
news.Content: This article first appeared on GuruFocus . Release Date: November 05, 2026 For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript . Positive Points ePlus Inc ( NASDAQ:PLUS ) delivered robust growth with net sales up 9.7% and gross profit up 11.2%, driven largely by organic growth across a diversified customer base. The company achieved record quarterly gross billings exceeding $1 billion, with open orders up nearly $750 million year-over-year, indicating strong future revenue potential. Adjusted EBITDA grew 14.3%, outpacing net sales growth, and operating income rose 15.8%, demonstrating improved operating leverage. ePlus Inc ( NASDAQ:PLUS ) raised its fiscal 2027 guidance, now expecting upper single-digit growth in net sales and gross profit, and low double-digit growth in adjusted EBITDA. The acquisition of Daymark Solutions broadens ePlus Inc ( NASDAQ:PLUS )'s Northeast presence and adds Microsoft Tier 1 CSP certification, enhancing capabilities in regulated industries. Data center and cloud net sales grew 39.2%, fueled by AI-related demand, and managed services revenue increased 11.9%, supporting recurring revenue. The balance sheet remains healthy with $381 million in cash, enabling investments in organic growth, strategic acquisitions, and shareholder returns. Negative Points Professional services revenue declined 11.3% due to project delays among large retail customers and a difficult comparison to the prior year's record quarter. Services gross margin decreased to 32.5% from 34.8%, and professional services margin fell to 35.4% from 38.2%, due to higher third-party costs and lower revenue. Operating expenses increased 9.2%, driven by higher salaries, benefits, and acquisition-related costs, which could pressure margins if growth slows. Supply constraints in high-end compute and networking, particularly memory, are causing delays and price increases, potentially impacting product availability and costs. Other expense of $0.5 million compared to other income of $5.2 million last year, due to lower interest income, foreign exchange losses, and a decrease in fair value of contingent consideration. Cash and cash equivalents decreased sequentially to $380.9 million from $448.9 million, primarily due to a significant inventory build-up for large customer projects. The effective tax rate remains elevated at 27.9%, though down from 29.3%, impacting net earnings growth. Q & A Highlights Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with PLUS. Is PLUS fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator. Story Continues Q : What is driving the large increase in open orders, and what was the year-over-year comparison? A : Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) explained that open orders rose about $300 million sequentially and nearly $750 million year-over-year, reaching over $1.8 billion versus roughly $1.1 billion last year. The backlog is concentrated in higher-end networking and data center projects, with overall activity building. Mark Maron (CEO and President) added that accelerating AI adoption, data center infrastructure demand, and cybersecurity emphasis fit squarely within ePlus's strengths in both services and products. Q : What conversion rate assumptions for open orders underpin the raised guidance for the second half versus the first half? A : Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) said the company is starting to see previously built open orders come to fruition, including inventory expected to ship in the second half. While a good portion of open orders will push into fiscal 2028, ePlus expects increasing growth as the year progresses. Q : What is the current state of supply constraints, particularly around memory, and when might relief come? A : Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) noted ongoing issues in high-end compute, especially GPU-related areas, with some delays spilling into high-end networking. However, these constraints are not broadly affecting the market with delays; the bigger impact is price increases rather than supply shortages. Q : How are higher third-party costs in professional and managed services affecting customers and pricing, and can they be passed through? A : Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) said third-party cost increases are built into project pricing and passed through to customers. Elaine Marion (CFO) added that some of the higher third-party cost mix reflects the Bailiwick acquisition, which had a higher proportion of third-party costs in its business. Q : What drove the strong second-quarter growth and profitability improvement? A : Mark Maron (CEO and President) highlighted nearly 10% net sales growth and 11.2% gross profit growth, with adjusted EBITDA growing even faster. Operating income rose 15.8%, reflecting improved operating leverage expected to continue in the second half. Growth was largely organic and spread across a diversified customer base, supported by record gross billings exceeding $1 billion. Q : What is the strategic rationale behind the Daymark Solutions acquisition? A : Mark Maron (CEO and President) said Daymark broadens ePlus's presence in the Northeast market and brings a Microsoft Tier 1 CSP certification with expertise in highly regulated and data-intensive industries. The capabilities are expected to scale across all ePlus markets, complement existing offerings, and create opportunities to deliver integrated solutions to a broader customer base. Q : How is AI demand translating into business opportunities for ePlus? A : Mark Maron (CEO and President) said AI remains an important catalyst for technology investment and a significant long-term growth driver, with demand particularly across data center, agentic AI, and security. Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) added that AI-related customer engagements have increased significantly, ranging from use case validation to purchasing and implementation, contributing to a strong pipeline and open order buildup. Q : What drove the decline in professional services revenue, and what is the outlook? A : Elaine Marion (CFO) said professional services revenue fell 11.3% to $67.8 million due to continued project delays among large retail customers, against a difficult comparison with last year's strongest professional services quarter to date. ePlus remains actively engaged with these customers as they work through their plans. Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) noted continued investment in talent, including Field CTO and Principal Technologist teams, to drive strategic services engagements. Q : What is the updated fiscal 2027 guidance? A : Mark Maron (CEO and President) said that given strong first-half performance, a healthy demand environment, and significant growth in bookings and open orders, ePlus is raising fiscal 2027 guidance to upper single-digit growth in both net sales and gross profit, with adjusted EBITDA expected to grow in the low double-digits, reflecting operating leverage inherent in the business. Q : How is ePlus deploying its strong balance sheet and cash position? A : Elaine Marion (CFO) reported cash and cash equivalents of $380.9 million at quarter end, with capital allocation priorities including organic growth investment, strategic acquisitions, and shareholder returns. ePlus repurchased approximately 148,000 shares in the quarter, bringing first-half repurchases to about 400,000 shares for nearly $34 million, and declared a dividend of $0.27 per share payable December 16, 2026. Q : What drove the increase in inventory during the quarter? A : Elaine Marion (CFO) said inventory rose to $271.4 million from $146 million at June 30, 2026, related to several projects for a large customer expected to ship in the second half of the fiscal year. The cash conversion cycle improved to 36 days from 41 days at the end of the first quarter. Q : How did the product and services segments perform in the quarter? A : Elaine Marion (CFO) reported product segment net sales up 12.8% to $547.1 million, led by data center and cloud, where AI-related demand increased significantly, along with strength in security and collaboration. Managed services revenue grew 11.9% to $53.1 million on data center-related demand, while professional services declined 11.3% to $67.8 million due to project delays. Product gross margin expanded 130 basis points to 25.8%, while services gross margin was 32.5% versus 34.8% a year ago on mix shifts. Q : What recognition did ePlus receive from partners during the quarter? A : Darren Raguel (COO and President of ePlus Technology) said ePlus became the first company in North America to achieve Everpure Ambassador status, was named NetApp North American Flash Partner of the Year, and became a certified services partner in Anthropic's Claude Partner Network.
