news.Title: GlobalFoundries (GFS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Nov. 4, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Head of Investor Relations - Eric Chow

Chief Executive Officer - Tim Breen

Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer - Sam Franklin

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Thank you for standing by, and welcome to the GlobalFoundries Third Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during this session, you will need to press star one on your telephone. If your question has been answered and you would like to remove yourself from the queue, simply press star one again. As a reminder, today's program is being recorded. Now I would like to introduce your host for today's program, Eric Chow, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead, sir.

Eric Chow: Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to GlobalFoundries Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. On the call with me today are Tim Breen, CEO, and Sam Franklin, CFO. A short while ago, we released GF's Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results, which are available on our website at investors.gf.com, along with today's accompanying slide presentation. This call is being recorded, and a replay will be made available on our Investor Relations webpage. During this call, we will present both IFRS and non-IFRS financial measures. The most directly comparable IFRS measures and reconciliations for non-IFRS measures are made available in today's press release and accompanying slides. Please note that these financial results are unaudited and subject to change.

Certain statements on today's call may be deemed to be forward-looking statements. Such statements can be identified by terms such as believe, expect, intend, anticipate, and may, or by the use of the future tense. You should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements. Actual results may differ materially from these forward-looking statements, and we do not undertake any obligation to update any forward-looking statements we make today.

For more information about factors that may cause actual results to differ materially from forward-looking statements, please refer to the press release we issued today, as well as risks and uncertainties described in our SEC filings, including in sections under the caption Risk Factors in our annual report on Form 20-F and in any current reports on Form 6-K furnished with the SEC. In terms of upcoming events, we will be participating in a fireside chat at the UBS Global Technology and AI Conference in Scottsdale, Arizona, on December 1st.

Story Continues

We will begin today's call with Tim providing a summary update on the business environment and technologies, followed by Sam, who will provide details on our third quarter results and fourth quarter guidance. We will then open the call for questions with Tim and Sam. We request that you please limit your questions to one with one follow-up. I will now turn the call over to Tim.

Tim Breen: Thank you, Eric, and welcome everyone to our Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. GF delivered strong results in the third quarter, with revenue and non-IFRS profitability metrics at the high end of our guidance ranges. We delivered record non-IFRS gross margin, which demonstrates the meaningful progress we are making to enhance the mix of our business by ramping our differentiated technologies in high-value, high-growth applications. Our communications infrastructure and data center end market saw record levels of growth, led by accelerating demand in optical networking across our silicon photonics and silicon germanium platforms. We also delivered strong growth in automotive and home and industrial IoT, reflecting broad-based secular momentum across our key markets.

Thanks to the accelerated growth across several end markets, the proportion of revenue outside of smart mobile devices was the highest level in our company's history and is driving a richer, more diversified, more resilient revenue base. Thanks to the team's excellent efforts and execution, we are ahead of plans to deliver the strategic and financial targets we set out at our Investor Day earlier in the year. We will look back at 2026 being a pivotal year for GF. In recent weeks, we have made several significant announcements that meaningfully advance our strategy, support our financial objectives, and reinforce our foundation for durable long-term growth.

We are proud to have announced a significant number of new customer and investment partnerships, such as our agreements with Marvell to accelerate capacity for our industry-leading high-performance SiGe, with Monolithic Power for critical power management solutions, with TSMC to establish a U.S.-based supply of silicon interposers for the CoWoS ecosystem, and the landmark U.S.-Japan fab expansion plan that will transform our Malta, New York site. Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Mehdi Hosseini from Susquehanna International. Your question, please.

Mehdi Hosseini: Yes, sir. Thanks for taking my question. I want to dive into communication infrastructure. Tim, can you please update us on how you see the mix between SiPh and SiGe changing into 2027 and 2028? I ask the question in this context because last time, you highlighted that in 2026, SiGe mix is higher than SiPh. Again, I wanted to see how that mix is changing over the next couple of years. I do have a follow-up.

Tim Breen: No, thanks, Mehdi. I think the story, I would say, is very simple. The optical transition is pulling both of them very strongly. I would say SiGe is getting particular pickup because of the transition to 200 G per lane speeds. I think that is going to continue going forward. We are sold out effectively of both. We are adding capacity for both. We have an excellent roadmap for both. I think our strategy will continue to operate on that basis. I think both are going to see very strong growth going into 2027 and beyond.

Like I say, customers are now willing to put their balance sheets to work to help us invest and add capacity, again, in both those end markets are very strong. You didn't ask it, but I will answer anyway. The transition to technologies like NPO are going to accelerate that story even further because that requires even higher performance photonics, but also extra SiGe content as well. So those are tailwinds for the business going forward.

Mehdi Hosseini: I was actually going to follow up on NPO, which is kind of a black box, in my opinion. NPO is more about integration, heterogeneous integration. You have PIC and EIC, which is quite different than discrete components associated with a pluggable transceiver. My follow-up question for you is, how do you see GlobalFoundries' content changing from pluggable to NPO transceivers?

Tim Breen: Yeah. No, it's a great question. I'd say overall, the transition from pluggables to NPO and to CPO, by the way, which we still believe will continue to happen, all of that creates a growing content opportunity for us. Because obviously, as you go forward in high performance, the PIC has to do more, right, in different applications. You have more SiGe content in each of those applications. Then as you get closer to the XPU, you have some of the packaging components, be that fiber attach, die-to-wafer bonding, and so on, also play an important role. So I'd say the opportunity increases as you get closer to the ultimate chip.

Therefore, our investments in R&D, building the scale platform, and others have really begun to pay off very well in terms of customer interest and traction for long-term roadmap in those areas.

Mehdi Hosseini: Great. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Harlan Sur from JPMorgan. Your question, please.

Harlan Sur: Yeah. Good morning. Thank you for taking my questions, and great job on the quarterly execution. June quarter utilizations were in the high 80% range. Did that increase in the September quarter maybe towards the 90% range? That would imply the team still has another 8-10 percentage points of utilization increases ahead. If that's the case, I mean, by my calculations, you still have roughly about 400 basis points of gross margin improvements in front of you just from utilizations, right? How much of that potentially gets unlocked in 2027 as manufacturing activity and utilizations continue to increase?

Sam Franklin: Yeah. Hey, Harlan. Good morning. Maybe just to pick up on that, you're right. Utilization in the high 80s in the second quarter. Utilization in the third quarter was also in the high 80s. One of the reasons for that is that we've been investing CapEx through this year. We've been adding to the capacity, which in effect adds to that denominator for the purposes of calculating utilization. You're right, we do still see utilization upside as an opportunity from a margin point of view.

But as you heard on the call, we're going to be continuing to invest in that capacity and really sort of grow the overall corridors where we see strong demand to be able to expand margins from a mix point of view, but also from a utilization point of view into 2027. At this point, headroom to certainly grow into from a utilization point of view, and we think we're going to keep growing that denominator as we invest CapEx dollars to grow our capacity.

Harlan Sur: No, I appreciate that. Then for Tim, on the photonics front, lasers are also in tight supply, right? High-quality lasers, very, very tight supply situation. I mean, Marvell is paying a healthy premium to acquire Lumentum, right, partly for their indium phosphide laser portfolio. The GF team has done a very good job in compound semiconductors, right? Silicon germanium you talk about quite a bit, targeted for high-quality TIAs and drivers is a good example. Indium phosphide lasers would also add to your SiPh capabilities and portfolio. Is the team considering adding indium phosphide manufacturing to your technology offerings?

Tim Breen: No, it's a great question, Harlan. You're definitely seeing a strong interest in that part of the value chain expressed by the transaction you mentioned, but also other investments that we're hearing about in the industry. We're focusing on integration of indium phosphide into our technologies, right? I think part of the roadmap is about having integrated lasers, integrated SOAs for future optical applications. By the way, just like we're also investing in novel materials for future enhanced modulation to go to 400 G per lane and beyond.

Harlan Sur: Yes.

Tim Breen: Part of our roadmap, what we can invest at the silicon level. Discrete laser manufacturing, not on our current roadmap, but obviously we'll continue to be open to opportunities going forward.

Harlan Sur: Oh, thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Joseph Moore from Morgan Stanley. Your question, please.

Joseph Moore: Great. Thank you. In the last cycle, it seemed like a lot of the focus on wafer securing was coming from automotive, and you had big automotive OEM deals that were working with GlobalFoundries, and obviously we had a shortage of cars that was driven by all of this. As I look at things now, I mean, your automotive business is doing fine, but I worry about looking at all the capacity going to interposers and silicon photonics and AI. These fabs are getting full. Do you think we could be looking at another capacity crunch in the automotive space? I guess, how are you thinking about that, and how are your customers thinking about that?

Are you seeing people start to focus on those supply chains in the way that they did a couple of years ago?

Tim Breen: Yeah. Thank you, Joe. It doesn't get as much of the limelight, but I think the sector continues to be advancing forward in terms of, the automotive sector that is, in terms of its thinking on supply security. We have a lot of conversations with automotive players, not just for the next 12 months, but the next kind of three to five years. For a lot of them, they're very keen also to see that geographic supply diversification as well, and that plays particularly well for us, given our U.S. footprint and our European footprint. So I would expect continuous investments, more engagement, more direct business opportunities in auto as well.

Many of them are doing that, both OEMs and tier ones. That also plays, by the way, into our custom business, where a part of what we've announced in our prepared remarks was progress in things like custom radar, which is another area we're developing further within the platform. So I'd say automotive continues to be, in line with what we talked about at our Investor Day, strong, consistent growth opportunity in which GF is really very well positioned to play across multiple technologies and with multiple end customers.

Sam Franklin: Joe, maybe just more broadly, as you think about some of the CapEx that we've guided to today for 2027, as you'd expect, a lot of that is going into interposers, silicon photonics, SiGe, data center applications. We're not leaving our other end markets behind, and automotive is a key component of that. As we think about driving towards that low double-digit percentage growth, investing into some of our automotive capacity corridors across the footprint will also feature within that overall $4 billion net CapEx that we indicated for next year.

Joseph Moore: Yeah, that's helpful. Thank you. In terms of the OEMs, you mentioned that those relationships are direct. I mean, I feel like that's what's been unique about the last few years, is that you're getting automotive OEMs showing awareness of foundry supply chains and things. Is it still, I guess, are they emphasizing it enough, do you think? Is it still very much a focus on the geographic sourcing? Is that coming from the tier ones, or is that coming from the OEMs?

Tim Breen: I think it's both, and I think part of it also is increased differentiation. I mean, if you look at today's car, the content growth has just tremendously increased over the last years, and all of them have roadmaps to do more, right? As you move to different architectures, some of that's linked to electrification, but some of it's just linked to performance and feature sets of the cars. I think it's also been led by the more kind of silicon-native OEMs. By the way, I would cite, obviously, Tesla, but I would also cite the Chinese players that are increasingly setting the tone globally for what the automotive industry needs to do in terms of performance.

I just think you've got a much more aware end market, and that creates a lot of opportunities for players like us.

Joseph Moore: Great. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Krish Sankar from TD Cowen. Your question, please.

Krish Sankar: Yeah. Hi. Thanks for taking my question. I had two of them. First one, Tim or Sam, can you give an update on the silicon photonics competitive landscape? Obviously, there is TSMC, Tower, STMicro, now UMC, and also along the same path, I think the Marvell-Lumentum merger highlights one of the bear aspects which people worry is that you could be into optical transceiver overbuilding 2028. I am just kind of curious if you have any thoughts around that, and then I had a quick follow-up.

Tim Breen: Yeah. No, great questions, Krish. Look, overall, it is great to see other players believing the same thing we believe, that the optical transition is just getting started, and that is why you are obviously seeing people enter the space who previously weren't very engaged in photonics. We have been doing this for 10 years. We have got a very strong technology roadmap and positioning today. We have also got a lot of investments beyond the PIC level into the packaging side, which I think will play more and more into those new applications we talked about earlier, like NPO and CPO.

I think perhaps even more important right now is you have got the scalable fab footprint to invest and grow with our customers without adding fab space for it, particularly for photonics and SiGe, where they need that capacity rapidly. That is one thing they are betting on in terms of coming to GF for more of their capacity. So, I think we feel very confident in our competitive position within that landscape. Look, I view the recent announcement, the Marvell-Lumentum announcement, again, as a really strong endorsement of that optical transition, both betting a bit, if you like, their future on optical, which I think is reassuring.

Both, by the way, are close partners with GF, we have been public about that as well. So, we think this is a great opportunity for all of us to do more, to innovate faster, and to grow the business. So, I think it is a tailwind.

Krish Sankar: Great. Thanks for the time. Then a quick follow-up on the TSMC CoWoS interposer agreement. It's like a $2 billion manufacturing agreement. Is any of this flowing through CapEx next year? Will the wafer supply there be dedicated to TSMC for the first five years, or do you have flexibility over that?

Tim Breen: Yeah. So, it's part of the CapEx that Sam has talked about, so definitely that's included within the $4 billion number that he shared. Look, our strategy in interposer is a critical technology for all forms of high-performance compute where you're integrating multiple die with HBM and so on. So, we've had a roadmap for some time in that. The TSMC agreement stands on its own, and that's accretive in its own right. But we're also engaging with a number of other customers for future interposer requirements, and these are getting increasingly sophisticated with integration of deep trench capacitors and so on.

So, I think it's actually a very interesting area that we're spending R&D money and effort to actually build more for the future, because it fills our sweet spot in terms of technology mix.

Krish Sankar: Thank you, Tim.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Atif Malik from Citi. Your question, please.

Atif Malik: Hi. Thank you for taking my questions. You guys have been busy with the partnership announcements with TSMC, Marvell, Monolithic Power. To what extent are these partnerships incremental to the long-term model shared at the Investor Day?

Tim Breen: I think, yeah, Sam commented on that a bit earlier. The way I think about it, Atif, is that we set out, only six months ago, a set of strategic goals, which I think are both appropriate for the business and very much strategically aligned with where we have a right to win. These are evidence points that we are winning in those directions with those customers. So, too early to update the numbers of our strategic goals, but as Sam said, all of these give us increased confidence that we're on the right track to deliver and exceed those goals over time.

Atif Malik: Great. Sam, what is the satellite communications exposure within CID, and what's the gross margin profile?

Sam Franklin: Look, we don't break out the individual components. I will say that in 2025, we gave a little bit of color around SATCOM. We delivered about $100 million of revenue within that component of the end market from a relative standing start in the prior year. You've seen publicly, we've made some announcements that associate ourselves with some of those key players within the satellite communications market more broadly. You've only got to look at low-earth orbit satellite launches and the continued momentum within that end market to see that it's an important growth vector within comms and for data center for us.

Look more broadly, this is a technology that we're servicing that demand with, which is accretive to the long-term goals that we've set out.

Tim Breen: Maybe just to add on my side, I mean, I think one of the reasons we are seeing strong long-term momentum in technologies like SiGe beyond the data center is actually things like satellite communications, right? When you want to launch a satellite 300 mi in space and have a high-performance, high-bandwidth solution, bringing that bandwidth back to Earth, you need high-performance RF technologies. We have been doing that for a very long time, and SiGe is getting also traction from those areas as well. Very encouraging.

Atif Malik: Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our final question for today comes from the line of Chris Caso from Wolfe Research. Your question, please.

Chris Caso: Yes, thank you. Good morning. My first question is with regard to the CapEx and the $4 billion number you mentioned. It is a big number relative to what you guys have spent in the past. So, a few questions on that. One is, if you could discuss, given some of the prepayments and credits in that, how much of that is cash out the door from GlobalFoundries that would affect your cash flow for next year? Just kind of separating out what is supported by others and what you are putting out yourself. Then, in terms of when that turns into revenue, and kind of the timing of that.

I guess what I would really like you to answer, which you probably won't, is how much revenue gets generated by $4 billion CapEx, but I will settle for the when.

Sam Franklin: Yeah, Chris, I think that we've been relatively under-investing from a CapEx point of view over the last, call it, three years. If you look at the aggregate over the last three years, it's only been a little north of 10% of revenue versus what we said previously was targeting a 20% net CapEx to revenue and what we reiterated earlier this year. The principal reason for that is the foundation of our investment decisions into capacity is demand. We've seen a step change function in that demand outlook as we go through this year. It's for technologies across silicon photonics, FDX, advanced packaging, SiGe, more recently what we announced with TSMC on interposer.

This has been the single biggest change in terms of how we think about that investment into the footprint. Our customers recognize that as well. Actually, to Tim's earlier comments, there's been very, very constructive conversations in terms of the prepayment capacity reservations for incremental capacity discussions that we've been having. We expect those largely to close in, call it, the fourth quarter and into early 2027 as well. That $4 billion net number that I gave you, obviously we don't net customer prepayments from that in terms of how we calculate net CapEx.

Think of that as $4 billion net CapEx to GF, but within that $4 billion, we expect that we'll get about, call it, a third of that supported by customer prepayments. You won't see that flow through as a net to CapEx, but you will effectively see it flow through towards our free cash flow. That's why we feel good about still remaining the targets around our free cash flow margin for 2027. Then the other dynamic, as you said, is around government grants and broader support frameworks. If I take the ITC as an example, that's now 35%. We don't get all of that 35% in year.

In fact, some of what we'll get as a net for CapEx next year will be from ITC that was accrued in, call it, the 2025 timeframe. We will, however, get as an offset to CapEx next year the government grants that we've announced during the course of this year. Some of that is in relation to quantum computing. We've also got the $955 million repurposing from the original CHIPS office grants. About 80% of that $955 million we expect we'll allocate towards CapEx. Not all of that will be allocated in 2027 as an offset, but we'll probably get the majority of that coming through in 2027 as well.

All points towards good indicators from a free cash point of view. Then look, the way we think about the ROI is really a function of payback. When you take that combination of the government grants, the ITC, the offset to our overall CapEx burden, we see strong paybacks inside a sort of two-year time horizon for most of those technologies that we outlined. It forms an important part of our investment decision-making. Given the margin profile and the mix associated with these corridors, we see a strong ROI and a relatively quick ramp to demand and revenue. Obviously, it's really a function of how quickly you can get those tools installed, qualified, and ramped.

The beauty of our expansion footprint is that we can do it within our existing four walls. So, we're not reliant like some others are around building incremental capacity to do it. We can do it within our existing four walls. So, that accelerates the time to revenue as well.

Tim Breen: I mean, the way we've been thinking about this is, it's a unique moment for us to accelerate our business with the participation of our customers, with the participation of governments, maintaining a very strong balance sheet, maintaining our free cash flow generation objectives. It's the right way to navigate the current situation that we're in.

Operator: Thank you. This does conclude the question and answer session of today's program. I'd like to hand the program back to Eric Chow for any further remarks.

Eric Chow: Thank you very much for joining today. We look forward to seeing you at the UBS conference on December 1st. Thanks again.

Operator: Thank you, ladies and gentlemen, for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect. Good day.

This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Revenue: $1.899 billion, up 6% sequentially and 13% year-over-year.

Wafer Shipments: Approximately 647,300 300mm-equivalent wafers, up 4% sequentially and 7% year-over-year.

Revenue Mix (Manufacturing Services): Approximately 88% of total revenue.

Revenue Mix (Technology Services): Approximately 12% of total revenue; expected ~12% for full-year 2026 at upper end of range.

Communications Infrastructure & Data Center Revenue: ~17% of Q3 revenue; up 14% sequentially and 81% year-over-year; expected to grow 60%70% in 2026.

Automotive Revenue: ~19% of Q3 revenue; up 11% sequentially and 20% year-over-year; expected low double-digit growth in 2026.

Smart Mobile Devices Revenue: ~32% of Q3 revenue (lowest in company history); down 5% sequentially and 19% year-over-year; expected low-teens percentage decline in 2026.

Home & Industrial IoT Revenue: ~20% of Q3 revenue; up 16% sequentially and 49% year-over-year; expected 10%15% growth in 2026.

Silicon Photonics Revenue: $0.5 billion expected in 2026; ~$1 billion annualized run rate expected exiting 2027.

Gross Profit: $597 million.

Gross Margin: ~31.4%, up 540 basis points year-over-year; company record and at high end of guidance.

R&D Expense: $164 million.

SG&A Expense: $93 million.

Total Operating Expenses: $257 million (~14% of revenue), up 9% quarter-over-quarter.

Operating Profit: $340 million at 17.9% operating margin, up 250 basis points year-over-year.

Net Interest Income: $9 million; other expense $6 million.

Tax Expense: $45 million.

Net Income: ~$298 million, up ~$66 million year-over-year.

Diluted EPS: $0.53 per share, at high end of guidance; ~558 million fully diluted shares.

Cash Flow from Operations: $341 million.

CapEx (Net of Government Grants): $205 million (~11% of revenue).

Adjusted Free Cash Flow: $136 million, benefiting from ~$150 million of customer prepayments and government grants.

Total Debt: $1.1 billion; $1.5 billion revolving credit facility undrawn.

Q4 Operating Expense Guidance: $235 million, plus or minus $10 million (excluding share-based compensation).

Q4 Operating Margin Guidance: 19.8%, plus or minus 170 basis points.

Q4 Diluted EPS Guidance: $0.59, plus or minus $0.05, on ~575 million fully diluted shares.

2026 Net CapEx: Expected ~15%20% of revenue; free cash flow margin ~10%.

2027 Net CapEx: ~$4 billion expected; ~one-third of net CapEx supported by customer prepayments.

Release Date: November 04, 2026

For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript .

Positive Points

GLOBALFOUNDRIES Inc ( NASDAQ:GFS ) delivered record non-IFRS gross margin of 31.4%, up 540 basis points year-over-year, with revenue and profitability at the high end of guidance.

Communications infrastructure and data center revenue grew 81% year-over-year, marking the eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, driven by silicon photonics and silicon germanium demand.

The company expects silicon photonics revenue to reach a $1 billion annualized run rate by exit 2027, a full year ahead of prior expectations, with plans to triple capacity.

Strategic partnerships with Marvell, TSMC, and the US government (including $955 million in CHIPS Act reallocation) enhance capacity, technology, and financial flexibility.

Revenue diversification reached a record with over two-thirds from outside smart mobile devices, and blended ASPs increased year-over-year for the first time since 2023.

Negative Points

Smart mobile devices revenue declined 19% year-over-year and is expected to decline by a low-teens percentage for the full year 2026, remaining a significant drag.

The company expects a significant increase in net CapEx to approximately $4 billion in 2027, which could pressure free cash flow despite customer prepayments and government support.

Utilization remained in the high 80% range, and while there is room for improvement, capacity additions may keep utilization from rising quickly, limiting margin expansion.

Automotive revenue growth is expected to be low double-digit in 2026, but concerns about a potential capacity crunch in the automotive space due to AI demand could pose risks.

The issuance of equity to the US government (totaling ~7% ownership) will increase the diluted share count to approximately 600 million shares in 2027, potentially diluting earnings per share.

Q & A Highlights

Q : With silicon photonics pulled in by a year and a structurally richer mix, how is the portfolio of changes impacting your gross margin trajectory into 2027 and 2028? A : CFO Sam Franklin said GF has delivered nearly 500 basis points of year-over-year margin growth this year and is on track with the targets set at Investor Day in May, including exiting Q4 2026 with a 30% gross margin handle, which guidance now exceeds by about 1.5 points. He noted there is still a bridge from 31.4% in Q3 to the 40% target for exiting Q4 2028, but mix and continued investment in high-demand corridors are pushing margins in the right direction. CEO Tim Breen added that wins with leading customers, many new to GF, support accelerating capacity investments and confidence in the trajectory ahead.

Q : How much of your 2027 and 2028 silicon photonics capacity is now under signed commitments, and are those agreements reaching into 2029 as NPO and CPO potentially come in? A : CEO Tim Breen said optical communication demand is skyrocketing as optical links replace copper across the data center. GF is fully booked through 2027 and increasingly booked through 2028, with customers seeking capacity assurance through 2029 and beyond and willing to put their balance sheets to work to support investments. He said executioninstalling tools and driving productivityis now the key, and that GF is doing better than expected in 2026 due to accelerated investments and fast tool ramps.

Q : With blended ASPs up year-over-year for the first time since 2023, should pricing be viewed as additive to the 40% gross margin target, and how much does the TSMC interposer agreement add to corporate gross margins? A : CFO Sam Franklin said Q3 blended ASPs rose about 2.5% sequentially and almost 5% year-over-year, with pricing now a more constructive dynamic across end markets. He expects roughly a 10% uplift in blended ASP mix in 2027 from richer mix and pricing actions, but noted pricing is less impactful than mix, utilization, depreciation and productivity. He did not change the long-term margin targets but said recent announcements give greater visibility and certainty, and the TSMC interposer ramp in the first half of 2028 should be margin accretive.

Q : Where do you see utilization, pricing and mix going into the first half of 2027, and can gross margins at least stay flat? A : CFO Sam Franklin said mix benefits from non-mobile end markets are a tailwind into next year, and structural shifts should make Q4-to-Q1 seasonality slightly less pronounced than in prior years. CEO Tim Breen added that GF has spent three years making its manufacturing footprint more flexible so capacity can shift between markets, which is helping improve utilization this year and into next year.

Q : How do you see the mix between silicon photonics and SiGe changing into 2027 and 2028, and how does GF content change from pluggable to NPO transceivers? A : CEO Tim Breen said the optical transition is pulling both silicon photonics and SiGe strongly, with SiGe getting a particular pickup from the transition to 200 gigabit per lane speeds. GF has effectively sold out of both and is adding capacity for both, with customers willing to help fund investments. He said the shift from pluggable to NPO and CPO increases GF's content opportunity, as higher-performance photonics requires more SiGe content and packaging components such as fiber attach and wafer bonding.

Q : Utilization was in the high 80% range in the June quarterdid it increase in the September quarter, and how much of the roughly 400 basis points of gross margin improvement from utilization could be unlocked in 2027? A : CFO Sam Franklin said Q3 utilization was also in the high 80s, partly because CapEx investments added capacity to the denominator. He said there is still utilization upside as a margin opportunity, but GF will continue investing in capacity to grow the corridors with strong demand, expanding margins through both mix and utilization into 2027.

Q : Is GF considering adding indium phosphide manufacturing to its technology offerings given tight laser supply? A : CEO Tim Breen said GF is focused on integrating indium phosphide into its technologies, including integrated lasers and semiconductor optical amplifiers for future optical applications, and is also investing in novel materials for enhanced modulation to 400 gigabit per lane and beyond. Discrete laser manufacturing is not on the current roadmap, but GF will remain open to opportunities.

Q : Could the capacity going to interposers, silicon photonics and AI create another capacity crunch in automotive, and are customers focusing on supply chains again? A : CEO Tim Breen said automotive players are increasingly focused on supply security and geographic diversification over the next three to five years, which plays well to GF's US and European footprint. He expects continued investment and more direct business opportunities with OEMs and Tier 1s, including in custom silicon such as radar. CFO Sam Franklin added that the $4 billion net CapEx plan for 2027 includes investment in automotive capacity corridors alongside silicon photonics and SiGe.

Q : How do you view the silicon photonics competitive landscape, and are you concerned about potential optical transceiver overbuilding in 2028? A : CEO Tim Breen said it is positive that other players now believe in the optical transition, which GF has pursued for 10 years with a strong technology roadmap and investments in packaging for NPO and CPO. He said GF's key advantage is its scalable fab footprint, which allows it to grow capacity with customers without adding new fabs, particularly for photonics and SiGe. He views the Marvell-Lumentum deal as a strong endorsement of the optical transition and a tailwind for GF, a close partner to both companies.

Q : Is any of the $2 billion TSMC interposer manufacturing agreement flowing through CapEx next year, and will the wafer supply be dedicated to TSMC for the first five years? A : CEO Tim Breen said the TSMC agreement is included in the $4 billion net CapEx plan for 2027. He said interposers are a critical technology for high-performance compute integrating multiple die with HBM, and GF has had a roadmap in this area for some time. The TSMC agreement stands on its own and is accretive, while GF is also engaging with other customers for future interposer requirements,

news.Title: What a $115 Billion Deal to Buy Lumentum Really Means for Marvell Stock Investors
news.Content:
Semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL) is all set to acquire Lumentum (LITE), a leading supplier of optical and photonic technologies, for $115 billion in an all-stock deal. Under the terms of the agreement, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell for each share of LITE stock they own. Marvell shareholders will own 67% of the combined company, while the rest will be held by Lumentum shareholders.

Marvell investors made their displeasure about the development clear, with shares ending almost 13% lower on Nov. 2 and down again today. They appear to believe the price tag of the deal is too high while the heavy dilution is also undesirable. Notably, the $115 billion consideration is an 86% premium to Lumentum's current market capitalization of $61.6 billion.

More News from Barchart

Why Investors Should Load Up on Google Stock Now

Billionaire Mark Cuban Says the Hardest Part of Fixing Health Costs Isn't the CEOs or Insurance Companies, 'Employees Fight Any Change'

Coca-Cola Pays Warren Buffett's Berkshire $848 Million a Year as Jim Cramer Says Buy KO Stock

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

However, Marvell management believes that the deal has the potential to result in cost savings of more than $1 billion. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come," said CEO Matt Murphy, describing the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market's focus on optical connectivity as a "once in a generation" opportunity. "By bringing together two leaders with highly complementary technologies, exceptional talent and specialized manufacturing capabilities, we intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity and create exceptional stockholder value."

About Marvell Technology

Founded in 1995, Marvell is an AI infrastructure company centered on data-center connectivity, custom silicon, optical interconnects, switching, and storage. Its custom silicon business in particular includes custom AI accelerators, XPUs, networking chips, storage and memory controllers, and data-center interconnect products. Marvell has an impressive customer base that includes Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT), and Alphabet (GOOGL), among others.

Marvell currently commands a market cap of $150.8 billion, with MRVL stock up an impressive 86% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. Notably, the stock also offers a modest dividend yield of 0.14%.

So, keeping the immediate market reaction aside, how will Marvell's impending acquisition of Lumentum impact its operations? Let's take a closer look.

Story Continues

Lumentum Is Legit for Marvell in the Long Haul

One rationale being bandied about the deal is that Marvell will gain access to Lumentum's expertise in optical transceivers, which allows for faster data transfer with less power. However, Marvell is buying more than faster optical transceivers. The bigger ambition of the deal is to control more of the technology connecting AI processors — from custom silicon and networking chips to lasers, optical modules, and optical circuit switches.

Notably, Marvell wants to design the electrical and optical signal chain together rather than optimize individual components separately. Bringing its silicon photonics, switching, and custom processors together with Lumentum's lasers and optical manufacturing could reduce engineering friction, simplify customer qualification, and shorten development cycles, resulting in the development of a vertically integrated semiconductor player that is harder to replace once its technologies are incorporated into a customer's design.

Meanwhile, Lumentum also brings indium phosphide capabilities and specialized laser production that complement Marvell's semiconductor design strengths. Additionally, optical circuit switching provides a separate growth opportunity beyond transceivers.

On Nov. 2, amid its first-quarter fiscal 2027 results, Lumentum said that optical circuit switch (OCS) demand visibility could support a business generating several billion dollars annually. Management also disclosed a second major win involving optics placed near or alongside processors, supported by purchase commitments exceeding $5 billion. Those commitments give the Marvell acquisition thesis more substance than a broad forecast for rising AI traffic alone.

Finally, with Lumentum, Marvell will be able to offer potential customers a more complete alternative to its larger peer and biggest competitor, Broadcom (AVGO). However, integration also creates a potential channel conflict. Customers that currently buy components from independent suppliers may hesitate if their supplier becomes a broader competitor. Marvell must preserve those relationships while pursuing more integrated sales.

Marvell Reports a Super Q2

Before examining Marvell's Q2 figures, we should look at the company's updated commentary on fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 revenue. Marvell raised its revenue outlook for both years, now projecting fiscal 2027 revenue of $12 billion and fiscal 2028 revenue of $18 billion, up from previous guidance of $11.5 billion and $16.5 billion, respectively. Within the fiscal 2028 outlook, Marvell anticipates data-center revenue growth of 60%, underscoring continued strength in the largest segment of the AI infrastructure buildout.

That momentum was visible in the latest quarterly results as well. Marvell reported record net revenue of $2.74 billion in Q2 fiscal 2027, representing a 37% increase from the prior year. Although that absolute figure set a new high, the growth rate lagged Broadcom, which recorded a 48% rise in its corresponding Q2 results. Meanwhile, Marvell's data-center revenue advanced 46% year-over-year (YOY) to $2.17 billion in Q2.

Gross margins contracted modestly to 58.9% from 59.4% in the year-ago period as stock-based compensation rose to $15.9 million from $13.4 million. Nevertheless, EPS increased 40% YOY to $0.94, just above the consensus estimate of $0.93.

For Q3, Marvell guided EPS between $1.05 and $1.15. Gross margins for Q3 are expected to fall in the range of 57.5% to 58.5%.

Net cash from operating activities improved to $605.5 million from $461.6 million in the prior year. Overall, Marvell closed Q2 with $3.93 billion in cash and no short-term debt. Long-term debt of approximately $5 billion, however, continues to appear as higher interest expense on the income statement. Interest expense rose to $61.6 million from $51.9 million in the same period last year.

Meanwhile, the searing rally in MRVL stock this year has led to punchy valuations. Its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 56.1 times, price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 18.3 times, and price-to-cash flow (P/CF) multiple of 47.1 times are all above the sector medians of 21.1 times, 3.2 times, and 18.7 times, respectively.

What Do Analysts Think of MRVL Stock?

Taking all of this into account, analysts have a consensus "Strong Buy" rating for MRVL stock overall. Out of 39 analysts covering the stock, 28 have a "Strong Buy" rating, three have a "Moderate Buy" rating, and eight have a "Hold" rating. The mean target price of $317.05 denotes potential upside of 102% from current levels.

news.Title: Marvell's Deal to Acquire Lumentum Could Be a Game Changer for the Stock
news.Content:
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) has been a big winner this year, with the stock up more than 130% in 2026, as of the end of October. However, an announced deal to acquire Lumentum (NASDAQ: LITE) could be a game changer for what has already been a good story.

This deal is all about optical networking, as it will combine Marvell's leadership in optical interconnects with Lumentum's strength in lasers. Marvell called the deal a "once-in-a-generation opportunity to define and lead AI connectivity in the era of integrated optics," as it will provide the company with end-to-end design capabilities that will allow it to accelerate its time to market and solve the increasing complexity of scale-up and scale-out networks.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's see what this could all mean for investors.

Complementary technologies

The two companies' optics technologies are very complementary. In an optical network, Marvell provides electronic components such as DSPs (digital signal processors) that prepare data to be converted into optical signals; transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs) that convert light signals back into electrical signals; and silicon photonics (SiPho) engines that combine hundreds of components to improve the performance and energy efficiency of optical interconnects.

Lumentum produces high-power indium phosphide (InP) lasers and gallium arsenide (GaAs) vertical cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs) that convert electricity into light for high-speed data transmission. It is one of a handful of companies with this technology for these advanced lasers. Designing and manufacturing these lasers is a complex task, and the company holds over 1,000 patents and owns specialized semiconductor fabs (manufacturing facilities).

Marvell said that the acquisition will allow it to go from producing components to full modules. It will also create meaningful design and operational efficiencies for its customers. It believes that integrating its technology with Lumentum is ultimately needed to take bandwidth, latency, and power efficiency to the next level.

The deal will combine what are expected to be two of the S&P 500 's fastest-growing companies by earnings per share (EPS) from 2026 through 2028. Meanwhile, Marvell believes its combined total addressable market (TAM) will be around $550 billion by 2030. It sees $1 billion in potential annual synergies with the deal, largely coming from a reduction in cost of goods sold. Excluding synergies, the company will have a $17.7 billion annual revenue run rate with 57% gross margins and 39% operating margins .

Story Continues

As part of the deal, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own. The deal valued Lumentum at an enterprise value of $115 billion, or about $1,132 per share, at the time of the announcement. That represents about a 24% premium to its closing price before the announcement. The deal is expected to close in the first half of calendar 2028.

Time to buy the stocks

Both Marvell and Lumentum have been riding the shift in AI data centers from copper wire to optical networks, which offer better bandwidth and lower energy costs. As AI innovation continues to advance and systems become more powerful, the need for optical networking should only grow.

Both companies are already seeing strong growth individually. Lumentum reported its fiscal first-quarter results the same day as the merger announcement. It grew its revenue by 137% to $1.26 billion, while its gross margins climbed 1,700 basis points to 51%. Meanwhile, Marvell had guided for its current quarter revenue to increase by 52%, with data center revenue surging 75%. The combined company will become a juggernaut in the optical space.

Marvell is more than optics, though, as it is also a leader in custom AI chips. It provides important IP (intellectual property) for both Amazon 's AI Trainium chips and Microsoft 's newer Maia chips. It also recently won a deal to supply Alphabet 's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) architecture with important attach components, such as inference accelerators, storage controllers, NICs, memory interface controllers, and near-memory compute.

Marvell's pending acquisition of Lumentum, plus its strength in custom AI chips, gives Marvell one of the best long-term growth outlooks in the AI infrastructure space. That makes the AI stock a buy, with Lumentum being a discounted way to own Marvell -- although there is always some risk that a deal may not go through.

news.Title: GlobalFoundries Q3 Earnings Call Highlights
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in GlobalFoundries Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

Q3 revenue rose 13% year over year to $1.899 billion , while record non-IFRS gross margin reached 31.4%. More than two-thirds of revenue came from outside smart mobile devices, which declined 19% year over year.

Communications infrastructure and data center revenue grew 81% year over year, driven by optical networking. GlobalFoundries expects about $500 million in silicon photonics revenue in 2026 and a roughly $1 billion annualized run rate by the end of 2027, a year ahead of its previous outlook.

For Q4, the company forecasts $2 billion in revenue and diluted EPS of $0.59. It expects about $4 billion in net capital expenditures in 2027 to expand specialty-chip and advanced-packaging capacity, with customer prepayments expected to fund roughly one-third.

GlobalFoundries' $21 Billion Deal Could Change the Economics of Chipmaking

GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ:GFS) reported third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.899 billion, up 6% sequentially and 13% from a year earlier, as stronger demand in communications infrastructure, data center, automotive and industrial markets continued to reshape the company's revenue mix.

CEO Tim Breen said revenue and non-IFRS profitability metrics reached the high end of the company's guidance ranges. The company recorded non-IFRS gross margin of 31.4%, a company record and a 540-basis-point increase from the prior-year quarter.

→ 3 Waste Services Stocks With More Growth Than You Might Expect

Micron's $250 Billion Bet Could Reshape the AI Memory Race

"For the first time in our history, more than two-thirds of our Q3 revenue came from outside smart mobile devices," CFO Sam Franklin said. The company said the increasingly diversified mix has supported margin expansion, particularly as it ramps differentiated technologies including silicon photonics, silicon germanium, advanced packaging and technology services.

Data Center and Optical Networking Drive Growth

Communications infrastructure and data center revenue accounted for approximately 17% of third-quarter revenue. The segment grew 14% sequentially and 81% year over year, driven primarily by optical networking demand for silicon photonics and silicon germanium technologies.

→ AbbVie's Humira Era Is Fading, But Its New Growth Engines Face Another Test

Quantum Computing's Commercial Breakout Has Arrived

Franklin said the third quarter marked the eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit year-over-year growth in communications infrastructure and data center. GlobalFoundries expects that market to grow between 60% and 70% during 2026.

Story Continues

Breen said the company now expects to generate about $500 million in silicon photonics revenue during 2026 and to exit 2027 at an annualized silicon photonics revenue run rate of approximately $1 billion. That milestone is expected a year earlier than the company's previous outlook.

→ Big Tech Is Spending Billions on AI—These 5 Stocks Are Getting Paid

GlobalFoundries plans to approximately triple silicon photonics capacity during 2027 to address demand expected in 2028 and beyond. Breen said the company is actively working with more than 50 silicon photonics customers, including seven of the top 10 optical-transceiver suppliers. Active customer designs are expected to ramp in 2027 and 2028.

The company also cited demand for silicon germanium, which is used in optical transceivers for components such as transmit drivers and receive amplifiers. GlobalFoundries said it is accelerating silicon germanium capacity investments, supported by customer prepayments. Its recently announced multiyear partnership with Marvell is intended to support expansion at the company's Burlington, Vermont, facility.

Partnerships Expand U.S. Manufacturing and Packaging Plans

During the quarter, GlobalFoundries announced several customer and government partnerships, including agreements with Marvell, Monolithic Power Systems and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

Under a five-year, $2 billion manufacturing agreement with TSMC, GlobalFoundries plans to establish a U.S.-based source of silicon interposers for TSMC's CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem. Volume production is expected to begin at GlobalFoundries' Malta, New York, site in the first half of 2028.

Breen said the interposer agreement will establish a multiyear revenue stream with gross margins above GlobalFoundries' long-term targets, while TSMC will co-invest in the capital required for the project.

The company also highlighted a U.S.-Japan fab expansion initiative for its Malta facility. Breen said the structure is intended to expand capacity without GlobalFoundries investing capital directly, relying instead on technology, construction and operations fees, cost reimbursements and EBITDA sharing. He said the arrangement is designed to produce profit per wafer comparable with a model in which the company built and owned the capacity itself.

GlobalFoundries also reached an agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce to reallocate $955 million from its existing CHIPS and Science Act award toward investments in Malta and Burlington. The funding is aimed at silicon photonics, silicon germanium and advanced-packaging capabilities, including silicon interposers.

The company said a separate agreement will provide the U.S. government with a 4% equity stake. GlobalFoundries expects total U.S. government ownership to reach approximately 7% after all related agreements are finalized. Franklin said the expected equity issuances would increase the company's fully diluted share count to about 600 million beginning in 2027.

Other Markets and Third-Quarter Results

Automotive: Represented about 19% of third-quarter revenue, rising 11% sequentially and 20% year over year. GlobalFoundries continues to expect low-double-digit percentage automotive growth in 2026.

Smart mobile devices: Represented approximately 32% of revenue, its lowest share in the company's history. Revenue declined 5% sequentially and 19% year over year. The company maintained its expectation for a low-teens percentage decline in the market for 2026.

Home and industrial IoT: Accounted for roughly 20% of revenue, growing 16% sequentially and 49% year over year. GlobalFoundries expects segment growth of 10% to 15% in 2026.

GlobalFoundries shipped approximately 647,000 300-millimeter equivalent wafers during the quarter, up 4% sequentially and 7% year over year. Manufacturing services represented approximately 88% of revenue, while technology services accounted for 12%.

The company reported non-IFRS operating profit of $340 million, representing a 17.9% operating margin, and net income of approximately $298 million. Diluted earnings were $0.53 per share, based on approximately 558 million fully diluted shares.

Cash flow from operations totaled $341 million, while adjusted free cash flow was $136 million. The company ended the quarter with approximately $3.2 billion in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities, compared with $1.1 billion in debt.

Fourth-Quarter Outlook and Accelerated Investment

For the fourth quarter, GlobalFoundries forecast revenue of $2 billion, plus or minus $25 million, and non-IFRS gross margin of approximately 31.5%, plus or minus 100 basis points. The company expects non-IFRS operating margin of approximately 19.8%, plus or minus 170 basis points, and diluted earnings per share of $0.59, plus or minus $0.05.

Franklin said blended average selling prices increased about 2.5% sequentially and nearly 5% year over year in the third quarter, marking the company's first year-over-year blended pricing improvement since 2023. He said the company expects approximately a 10% uplift in blended pricing and mix during 2027.

GlobalFoundries expects net capital expenditures of about $4 billion in 2027 as it expands capacity for silicon photonics, silicon germanium, FDX, advanced packaging and interposers. About one-third of that spending is expected to be supported by customer prepayments, according to Franklin, while government grants and investment tax credits are also expected to offset investment costs.

"We see strong paybacks inside a sort of two-year time horizon for most of those technologies," Franklin said, adding that the company can expand much of the capacity within its existing manufacturing footprint.

About GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ:GFS)

GlobalFoundries Inc (NASDAQ:GFS) is a semiconductor manufacturer that operates as a contract foundry, producing chips designed by other companies. The company provides wafer fabrication and related services for customers in the automotive, communications infrastructure, aerospace and defense, industrial, and consumer electronics markets.

GlobalFoundries specializes in differentiated semiconductor technologies rather than competing primarily in the most advanced logic-processing nodes. Its offerings include radio-frequency and silicon-on-insulator technologies, embedded memory, power-management solutions, high-voltage processes, silicon photonics, and other specialty platforms used in connectivity, sensing, automotive electronics, and edge-computing applications.

The company was established in 2009 through the separation of Advanced Micro Devices' manufacturing operations, with investment from the Abu Dhabi-based Advanced Technology Investment Company.

news.Title: Marvell Stock Has Plunged 46% Since Jensen Huang Called It the Next $1 Trillion Company. Here's Why.
news.Content:
In early June, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) the next trillion-dollar company. Huang explained that Marvell's connectivity solutions are essential for coordinating large clusters of processors powering artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

Wall Street initially embraced this optimism. Marvell shares surged to about $291 on June 2 and reached a record closing price of nearly $316 just two days later. However, enthusiasm around Marvell seems to have evaporated. As of Nov. 2, Marvell stock traded at $171, representing a decline of 46% from its peak.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

MRVL data by YCharts

The sell-off follows Marvell's announcement that it is acquiring optical networking specialist Lumentum (NASDAQ: LITE) in a $115 billion deal . Let's unpack why Wall Street is reacting so negatively to this news and assess whether investors are overlooking the long-term opportunity.

Why Jensen Huang sees trillion-dollar potential in Marvell

Marvell is quietly becoming an important supplier to the AI infrastructure supercycle. The company's custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) allow hyperscalers to build processors optimized for particular training and inference workloads, while its networking and connectivity products help transfer information between chips and servers.

Nvidia recognized this opportunity early on, announcing a $2 billion investment in Marvell and a partnership involving its NVLink Fusion platform. The collaboration allows AI developers to combine custom silicon designed by Marvell with Nvidia's broader computing and networking architectures.

Why the Lumentum acquisition sent Marvell stock plunging

On Nov. 2, Marvell announced an agreement to acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction carrying an implied enterprise value of approximately $115 billion. The acquisition values Lumentum at approximately $1,132 per share, representing a 24% premium to its closing price on Oct. 28, right as speculation about the deal surfaced.

The transaction's structure is important to understand. Rather than paying cash or taking on debt to finance the acquisition, Marvell will issue 4.5 new shares for every outstanding Lumentum share. Following the transaction, Marvell shareholders will own 67% of the combined company while Lumentum shareholders will control the remaining 33%.

Story Continues

This means Marvell's investors are effectively surrendering one-third of the combined company's ownership to acquire Lumentum. That dilution explains Wall Street's negative reaction. However, since the agreement uses a fixed exchange ratio rather than a guaranteed cash price, the value Lumentum shareholders ultimately receive will fluctuate with Marvell's stock price. In other words, the acquisition's headline valuation isn't necessarily the price Marvell will actually pay.

Is Wall Street overlooking Marvell's long-term potential?

Despite the dilution, I think there are some meaningful benefits to this deal. Marvell's portfolio includes digital signal processors (DSPs), networking chips, and connectivity solutions that enable data to move through AI systems. Lumentum complements those capabilities with lasers and optical components used to transmit information at low latencies. Combining these solutions allows Marvell to offer customers a more complete optical connectivity suite.

Management expects the transaction to generate more than $1 billion in annual run rate cost synergies and become accretive to adjusted earnings per share (EPS) during the first year post-close.

Although the market's reaction has been severe so far, investors should not lose sight of Marvell's long-term potential. During its investor day last month, management estimated that its total addressable market (TAM) could reach $400 billion by calendar 2030. Following the proposed Lumentum acquisition, the combined company's addressable market is expected to expand to $550 billion.

Another important development involves Alphabet . In August, Marvell disclosed an agreement to develop custom semiconductors supporting Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) ecosystem. As part of the arrangement, Google received warrants to purchase 59 million Marvell shares at $206.58 each.

I think the agreements with Google and Nvidia reinforce Marvell's rising position as an important partner to some of the world's largest AI infrastructure customers. Ultimately, Marvell's acquisition of Lumentum could strengthen its competitive position by bridging optical components and semiconductor design under one roof.

Nevertheless, the market seems to be focusing on what existing shareholders need to give up in the short term. Huang's trillion-dollar prediction remains ambitious, but the strategic rationale behind his enthusiasm hasn't disappeared just because Marvell's stock price is falling.

For investors willing to tolerate volatility in the near term and wait a few years for the acquisition's benefits to materialize in both revenue and profit, Marvell's sell-off could represent an attractive opportunity to buy the dip.

news.Title: 3 Reasons to Hold Amkor Stock Despite Its High Premium P/E

Amkor Technology AMKR is gaining traction in advanced semiconductor packaging for artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing and automotive electronics. However, its valuation premium, recent share-price weakness and falling earnings estimates suggest investors should resist chasing the stock. AMKR Stock Lags Industry and Key Peers

Over the past three months, AMKR's shares declined 30.2%, underperforming the Zacks Electronics - Semiconductors industry's 18.1% loss and the Computer and Technology sector's 7.7% fall.

AMKR's recent share-price performance also stands out against its peers, including ASE Technology Holding ASX, Entegris ENTG and Synaptics SYNA. Over the past three months, ASE Technology Holding's shares gained 6.1%, Entegris returned 4.9% and Synaptics appreciated 17.2%. The stronger performance of ASE Technology Holding, Entegris and Synaptics, despite their different business models and semiconductor industry exposures, highlights relatively weaker investor sentiment toward Amkor.

Three-Months Price Comparison

AI and Data Center Packaging Could Sustain Growth

Third-quarter 2026 Computing revenues increased 37% year over year and 25% sequentially to a record, helped by the ramp of Amkor's flagship high-density fan-out (HDFO) CPU program. Another hyperscaler HDFO CPU program began ramping in the quarter, while two 2.5D networking and data center programs were expected to come online in the fourth quarter. Management anticipates more than 50% year-over-year Computing growth in the fourth quarter.

Management also indicated that Computing revenues could grow more than 30% in 2026, with a similar or higher growth rate possible in 2027. These programs broaden Amkor's AI infrastructure opportunity and provide a potential multiyear growth driver. Its expanding HDFO and 2.5D capabilities could also strengthen its competitive positioning against companies such as ASE Technology Holding. Growing demand for advanced packaging could enable Amkor to capture a larger share of AI infrastructure spending and diversify its revenue base.

Story Continues

Richer Product Mix Is Improving Profitability

Third-quarter net sales were nearly flat year over year at $1.99 billion, but earnings rose to 76 cents from 51 cents per share. Gross margin expanded 400 basis points to 18.3%, while operating margin improved to 11.3% from 8% a year earlier. Management attributed gross margin expansion primarily to a richer mix of high-value advanced packaging, including products with lower material content.

Automotive and Industrial revenues advanced 37% year over year, supported by demand for advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), in-car computing and industrial products. This mix shift supports earnings resilience even as Communications remains exposed to smartphone demand. Communications accounted for 37% of quarterly sales, down from 51% a year earlier, while Computing increased its contribution to 26% from 19%.

The improving contribution from Computing and Automotive and Industrial provides evidence that Amkor is gradually diversifying beyond its traditional Communications exposure. A richer advanced-packaging mix and stronger contributions from higher-growth end markets could support further margin improvement. Nevertheless, component shortages and changes in customer production schedules remain potential constraints.

Customer Commitments Support Capacity Expansion

Amkor's long-term customer relationships and advance-payment arrangements provide greater visibility into future demand and help support its capacity expansion. Management stated that the company had executed advance-payment arrangements with a dozen customers since 2025, primarily supporting advanced-packaging capacity in Korea and Arizona.

Additionally, an October 2026 customer agreement is expected to provide approximately $1.3 billion in advance payments during 2027. These arrangements should help fund planned investments and reduce some of the near-term financing burden.

Phase 1 of the Arizona advanced-packaging and test campus is scheduled for completion by the end of 2027, while Phase 2 is expected to break ground in late 2027. Together, the two phases represent an estimated investment of $12 billion. The expansion, alongside ongoing investments in Korea and Vietnam, should strengthen Amkor's geographic footprint and ability to serve customers seeking advanced packaging and test capabilities.

Near-Term Outlook and Spending Remain Challenging

For fourth-quarter 2026, Amkor expects revenues of $1.9-$2 billion, gross margin of 18%-19% and earnings of 65-75 cents per share. Communications weakness, component shortages and the system-in-package migration from South Korea to Vietnam remain headwinds. Full-year capital expenditures are projected near $2.5 billion, with higher spending expected in 2027. Free cash flow was negative $319 million in the first nine months of 2026, versus negative $13 million a year earlier. At September-end, cash and short-term investments of $2.4 billion roughly matched total debt of $2.5 billion, while the top 10 customers accounted for 66% of third-quarter sales. This concentration makes disciplined execution important.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fourth-quarter 2026 earnings per share (EPS) fell to 71 cents from 80 cents over the past 30 days. The first-quarter 2027 EPS estimate fell to 49 cents from 57 cents. The full-year 2026 EPS estimate declined to $2.50 from $2.60, while the 2027 estimate slipped to $2.59 from $2.72.

Conclusion

Amkor's expanding advanced-packaging pipeline, improving product mix and longer-term customer commitments provide sound reasons for existing investors to stay invested rather than sell after the pullback. However, the premium forward P/E, negative free cash flow, smartphone exposure and downward earnings revisions limit the case for aggressive buying.

Investors can hold AMKR while monitoring HDFO and 2.5D program execution, capacity utilization and a recovery in earnings estimates. A sustained improvement in free cash flow and evidence that new capacity can generate attractive returns would further strengthen the investment case. New buyers may prefer clearer evidence that heavy investments will translate into sustainable cash generation.

news.Title: How to Play the Selloff in Arm Stock
news.Content:
The recent tech selloff has been especially tough on semiconductor stocks, with Arm Holdings (ARM) suffering the most. Shares fell more than 11% during the Friday trading session on Oct. 30, before recovering somewhat to end down by around 10%. The selling sentiment continued on Monday, though ARM had been bouncing back to around $203.71 during Tuesday's session before dropping again as trading kicked off Wednesday morning.

Importantly, the decline wasn't caused by poor earnings results from Arm itself. Rather, concerns over returns from investments in AI infrastructure have been putting a lot of pressure on the overall semiconductor group. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Nvidia (NVDA), and Broadcom (AVGO) have all seen significant declines. Nevertheless, with Arm set to report earnings on Nov. 4, there are additional reasons to rethink the company's valuation and prospects for growth.

More News from Barchart

Why Investors Should Load Up on Google Stock Now

Billionaire Mark Cuban Says the Hardest Part of Fixing Health Costs Isn't the CEOs or Insurance Companies, 'Employees Fight Any Change'

Dear Qualcomm Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 4

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

About Arm Stock

Based in Cambridge, England, Arm Holdings develops and licenses semiconductor IP, including energy-efficient CPU architectures that are used in a wide array of applications ranging from smartphones and data centers to automotive systems and AI devices. Instead of selling chips itself, Arm makes its money mostly from licensing and royalties; however, the recent move into producing its own silicon has changed that somewhat. At Monday's close, the company had a market cap of around $210 billion.

Although the company has seen a noticeable correction, ARM stock has performed well this year. Shares have been up by around 86% year-to-date (YTD), easily outperforming the 12% gain in the Nasdaq-100 Index. Nevertheless, the stock has lost about 34% over the past month and currently sits at around 55% below its 52-week high of $452.70.

The most serious concern right now is valuation. ARM trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 178.76x and a P/S ratio of 44.71x. In contrast, a peer group valuation dataset for semiconductors puts the median price-to-sales (P/S) ratio at around 14.6x.

Therefore, even despite this steep selloff, Arm still looks expensive. Investors are paying a very high price for the company's exposure to AI infrastructure and for its ability to generate more revenue per generation of chips.

Story Continues

Beats on Earnings as AI Demand Accelerates

The recent earnings results of Arm provide quite a different story compared to the recent price performance. During the July 29 conference call, the company reported Q1 2027 earnings that beat expectations on both top and bottom lines. Revenue came in at $1.29 billion, rising 22% year-over-year (YoY) and beating Wall Street's expectation of approximately $1.26 billion. EPS was $0.45, above the consensus of $0.40 and up 29% from the year before.

What attracted my attention was the performance of Arm's royalty business, which saw its revenue rise by 22% to $715 million, while licensing revenue increased 23% to $574 million. Importantly, data center royalties have grown more than two times YoY, implying that Arm is now benefiting more and more from the transition to power-efficient AI infrastructure.

Moreover, Arm's newly introduced AGI CPU provides another opportunity. According to management, the demand for the product from customers now exceeds $2 billion over fiscal years 2027 and 2028, compared to the previously mentioned initial $1 billion opportunity. However, it shouldn't be confused with actual revenue recognition, since the company is still struggling with increasing manufacturing capacity.

There are also some worries. While reporting robust revenue growth, the company's GAAP operating income decreased by approximately 20% YoY to $91 million. That was due to higher operating expenses and investments in R&D. With Arm moving beyond its traditional licensing business model, execution and profitability have now become more and more important.

Looking forward, the company guided Q2 revenue to be around $1.38 billion, ±$50 million, and EPS to be $0.47, ±$0.04. Wall Street expects the company to bring in approximately $1.38 billion in revenue and earn $0.48 in EPS, meaning that analysts expect another quarter of double-digit revenue growth.

It has been confirmed that Arm will publish its Q2 2027 results on Wednesday, Nov. 4, after the market close. Given the recent volatility, the upcoming earnings report may be quite critical for determining whether shares stabilize or suffer another correction.

What Do Analysts Expect From ARM Stock?

Despite the sharp drop, Wall Street has remained fairly optimistic about Arm's outlook. Analysts assign ARM stock a "Moderate Buy" rating consensus with a mean price target of $289.14. Based on the recent price of $199, its mean target implies a potential upside of approximately 47%. At the same time, the highest price target of $480 implies a potential upside of approximately 136%, while the lowest target of $130 offers a potential downside of roughly 34%. This rather large range reflects the uncertainty concerning Arm's earnings potential and its valuation.
